chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.html:
They say the universe began with silence.

Even the Titans, for all their thunder, died quietly.

When Amphoreus broke, the sound took centuries to arrive—a tremor slow as grief, rippling through the marrow of creation. The great body cracked, bleeding light and memory into the void. From that wound spilled dust, heat, and the bones of gods.

The fragments drifted outward, cooling as they went. Continents formed in the hollows of ribs; oceans pooled in eye sockets. Gravity gathered the debris into orbits, and where Titan blood met vacuum, it hardened into light —rings circling what had once been one divine body.

That is how the new worlds were born: bright shards trailing the ruin of Amphoreus, each pulsing with a trace of its maker’s marrow.

The Titans had no destiny—only appetite. They devoured until they collapsed beneath their own hunger. When the last of them consumed the wrong star, the universe cracked its knuckles and began again. From their remains, civilizations crawled forth: small, radiant things that built cities from cooled godflesh and called themselves heirs.

And perhaps they were.

Time passed, as it always does. The Titans became myth, their bones became trade goods, their festivals excuses for pageantry. Reverence turned to routine. The old questions—what shaped us? what remains of them?— faded beneath a newer one: who owns what?

And when a species learns to covet, empires are inevitable.

Two fragments shone brighter than the rest, circling the void where Amphoreus’s heart once burned. One gold, one red.

They shared no language, no faith, not even air—only conviction that the other was wrong.

Naturally, they went to war.

They say Kephale, the Worldbearer, was the gentlest Titan, second to only Georios. When he fell, a single shard of his spine drifted into the broken system and became Okhema—the city that never touched ground.

Its continents hover among auroras that pulse like slow heartbeats, tethered by cords of aether spun from Kephale’s lingering breath. The cords feed on resonance—on feeling. When the people laugh, the roots tighten. When they grieve, the cities sink. Storms of sorrow can drag whole skylines from the heavens. Weddings can send them soaring.

For Okhemians, emotion is physics.

Their cities grow like coral, humming faintly underfoot. Gold-veined bridges stretch between floating islands, carrying the echo of every heartbeat that helped shape them. The people glow from within— bioluminescent pigments blooming under their skin in shades of amber and azure. Amusement flickers blue across the throat; affection warms gold in the palms. Arguments are silent, fought in dimming light.

To outsiders, it all seems unbearably polite. But composure is survival. The cities themselves are alive, and one stray surge of emotion can ripple through the atmospheric lattice, undoing years of balance.

Seen from orbit, Okhema resembles a miniature sun—its light steady on calm days, flickering like a heartbeat when unrest brews below.

To be calm is to build. To feel too deeply is to destroy.

And so they live as Kephale did—shoulders steady beneath invisible weight, carrying their shining world through the sky.

If Okhema is the sun, Kremnos is its moon.

Quiet, enduring, unbothered by the need to shine.

They say it was carved from the body of Nikador, Titan of Strife—his bones hardened into crust, his blood into twin seas of gold and red. His final breath became gravity itself, pressing down like an oath.

Here, nothing comes easily. The air is heavy, the storms unending, the ground veined with molten light. But struggle is sacred. The Kremnoans believe effort gives shape to existence. Their towers don’t scrape heaven— they defy it.

They are built like their world: strong, deliberate, forged under pressure. Laughter shakes the walls. Love is loud and certain. Even their faith is made of muscle and endurance. Every scar is proof that they refused to yield.

Their creed is simple: Struggle is proof of life.

And so, where Okhema polishes emotion into harmony, Kremnos hammers it into meaning. One seeks balance, the other, worth. Yet both burn with the same ancestral heat, two children orbiting the corpse of a god.

Their lights still cross in the dark—gold meeting red, sun meeting storm.

And somewhere between them, light-years away, a man named Phainon was staring into his fourth empty cup of coffee, trying very hard to remember what the hell “sacred” was supposed to feel like.

The station breathed.

That was what Phainon always thought when he was on the night shift— though technically, there was no night here, nor did he take shifts, just the dimmed lights of Ecliptica-6 humming low to mimic one. The walls sighed with quiet energy, the pulse conduits beneath the floor thrummed in measured time, and somewhere in the deep machinery, the station exhaled recycled air that smelled faintly of citrus.

He’d been awake for… well, long enough that the coffee cup in his hand had gone from full, to empty, to possibly a biohazard. But it was peaceful work, at least—monitoring emotional harmonics while the ship floated steady above the Meridian Rift.

Outside the viewport, the Rift sprawled across the void like a scar of light— endless, pale, and whispering. It wasn’t quite a storm, not quite space. It was something that simply hummed faintly against the hull when the station drifted too near. Most people found it unnerving. Phainon thought it beautiful.

“Deck Twelve’s stabilizing again,” Castorice said from his left. She stood over a projection panel, neat as ever in her uniform, her lavender hair pulled into a knot that never seemed to move even in zero-grav. “Ninety-eight percent coherence. I’ll log it, but you might want to double-check the southern harmonic node. It’s fluctuating.”

Phainon glanced up from his console, watching the data scroll lazily past. “Only by two decimals,” he said. “Could just be interference from the Rift’s edge.”

Castorice tilted her head, one eyebrow faintly raised. “Could be,” she said in the tone of someone who didn’t believe him but was too polite to argue.

He smiled. “You ever think we’re too calm for this job?”

Her eyes flicked to him, then back to the console. “Someone has to be.”

That earned a chuckle. The last time emotional coherence had dropped below eighty, the entire aft deck had flickered in what Command diplomatically referred to as atmospheric sensory leakage. He still found glittering gold dust in his boots some days.

“Alright, alright,” he said, holding up one hand. “Point taken. I’ll monitor it manually.”

Castorice hummed in approval. “Add that to your report while you’re at it. They’ll ask.”

Phainon set his coffee down and picked up his datapad, brushing a thumb along the smooth edge to wake it. “They always ask,” he muttered, then leaned closer to the screen as it lit up with the Okhemian crest—gold, radiant, and annoyingly bright for the hour.

“Ecliptica-6 to Command,” came a filtered voice over the comms. “Requesting confirmation on emotional harmonic data for Cycle 117.”

Phainon tapped the console, toggling the transmission line open. “Command, this is the Envoy Phainon of Okhema, responding from Ecliptica-6. Transmission link clear. You’re getting our data stream?”

“Confirmed,” the voice replied. “State your operational status.”

“Stable orbit around Meridian Rift,” Phainon said, professional cadence slipping easily into place. “Position holding five klicks off the inner boundary, trajectory locked at two degrees lateral drift. Harmonics steady at ninety-eight coherence, no empathic surges reported. We’re ready for traversal tests when you are.”

Castorice, silent beside him, monitored the readouts with faint concentration.

“Understood,” Command said after a pause. “Prepare for synchronization sequence. Expect confirmation within the hour.”

Phainon inclined his head slightly, even though they couldn’t see him. “Copy that. Ecliptica-6 stands by.”

The transmission clicked off.

Phainon leaned back in his chair, exhaling through a smile.

“Well,” he said, glancing at her. “Looks like we’re officially doing our jobs today.”

Castorice looked up from her monitor, entertainment flickering briefly across her face. “We should celebrate, I can offer you half a ration bar.”

“Tempting,” he said. “But I was saving my appetite for recycled air and despair.”

She smiled—barely—but it reached her eyes.

The moment held, easy and companionable, before the station’s ambient quiet was broken by a new sound: light footsteps and a voice that chimed like laughter through glass.

“Ooh! Snowy! Where are we going again?”

Both of them turned.

Standing in the doorway was Tribbie, one of the Tribios triplets—though Phainon still thought of her as the youngest, even if technically she was a third of a collective AI consciousness. Her frame flickered with faint golden light at the seams, and the air around her shimmered faintly as her projected scarf looped itself into a new pattern every few seconds.

“Tribbie,” Phainon said, a grin already tugging at his mouth. “Didn’t expect to see you up. Thought you and your sisters were still in rest mode.”

“We were,” Tribbie said cheerfully. “But we woke up! Trianne and Trinnon wanted to keep dreaming, though, so we came instead.”

Phainon set down his tablet, stretching his arms. “We,” he echoed. “Even when you’re alone, huh?” He assumed it was a bug at first but seems not.

“Of course,” she said, as if it were obvious. “We’re always us.”

Castorice turned, her tone softening. “It’s good to see you, Tribbie. We were starting to miss your drawings.”

Tribbie gasped, delighted. “You did? You noticed?”

“Hard not to,” Phainon said, and crouched so he was at her level. “But since you’re up…” He lowered his voice, eyes glinting. “Want to know where we’re headed next?”

Tribbie leaned closer, practically buzzing. “We do!”

Phainon’s smile changed into something conspiratorial. “We’re going to the Meridian Rift.”

Tribbie froze for half a second—then her eyes widened, twin pinpoints of starlight. “The Rift?”

“The one and only,” Phainon said, straightening again. “Don’t tell your sisters.”

Tribbie clasped her hands behind her back, expression all mock-seriousness. “We won’t. Probably.”

Castorice exhaled what might’ve been a laugh, and for a brief moment, everything seemed peaceful.

Then Tribbie blinked—once, twice—and the constellation of light around her shimmered strangely, fracturing into brief static before reforming. Her smile wavered.

“Snowy…” she said, voice thoughtful now, the faint reverb in her tone flattening as her processors shifted focus. “We might be detecting a signal.”

Phainon frowned, straightening slightly. “A signal?”

Castorice’s eyes lifted from her screen, one brow arched. “From the Rift?”

Tribbie tilted her head, as if listening to something distant. “Not sure. It’s… faint. And not supposed to be here.” Her voice dipped into a whisper of computation, digital notes rippling beneath her words. “It’s like static, but it’s singing back.”

Castorice’s fingers danced across her console, pulling up a schematic of their current coordinates. “No external comm signatures detected,” she said. “It’s likely interference from the harmonic edge. The Rift distorts just about everything that gets too close.”

Phainon hummed noncommittally, eyes still on his tablet. He wasn’t convinced, but he wasn’t particularly alarmed either. “Could be,” he said, returning to his work. “Or maybe it’s the Rift saying hello.”

Tribbie blinked, processing. “Rifts can’t say hello,” she said seriously, then paused. “Can they?”

“Depends how lonely they are,” Phainon murmured.

Tribbie frowned faintly. “Our database is… a little fuzzy right now. We know what the Meridian Rift is, but not much else.” She tapped her chest lightly, where her light-core pulsed. “Something about the data here causes interference in our archive memory. We tried syncing last cycle, but it keeps looping.”

Castorice glanced over, her expression softening. She reached out and patted Tribbie’s head with one gloved hand. “Don’t worry. I’ll run a full diagnostic once we finish the harmonic sweep.”

Tribbie’s eyes brightened instantly. “Thank you, Cas! We love it when you do a checkup.”

“Of course,” Castorice said.

Phainon, still half-focused on his screen, spoke without looking up. “Well, if it helps your data bank, the Rift isn’t really one thing—it’s more of a scar left behind when the Titans fell.”

Tribbie turned toward him, intrigued. “A scar?”

“Mhmm,” Phainon said, finally glancing up, his tone adopting the easy cadence he used when explaining things to the triplets. “When the Titans’ age ended, all that raw energy—what the old records call ‘residue’—didn’t just vanish. It condensed. Left fragments scattered across the void. The Rift happens to be one of the biggest deposits of that residue.”

He gestured toward the viewport, where the pale divide shimmered faintly in the darkness. “Titanal fragments are like… concentrated echoes of creation itself. They bend fields, distort signals, and—if you’re reckless enough—can power just about anything. Okhema’s Lattices run smoother with them. Kremnos uses them to strengthen their bioforges.”

Tribbie’s eyes widened. “Ohhh. So that’s why we’re here?”

“Partly,” Phainon said, flashing her a small smile. “Research. Observation. Making sure no one’s accidentally blowing up a chunk of reality.”

“And the other reason?” Tribbie asked, her digital gaze fixed on him.

Before Phainon could answer, Castorice spoke up. “There’s talk of collaboration,” she started. “Between Okhema and Castrum Kremnos. Something involving the Rift.”

Tribbie blinked, the light around her flickering as she processed this. “Collaboration?” she repeated slowly. “But… you hate each other.”

Castorice hesitated, while Phainon chuckled. “She’s not wrong,” he admitted. “But apparently it’s been decided we should play nice for once. No one tells the envoys why, of course—just that it’ll be historic, poetic, transformative…”

“Fifty years of cold conflict,” Castorice murmured, her gaze drifting to the Rift beyond the glass. “Over this same stretch of void.”

Phainon nodded. “Half a century of blockades, sabotage, posturing— because both sides wanted the same thing. Like I mentioned before… these fragments could power Okhema’s empathy lattices or strengthen Kremnos’s biostructures. You can imagine how that went.”

Tribbie tilted her head, her gaze wide. “Not well?”

“Not well,” Phainon agreed with a small, rueful smile. “But it’s poetic, isn’t it? Using the same thing that split us apart to bring us back together.”

Castorice’s sighed. “Assuming it does.”

Phainon’s smile dimmed slightly. “I suppose you’re right.”

Tribbie’s light flickered again, and she paused mid-motion, as though recalibrating. When her voice returned, it was bright, chirping with an upbeat tone that was as unmistakable as ever.

“Ooh! Aggie wants to talk to you guys!”

Phainon blinked, his brow furrowing slightly. “Aglaea?”

Tribbie nodded eagerly. “She said there’s a briefing soon. Something about a peace operation.”

Castorice straightened slightly, a hint of surprise crossing her face. “It seems we were right, then.”

Phainon’s eyes glinted. “Well, that’s… interesting.” He clapped his hands once, the sound sharp. “Alright then—let’s wrap this up fast. Castorice, check harmonic stability. Tribbie, you’re on assist.”

“Sure!” Tribbie said, her tone full of eagerness. “What do you need me to do, Snowy?”

Phainon paused for a moment, tapping his chin. “Start by syncing the pulse grid with the Rift’s outer frequency. Let’s see if we can get her singing back properly.”

Tribbie gave a tiny salute, her digital lights flickering in a mock-serious fashion. “On it!”

As Tribbie twirled toward the console, humming a melody that somehow synchronized with the station’s pulse, Castorice adjusted the alignment nodes in silence, focused as always. Phainon, meanwhile, turned back to the viewport, his gaze drawn to the Rift—a slow, deliberate pulse of light against the dark expanse of space.

For all its grandeur—the politics, the history, the ever-present tension—it still looked, to him, like a heartbeat suspended in time. And for a reason he couldn’t quite place, he couldn’t shake the feeling that it was listening.

The sound of Ecliptica-6 was steady enough to lull anyone else into forgetting they were orbiting a fault in reality. Phainon couldn’t.

He and Castorice moved through the hall in silence, boots whispering over metal. Her stride was short but brisk, calibrated; his matched it automatically. Years of running dispatches together had synced their pace without effort. The only real sound came from the small, translucent tablet in his hand, its interface flickering in layered data bands: spectral harmonics, navigation maps, Rift field readings, and the quiet rhythm of an impossible pulse—red, steady, deliberate.

Castorice’s wrist console answered it a moment later with a crisp electronic chirp. She glanced down, frowned, and said, “That nonexistent signal is now repeating in a coded pattern. Five-cycle intervals. Which means it’s evolved.”

Phainon’s tone was mild. “So nonexistent it’s registering across four frequencies. Ambitious for something that shouldn’t exist.”

“Ambitious,” she repeated under her breath, tapping her console. “Or bored.”

Behind them, Tribbie drifted with the easy, weightless poise of her projection—barely solid light, a shimmer of color cut through with data feed halos. “We traced the origin to approximately twelve degrees off the Rift’s polar axis,” she said, concerned. “Except there’s nothing there. Nothing charted, nothing visible, nothing mapped in the last two centuries.”

Phainon slowed, scanning the tablet. “Not nothing. Just something clever enough to look like it.”

The feed shifted with a flick of his wrist, pixels shattering into static, static condensing into shapes. Tribbie caught the cue and extended the projection mid-corridor, the light blooming outward into a three-dimensional lattice of noise. The grain moved—slowly, irregularly—then folded into angular symmetry. Faint outlines formed, then vanished again.

Castorice’s steps stopped first. “That looks like hull curvature.” Her brow creased. “Military grade. Pattern’s consistent.”

Phainon studied the formation, head tilted. “Formation?”

She nodded once. “Triangular. Tapered drives, long spines—design profile matches Kremnoan fleet architecture. Except they shouldn’t be here.” She scrolled her readings, muttering. “The Rift’s harmonics would’ve shredded any unauthorized entry.”

“Unless,” Phainon said quietly, “they found a way to walk through shredded space.”

Tribbie’s voice faltered, projection dimming. “That’s… not in their capacity range. Their vessels can’t even sustain prolonged exposure to Titanal residue. They’d corrode from the inside out.”

“Unless,” he repeated, “they learned.”

Castorice’s console beeped again. “Empathic sensors are clean. That’s not possible. Even if they’ve cloaked their visuals, we’d still pick up emotional residue from the crews.” She hesitated, then added softer, “Unless someone found a way to mask that too.”

Phainon smiled faintly. “Hide emotion. There’s a thought.”

Her reply came quick, defensive. “It’s impossible.”

But she didn’t sound like she believed it.

Tribbie’s tone lost its bounce. “We’re reading twelve distinct signatures. Same drive pattern. Same energy bleed.” She paused. “Do we… ping Command?”

“Not yet,” Phainon murmured. He enlarged the scan. Those shapes moved in unison, cutting through Rift distortion like knife edges through fog. They weren’t wandering debris or misread ghosts. They had formation discipline. Purpose. A fleet’s patience.

Castorice stepped closer. “Trajectory?”

“Vector drift toward the Rift’s outer rim,” Tribbie said. “They’re hugging distortion—masking in the pulse troughs. No registry match. Definitely not ours.”

The red pulse on Phainon’s screen matched their rhythm now, each beat like a quiet, slow warning. His reflection blinked inside the glass, and for the first time since the mission began, he felt the faintest tickle of unease at the back of his neck.

“New design?” Castorice asked, though she already knew the answer.

Phainon gave a soft exhale. “New. And very improved.”

Their eyes met—briefly, but long enough to say we know what that means without needing to voice it.

Tribbie’s voice came out small. “Aggie’s pinged again. Twice.” A flicker of static laced through her projection. “Should I tell her we’re about to ruin her afternoon?”

“Let’s keep her anticipation alive,” Phainon said lightly, closing the tablet with a flick. “Come on. She’ll want visual proof before she starts lecturing.”

Castorice sighed, falling into stride beside him as they resumed down the corridor. “You do realize she’s going to lecturing anyway.”

“She’d lecture at the sunrise if it wasn’t formatted properly.”

Tribbie laughed softly, spinning once midair. “She did last week.”

That drew the faintest giggle from Castorice, though her eyes stayed on the slit window.

The doors to the central deck parted with a low hiss.

Light unfurled ahead—the consoles lining the walls pulsing with soft data rhythms, and through the panoramic viewport, the stars shimmered like they were moving underwater.

Phainon stepped in first. The deck lights adjusted around him, soft gradients rolling outward under his boots. He braced one hand against the glass, watching faint ripples of reflected light travel up his sleeve. In the viewport’s curved surface, three reflections overlapped—his, Castorice’s, and Tribbie’s—half-solid, half-light.

“Still never gets old,” he murmured.

“Neither does hearing you say that every time we come here,” Castorice said dryly, already bent over the nearest console. The air shimmered faintly around her hands as she brought up the harmonic lock, the nested circles aligning one by one in a soft pulse. “Running synchronization.”

Tribbie’s voice piped up behind them. “Bandwidth’s jittery again. The Rift’s throwing electricity from all directions.” She bounded toward another terminal, flickering briefly as her holographic form stabilized. “Stabilizing transmission bandwidth—don’t move anything important for, uh, five seconds. Maybe six.”

“That’s not confidence-inspiring,” Phainon muttered, eyes on his own tablet as lines of command script danced up the screen.

“My code prefers accuracy to confidence,” Tribbie chirped.

“Those aren’t mutually exclusive,” Castorice said, without looking up.

Tribbie blinked, mock offense flickering across her projection. “I’m both!”

Phainon let a quiet laugh slip as he keyed in the final command. “Good. Then you’ll love this part.”

The air shifted.

From the deck’s center, concentric rings of light spiraled outward, their glow moving in smooth, perfect timing with each pulse. They spun faster, converging into a single point before expanding in a burst of pale gold.

A figure began to form—fragmented at first, a shimmer of lines and geometry that slowly resolved into shape. When the lattice stabilized, a woman stood at the center, tall and composed, her white-and-golden attire catching the light. Around her drifted soft orbits of shape—geometric constructs turning slowly like miniature constellations.

Castorice’s posture straightened, a reflex born of habit. “Hello, Lady Aglaea.”

The hologram’s eyes shifted immediately toward her. “Castorice.” Her tone eased, a soft undercurrent of familiarity. Then her gaze flicked to the man by the viewport. “And Phainon. You’re looking far too radiant for this hour, Envoy.”

Phainon gave her a wry smile, lifting his cupless hand as if in toast. “That’s because I sleep less than you do, Architect.”

A faint gleam curved Aglaea’s mouth. “An impossible metric. I don’t believe anyone does.”

Tribbie waved energetically, her form flaring slightly. “Bandwidth stable! Transmission’s clean across the field.”

“Excellent work, Tribbie,” Aglaea said. “You always bring the system more enthusiasm than it deserves.”

“I’ve been told that before.” Tribbie said proudly.

Castorice glanced sidelong at Phainon. “Usually after she crashes it.”

“That was one time!” Tribbie protested.

Phainon coughed, covering a smile. “Three, actually.”

Aglaea’s laughter came quiet but genuine—a low, melodic sound that filled the space without needing volume. It faded as her tone eased back into command, smooth as gravity reclaiming its pull. “It’s good to see you all,” she said. “Though I take it you know this isn’t a social call.”

“Unfortunately,” Phainon replied, finally letting his hand fall from the viewport. The stars refracted faintly across his palm. “You’ll want to see this.”

The last of the deck’s lights steadied around them.

Phainon adjusted the holo-tablet between his hands, its pale light running thin across the metal curve of his gloves. “Alright. Picking up from the sweep.”

At his cue, Tribbie flicked her fingers, and a projection shimmered to life above the central dais—an elegant, pulsing web of coordinates suspended in air. The Meridian Rift sprawled wide and jagged across the display, veins of light tracing where the distortion folded in on itself.

“Origin’s here,” she said, gesturing toward the edge of the polar quadrant. Her hand fuzzed slightly as it passed through the light. “Twelve degrees off the Rift’s axis, same as before. And before anyone reminds me—yeah, there’s nothing there. Not according to any map we’ve got.”

Aglaea’s image tilted her head, curiosity showing. “And yet you found something.”

Tribbie zoomed in. The hologram refocused, the map collapsing inward until it dissolved.

“That loop again,” Castorice murmured, already syncing her wrist-console. “Repeats every five cycles, clean intervals. Random noise doesn’t do that.”

Phainon scrolled through his display, lines of coded light shifting across his lenses. “Signal’s registering across four harmonic bands. Which shouldn’t even be possible unless it’s been structured manually.”

Aglaea’s brows rose slightly. “Intentional?”

“Without question,” Castorice replied before Phainon could.

“Not from Okhema, not from anyone friendly,” Tribbie added. “I checked every registry twice.”

Phainon flicked his wrist, expanding the feed. “Then we’re down to one explanation.”

The hologram deepened, static unfurling into hazy geometry—faint, glimmering, half-caught in the Rift’s distortion. Then, piece by piece, the shapes resolved into focus.

Angular hulls. Triangular silhouettes. Vessels slipping in and out of wavelength, as if surfacing and drowning in light all at once.

Castorice’s expression tightened. “They’re cloaked.”

Phainon’s tone stayed dry. “Fully functional stealth signatures. And get this —they’re bypassing empathic detection entirely. We ran a triple harmonic sweep and picked up nothing. No emotional residue, no energy displacement. Nothing.”

“That’s what confuses me,” Castorice said under her breath. “Empathic sensors are harmonically anchored. You can’t hide what you feel. That’s the entire point of them.”

“Unless someone finally cracked the threshold.” Phainon didn’t look up. “And I’d bet half my rations who did.”

Tribbie’s glow dimmed, almost nervous. “Cloaking tech’s banned, though. Has been since—”

“The Lycurgus Accord,” Castorice supplied. “Everyone signed it. Even Kremnos.”

“Yeah,” Phainon said quietly. “And yet—”

He zoomed in once more, the ships’ hulls catching faint light.

“Tell me that doesn’t look familiar,” he said.

No one answered.

Castorice finally exhaled. “Kremnoan construction. You can tell from the symmetry anchors on the fins.”

“Thought so,” Phainon murmured. “They’ve refined the design. Whatever they’re doing, it’s cleaner.”

Aglaea’s hologram watched silently as the image rotated. “You’re certain these readings are accurate?”

Tribbie straightened defensively. “The bandwidth’s been fluctuating, but the pattern’s stable. If it were a false echo, it wouldn’t hold formation that cleanly.”

“Which means,” Castorice said, “they’re operating with intent. Close to the Rift. Running tests they don’t want us to see.”

“Or,” Phainon countered, “tests we were never supposed to notice but did anyway.”

Aglaea’s voice cut through before either could continue. “That’s enough.”

The projection dimmed, pausing mid-flicker. The room’s low hum softened, matching the steady cadence of her voice.

“You’re right,” she said. “They are Kremnoan. Prototype scouts equipped with adaptive stealth arrays. They weren’t attacking, only performing calibration runs along the Rift perimeter.”

Phainon frowned. “Calibration. That far out?”

“It was sanctioned.” Aglaea’s tone didn’t waver, but there was something behind it. “Under new protocol.”

Her gaze swept over them one by one before she continued. “The arrays they’re using were developed through Okhema’s authorization.”

Silence rippled through the observatory. The soft glow beneath their feet seemed louder than it should’ve been.

Phainon blinked slowly, trying to make sure he’d heard that right. “… Ours?”

Castorice’s eyes sharpened. “We approved it?”

Aglaea inclined her head. “The High Council voted this cycle. The initiative’s formal now—Okhema and Kremnos will cooperate for the Meridian Rift’s recovery effort. The operation’s official title is the Meridian Recovery Initiative.”

Tribbie’s voice came out small. “Cooperate as in… us with them? I thought that was a joke.”

“Exactly that,” Aglaea said. “They’ll lead fleet security. We handle harmonic containment and research. The partnership’s already in motion.”

Phainon leaned back slightly, exhaling through his teeth. “Didn’t think I’d live to see the day.” He had expected a collaboration of sorts but not—

Castorice’s tone was mild, but it finished his thoughts for him. “I didn’t think I’d see us sponsoring them.”

Aglaea’s expression softened faintly. “It’s not sponsorship if it’s necessity. The Rift’s destabilizing faster than projected—this is our best chance to contain it.”

“That’s one way to call it,” Phainon muttered.

Aglaea continued as if she hadn’t heard. “The Council has selected both of you as Okhema’s liaisons for the operation. You’ll oversee harmonic relay calibration, and maintain contact between field divisions.”

Castorice nodded once, calm and already moving into work mode. “Understood.”

Then, slower to react, she let out a breath. “…Please tell me it’s not the same commander again.”

For the first time, Aglaea’s poise wavered. She coughed—delicately—and glanced aside. “I’ll send you the file.”

The silence that followed said enough.

The display bloomed into being, light fracturing upward in a clean column before unfurling into a projection between them. The text assembled piece by piece—headers, insignias, stamps of interstellar authorization—all glowing in Okhema’s pale azure code.

Phainon leaned forward a fraction, eyes catching the reflected data as the title resolved.

[MISSION FILE – JOINT RECOVERY OPERATION: MERIDIAN RIFT] AUTHORIZED UNDER: THE INTERPOLAR HARMONIC ACCORDS, REV. 1124 COLLABORATIVE OVERSIGHT: OKHEMA | KREMNOS | CENTRAL UNION

Below the formalities, paragraphs of technical data scrolled—a cascade of harmonic flux readouts, containment parameters, diplomatic hierarchy lists. Castorice was already scanning the brief with focus, her fingers flicking through screens like a conductor keeping rhythm. Phainon, on the other hand, only skimmed, attention half-latched on the motion, until one section caught his eye.

A single line, pulsing faintly in the Okheman system’s signature gold, almost like it wanted to be read.

[COMMANDER // MYDEIMOS]

He went very still for a moment. Then his lips curved—slowly, involuntarily.

“…It’s the Commander,” he murmured, and the words came out soft, dreamily almost, like he’d been waiting for the name to appear.

Castorice didn’t look up. “Of course it is.” Her voice was cool, like she’s been waiting for this headache to happen the whole week.

Phainon’s mouth quirked further. “What? You sound thrilled.”

Aglaea’s form, still projected beside them, did not dignify that with acknowledgment. “Mydeimos is representing Kremnos’s interests. You’ll meet upon arrival.”

At that, the empathic panels along the chamber walls warmed in response to Phainon’s sudden emotional spike—barely a flicker, but enough for the ship to register it. Light flowed gently across the edges of the room, a synchronized pulse like a heartbeat trying to smooth over the disturbance.

Castorice glanced sidelong. “You’re setting the room off again.”

He adjusted his sleeve, tone perfectly even. “Just calibrating.”

Tribbie pouted from their console. “You ‘calibrate’ every time he’s mentioned.”

“Maybe he’s got that effect,” Phainon said idly, voice lighter now.

Aglaea’s projection flickered once as she continued, businesslike. “Coordinates are transmitting now. You’ll dock at Port Eltarion—one of the original Meridian fringe stations. Expect unstable gravimetric tides; the Rift’s harmonic field has been volatile since the Titanal aftershocks.”

“Translation,” Phainon said. “Bumpy ride.”

“You’ll manage,” Aglaea replied without missing a beat.

The navigation panels at the far end of the deck thrummed—a shift in tone as the ship began recalibrating its own course. A faint ripple of golden light swept the length of the room as the pilot core awakened.

Phainon’s gaze flicked toward the motion. “Trinnon’s awake,” he muttered, half to himself. “Right on time.”

Aglaea went on, eyes narrowing slightly as if she’d caught the undercurrent in his tone. “And yes—the signal was Kremnoan. But they’re not here for battle. I expect you all to be on your best behavior.”

Her gaze sharpened on him specifically.

Then, bemused: “Everyone.”

Phainon raised his hands in mock surrender. “See? I’m not even doing anything yet.”

“Not yet,” Castorice said under her breath.

Aglaea ignored them both, though the faintest ghost of amusement passed across her face. “HapLotes-405—how are the triplet sync protocols holding?”

Tribbie straightened. “Stable! Mostly. Trianne tried to overload the resonance loop again, but we convinced her that would’ve vaporized the kitchen, so—success!”

“Progress,” Aglaea said mildly. “Keep it that way.” Her tone softened. “Safe travels, all of you.”

Her hologram fractured, light cascading upward before fading into the ship’s dim, ambient glow.

Castorice exhaled and flicked through her screen one last time. “Trinnon, ETA?”

A new voice emerged through the comm system—gentle, even-toned, laced with synthesized warmth.

[“Estimated arrival: twenty-three minutes, forty-eight seconds.”]

“Perfect,” Phainon murmured, collapsing the holo-display into a smaller window.

The ship shuddered lightly as thrusters adjusted for descent, their trajectory turning toward their landing point. Outside, the view stretched endless— ribbons of blue and gold distortion curling like silk, the gravity waves bending light in impossible arcs.

Phainon lingered at the viewport, hand braced on the transparent panel.

Beneath his palm, the empathic panel glowed once, registering a heartbeat just a touch too fast before dimming again.

Castorice noticed. She said nothing.

Phainon didn’t look away.

To say the trip had been bumpy was an understatement.

The Ecliptica-6 wasn’t flying so much as violently flinging itself through the Rift like a half-possessed comet. If anyone had been watching from the outside—and honestly, no one sane would’ve been—they would’ve seen the small Okheman craft streaking across a churning void that looked more like molten glass than open space.

Inside, it was bedlam.

The walls pulsed in frantic shades of blue and green, trying (and failing spectacularly) to keep the interior mood field stable. The entire ship groaned like it was personally offended by their flight plan.

Tribbie, stationed at the primary console, yelped as her holographic hands danced over a dozen shifting panels. “Okay! That’s another magnetic tide! If we hit it dead-on, we might lose the aft stabilizers—no pressure!”

From the pilot’s nest came Trianne’s gleeful cackle. “It’s the only course that doesn’t peel us in half!”

Oh, right. Trianne was awake also. He should’ve mentioned that earlier.

The Ecliptica jerked hard to port, and suddenly everyone was airborne. The artificial gravity stuttered, vanished, and then slammed back at double intensity. Castorice made a sound halfway between a grunt and a prayer as her hair floated, halo-like, for half a second before snapping down again.

Phainon barely moved—just a single hand braced against the overhead beam, boots steady, eyes calm. He looked less panicked and more vaguely entertained.

“Are we sure she was programmed for this kind of flight path?” he called, his voice carrying clear through the air as the ship’s resonance field compensated for the chaos.

“Define sure!” Trinnon shouted back, clinging to a safety rail and very much not helping. The smallest of the Tribios had plastered herself against Castorice’s sleeve like a terrified squirrel, her hologram flickering each time the ship jolted.

The lights strobed ultraviolet. The mood field reacted to collective panic by flickering into a migraine-inducing pulse. Somewhere in the background, something made a noise that sounded suspiciously like “krrrk-bzz-no-structural-integrity,” which was not reassuring.

“Hold—hold—HOLD!” Tribbie shrieked, half into static. “That was a gravitational shear! Trianne, what part of ‘subtle approach’ did you not understand!?”

“The part where you think subtlety keeps us alive!” Trianne hollered back.

The Ecliptica dipped nose-first into another pocket of turbulence so violently that even Phainon had to grab the nearest beam. His other arm shot out instinctively, catching Castorice before she could collide with the console.

“You alright?” he asked, leaning close to be heard over the rising vibration.

She’d gone pale, lips pressed tight. “Fine,” she managed, voice thin. “Just —space motion sickness.”

“Understandable,” he said lightly, shifting so her shoulder pressed against his chest for support. “Focus on my voice, not…whatever the hell this is.”

Trinnon, trying to be helpful, piped up, “Statistically, only a thirty-three percent mortality rate.”

“Not now, Trinnon!” Phainon snapped, eyes still on the viewport.

Outside, colors were twisting into glassy filaments. Through the shimmering haze, a faint metal silhouette appeared, distant but steady: a skeletal ring dotted with weak blue lights.

Port Eltarion.

He gritted his teeth, half for stability and half to keep from swearing. “I’ve got visual on the port! ETA?”

Trinnon squinted at flickering readings. “Uh—5 minutes if nothing else implodes!”

“Great,” Phainon muttered.

Panels screamed in six languages. The inertial dampeners pulsed erratically, their hum alternating between too loud and nonexistent. The empathic stabilizers tried to emit “soothing” frequencies that only made things worse —a high-pitched, cheery white noise paired with the faint, persistent scent of citrus.

“Is the ship trying to gaslight us into calmness?” Castorice muttered weakly.

“Yes,” Phainon said grimly. “And it’s failing.”

Then Trianne’s vioce. “On three, everyone!”

Tribbie froze mid-command. “Don’t you dare.”

“One!”

“Please no—”

“Two!”

“TRIANNE—”

“THREE!”

The Ecliptica dove.

Phainon’s instincts kicked in—he caught Castorice again, dragging her in against his chest and bracing his boots against the floor.

“Almost there!” He yelled out, laughing.

She looked green.

And then—suddenly, mercifully—the pressure eased.

The violent shuddering slowed. The lights dimmed. The only sound left was the low hum of the ship’s engines exhaling relief.

Silence.

Then, the faint hiss of the air filters kicking back in.

They’d landed.

…Or at least crashed softly enough to call it landing.

The artificial gravity stabilized a heartbeat too late, which meant everyone was flung down in a graceless heap. Castorice landed squarely on top of Phainon, who sighed and decided, for the sake of gallantry, to remain the human cushioning.

He blinked up at the flickering ceiling, waiting for the world to stop vibrating. “…Well,” he said finally, “that was a ride.”

Castorice groaned, face half-buried in his shoulder. “I’m starting to dislike space.”

“Good news,” he said, “space definitely hates us too.”

Trinnon dangled upside-down from a safety strap like a stunned bat. Trianne was still giggling somewhere up front. Tribbie, however, dusted herself off, straightened her holographic uniform, and, after a perfectly timed pause, cleared her throat.

“…Ahem. Welcome to Port Eltarion. We hope you enjoyed your flight.”

Silence.

Castorice exhaled one long, exhausted sigh.

“Never again,” she said flatly.

Phainon stayed on the floor a moment longer before his ribs pulsed with dull complaint. “Alright,” he groaned, “new rule—no Rift shortcuts. Ever again.”

Castorice made a sound halfway between agreement and nausea. She blinked down at him, realizing belatedly she was still sitting on his chest. “Oh. Right. Sorry.”

He waved her off with a grunt. “You’re fine. The floor’s worse off than me.”

She pulled him up. Phainon’s spine cracked audibly enough for Trianne to wince from across the deck. The ship’s viewplate still flickered slightly as he turned toward it—Port Eltarion came into view, floating along the edge like a shattered crown.

The ring was half-collapsed, three docking arms missing entirely, but light poured through the fractures in molten ribbons. Every few seconds, the glow shifted—orange to violet to pale gold—casting the broken metal in hues that almost looked intentional.

It wasn’t perfect. But in its own way, it was beautiful.

Behind them, Tribbie was muttering apologies to the ship’s systems. Trinnon hovered close to Castorice, holding out a slim water flask as if it might detonate.

“Hydration stabilizes biofeedback,” she said seriously. “And you should not stand. Standing is statistically correlated with—”

“—Vertigo,” Castorice finished weakly, taking the flask. “Got it.” She sank onto the lower deck steps, one hand pressed to her temple.

Phainon crouched beside her, resting an elbow on his knee. “Sorry for the trouble,” she apologized.

“Please,” he said, smiling faintly, “you handled that better than Trianne.”

“Hey!” came a distant squawk from the cockpit.

Phainon didn’t bother to look up. “You drove us through a dimensional pressure wave.”

“It was tactical improvisation!”

He arched a brow. “Sure. And my spinal alignment is a religious experience now.”

Castorice let out a laugh that cracked into a cough halfway through, but it was laughter all the same.

Trinnon, still hovering, pressed two small fingers against her wrist. “Let me tune the ambient field to your pattern,” she said, her tone almost gentle. The deck beneath them brightened from cold blue to warm amber. The hum softened, syncing with her pulse until her breathing eased.

She let out a slow breath. “That’s… better. Thank you.”

Phainon smiled at that and reached for the console nearby. Gold shimmered across his face as the holo-doc booted up, lines of encrypted script scrolling down. “Joint op files are still syncing,” he muttered. “Arrival window’s been moved forward. Again.”

She pinched the bridge of her nose. “Please excuse me, I feel like I’m going to throw up.”

“Then aim for Trianne.”

“Rude!”

Phainon stretched to his full height, groaning as something popped in his back again. He rubbed his side, grimacing lightly. “Alright. Let’s see what bureaucratic miracle wants us now.”

The words had barely left his mouth before Trinnon’s ears twitched. “Incoming transmission.”

Everyone froze.

The main comms array lit up, a slow bloom

spiraling from the floor to the ceiling. Then—suddenly—the pattern fractured, overwritten by a sharp red lattice. The Okheman circuitry flickered uncertainly as the Kremnoan neural-tech protocol forced its way through, refracting light across the panels like crystallized blood.

Castorice leaned forward, squinting. “They’re pinging an open line. Kremnoan command signature.”

As if the dramatic color scheme hadn’t given it away.

“How soon?” Phainon asked, already straightening.

Trinnon blinked at the display. “Transmission strength—ninety-eight percent. So… now.”

Phainon sighed through his teeth. “Of course it is.”

He stepped to the console, massaging his side absently as he keyed in the handshake sequence. The red light sharpened, focusing into the silhouette of a man.

The hologram resolved fully: tall, broad-shouldered, silver at the temples. The lines of his uniform were severe enough to look weaponized, and his eyes carried that unblinking steadiness that came only from decades of command.

Krateros.

Phainon’s posture straightened instinctively. “General.”

The older man inclined his head. “Envoys of Okhema. I trust your transit through herw was… survivable.”

Castorice smoothed a stray lock of hair behind her ear. “Barely.”

Krateros’ gaze flicked to the background—the flickering panels, the scorch marks along the hull visible through the viewport—and back again. “Rift traversal remains a high-risk maneuver for non-Kremnoan craft. Consider your arrival… fortunate.”

“That’s one word for it,” Phainon said lightly, arms folding.

“Your efficiency is noted. Our fleets are still en route from the inner corridor. You will hold orbit at Eltarion until the forward relays are operational. Once synchronization is complete, we’ll begin anchor alignment.”

Phainon nodded once. “Understood.”

“Expect the first relay drones within the hour. Your systems will need to adapt to Kremnoan harmonics.”

Castorice glanced at her console. “We can accommodate. HapLotes405 will manage calibration once the signal stabilizes.”

Krateros inclined his head. “Acceptable. The Commander will join the transmission upon arrival. He intends to debrief you personally.”

Phainon’s brow twitched, ever so slightly. “Of course he will.”

Krateros ignored him. “Until then, Envoy. Keep your systems steady.”

The projection fractured into shards of light and vanished, leaving the room bathed once more in warm Okheman gold.

For a long moment, no one spoke.

Then Tribbie sighed, brushing her hands down her holographic clothes. “Well. That was intense. Anyone else suddenly craving a systems diagnostic?”

Castorice groaned softly into her hand. “I’m craving gravity that doesn’t shift moods every five minutes.”

Phainon scrubbed a palm over his face. “If by ‘intense’ you mean ‘a bureaucratic migraine waiting to happen,’ then yes. Completely intense.”

She pushed herself up, more balanced now. “At least we made it,” she said, gazing out through the viewport at the fractured ring beyond.

Phainon followed her line of sight. “Yeah,” he said quietly. “One piece is better than none.”

For now, they’d left the aftermath to the Tribios to deal with.

Trinnon had insisted they could handle the inbound calibration work—“a minor synchronization issue,” he’d said, as if merging two civilization-grade comm arrays across two cultures with diametrically opposed physics models was as simple as adjusting a radio dial. Phainon hadn’t argued. The small ones were frighteningly competent when left to their own devices, and besides, it gave him an excuse to get Castorice off the ship.

“Maybe you’d like some fresh air?” he’d offered, leaning in the doorway.

She had looked up from her terminal, arching a brow. “Fresh air? On a derelict ring station?”

“You’ll like it,” he said. “Eltarion’s dome filtration system still runs on original Okheman design. O₂ purity’s better than what we get on the homefront.”

“Lead the way, Snowy.”

And that was how they’d ended up here, twenty minutes later—leaving the Tribios to the diagnostics, while the two of them stepped out into the fractured grandeur of Port Eltarion.

Now, the present hums around them.

The outer decks breathe with faint light—half-living conduits pulsing underfoot, their blue glow tracing veins through the corroded metal. The dome overhead, fractured but whole enough, filters light into trembling shades violet. Below, the silent skeleton of the place stretches into the curve of the horizon, every ruin suspended in gravity’s half-forgotten memory.

Castorice stands near the observation railing, steady now. “You were right,” she says. “The air’s… clean.”

“Told you.” Phainon rests his elbows against the railing, eyes tracing the shimmer of field generators below. “Okhema built things to last.”

“Built them so well they fell apart poetically,” she murmurs, and he glances sideways.

“Hard to believe this used to be one of the major trade rings,” Castorice says.

He hums. “Harder to believe it’s still standing.”

Then she stills, head tilted slightly toward the viewport.

“Phainon,” she murmurs.

He follows her gaze—and sees it too.

“Docking sensors are activating,” he says under his breath, watching the readouts bloom across his wristplate.

The air pressure shifts around them; the dormant sirens shudder awake, casting resonant pulses through the hull. And then, with a slow, seismic grandeur, the first shadow breaches the fog.

The Kremnoan fleet arrives like the surfacing of continents.

Ships, if one could still call them that, unfold from the distortion—vast, triangular hulls of obsidian and red, their edges etched in molten veins that pulse like magma.

Phainon feels it before he sees it—the low, chest-deep vibration as gravity fields shift to accommodate their mass.

Even from a safe distance, the air itself seems to bow beneath their presence. The red-gold illumination paints the walls and the two Okhemans in soft, bleeding color.

“Never seen anything like that up close,” Castorice breathes, awe threaded through her voice.

Phainon lets out a low whistle. “Most people haven’t.”

He flicks his wristplate, the projection blooming into a curved comm-interface. “Let’s make sure they know we’re not standing in the blast zone.”

“This is Phainon of Okhema,” he says. “Station Eltarion welcomes the incoming fleet. Your approach vector is clear and registered.”

For a few seconds, nothing. Then: a voice.

“Eltarion Command, this is the Kremnoan Vanguard Serev-Kai. Your coordinates are stable. Visual descent will commence shortly.”

The clarity of the tone almost startles him. He glances toward Castorice, who raises a brow but says nothing.

“Well,” he murmurs. “Either we’re very important or very doomed.”

A flicker ripples across the interface, coalescing into a faint holo— Krateros, once again, crystalline eyes glinting like volcanic glass.

“Okhemans,” he greets, curt. “Our thanks for securing the perimeter. Transmission received with minimal deviation.”

“Glad to hear it,” Phainon replies. “Your fleet made excellent time.”

Krateros inclines his head slightly. “Efficiency is a matter of habit. Our escort divisions will synchronize docking in thirty standard minutes. Containment barriers will stabilize soon after.”

“Perfect.” Phainon nods, then adds lightly, “Would you mind sending someone to meet us once you’ve landed? Your ships are larger than ours, and I’d hate to wander into the wrong airlock and dissolve.”

A faint, almost imperceptible pause from Krateros. “Understood. An escort will be dispatched upon touchdown.”

“Much appreciated,” Phainon says. “We’ll be standing by.”

The connection flickers out, leaving a trace of harmonics hanging in the air.

He exhales slowly, lowering his wrist. “Thirty minutes,” he mutters. “Their estimate was six hours.”

Castorice doesn’t answer immediately. She watches the massive silhouettes align for descent, thoughtful. “They like to make an entrance.”

“Or a statement.”

The first of the ships begins to lower.

There’s no sound at first—just light, rippling in liquid waves over their hulls as they pierce the atmosphere’s thin membrane. Then the resonance hits: a deep, rolling hum that vibrates through every bone in his body. For a moment, the entire station feels alive again.

Microfractures skitter across the plating beneath their boots—harmless, caught by the stabilizers—but still, Phainon can feel the strain, the scale. The ships settle into the ring’s outer bay with the predatory grace of something ancient returning home.

The comm-plate chimes again, voice automated but unmistakably Kremnoan:

“Escort en route. Please remain within the designated perimeter.”

He glances toward Castorice. “Guess that’s our cue.”

She tucks a stray strand of hair behind her ear. “Please try not to offend anyone before we even step aboard.”

“No promises.”

As expected, the inside looked even better than the out.

Eltarion’s outer hull hadn’t done justice to what lay beneath its molten skin. Inside, the flagship of Kremnos was less a vessel and more a cathedral grown from the planet’s marrow. The walls gleamed in deep red and black-gold gradients, crystalline veins branching like rivers of light beneath the surface. When the air shifted, the glow inside them shifted, too, humming like a heart caught between mechanical rhythm and biological beat.

The escort leading them said nothing. His armor—if that’s what it was— looked forged from the same substance as the ship itself, a volcanic alloy so dense that even the sound of his steps seemed swallowed by it. Phainon couldn’t decide if there was a man under it or just another of Kremnos’s living constructs, one of those half-breathing guardians molded from the planet’s own core.

Castorice walked beside him, hands loosely clasped behind her back. The pale light caught the lavender sheen of her hair and the faint opalescence of Okhema’s standard uniform—soft white fabric trimmed in gold, a color palette that made them both look like stray sunlight wandering through the underworld.

When they entered the diplomatic hall, even Phainon—professional, unflappable—found his breath catching for half a second.

It was immense. Columns of white crystal spiraled up into vaults of molten glass, their tips refracting light like slow lightning. The floor was cut obsidian (?), smooth enough to reflect their faces in the glow.

“They built this to impress,” Castorice murmured, gaze trailing up one of the glimmering arches.

Phainon smiled faintly. “Or to intimidate.”

She considered. “Same thing, really.”

Their escort finally stopped at the hall’s center and gestured forward. Around them, Kremnoan officers stood in quiet formation, their armor a spectrum of metallic colors, their crystalline eyes catching and scattering the ship’s internal glow. The tallest among them—a beautiful looking woman—stepped forward and bowed, an elegant arc of formality.

“Okhema’s envoys,” she said, voice rich. “You honor the Vanguard with your presence.”

Phainon inclined his head in return, every movement polished. “And Okhema appreciates the welcome. It seems we’re in excellent hands.”

“The best our fleet can offer,” she replied, tone smooth. “The Vanguard awaits your findings.”

Phainon smiled faintly.

“You’ve made remarkable time through the Rift,” Phainon said, eyes on one of the shifting patterns. “Our instruments logged turbulence along your vector—most fleets would’ve diverted.”

Rhyktas, a captain with garnet skin marbled by black mineral veins, offered a small, tight smile. “Kremnos adapts. Our traversal algorithms refine themselves through repetition. Efficiency is a virtue.”

“Efficiency,” Phainon echoed, tone mild. “And stealth.”

A pause.

“Stealth,” Rhyktas said at last, “is a side effect. Never an intent.”

“Intent,” Castorice said pleasantly, “tends to be a flexible thing.”

That earned the faintest twitch at the corner of his mouth before the conversation drifted elsewhere.

Another officer, this one with quartz-bright eyes, turned toward them. “We’ve heard your readings from the outer sectors show a rise in empathic frequencies. Beyond predictive range?”

Castorice’s voice was gentle but deliberate. “They’ve been… irregular, yes. Nothing outside operational limits. The Rift is volatile, it reacts to any conscious field nearby. You understand how it is.”

That, of course, was a diplomatic lie. And Phainon could feel the moment every Kremnoan in the room recognized it.

By the time they reached the inner chamber, both delegations had exchanged far more sentences than secrets. Still, they’d both gotten what they came for: Kremnos’s interest wasn’t academic. Mydeimos’s personal detachment—his elite specialists—was onboard.

Curious.

The next chamber opened with a sound like a forge exhaling. The doors parted, and the temperature shifted. It was warmer, heavier.

Waiting within stood Krateros, this time in human form. Beside him, Commander Vireth—the arm still bearing the fracture scar from a skirmish with the Luofu Phainon remembered far too vividly—and Hekron, quiet, luminous-eyed.

Phainon and Castorice exchanged a glance. So the council had sent more than diplomats.

“Envoy,” Krateros greeted. “Adjunct. An honor to finally meet in person.”

“Likewise,” Phainon returned smoothly. “Your ship is… breathtaking. I’d almost call it holy.”

“The Kremnoan design strives for function and reverence,” Krateros said. “I imagine Okhema does much the same.”

“Oh, we prefer subtlety,” Phainon said, smiling faintly. “But I’ll admit, you’ve outdone us.”

Castorice, ever composed, added, “And efficient, too.”

Krateros’s eyebrow rose slightly. “Efficiency,” he said, amused at hearing the word again. “A shared principle, then.”

Phainon would’ve continued talking, but he was waiting for the right moment.

And then it came.

The chamber’s glow dimmed, turning from gold to a deep ember. The frequency beneath their feet shifted tone, low and resonant.

Phainon’s hand tingled. The small harmonic focus crystal he’d kept tucked in his sleeve—an instrument designed to measure resonance—suddenly thrummed to life, vibrating so violently he nearly fumbled it. Its readings spiked off-scale before the device began to burn hot against his palm. He slid it into his coat pocket fast, pretending to adjust his sleeve.

The doors at the far end split apart.

Two figures stepped through the haze first—one unmistakable.

Hephaestion—Phainon knew him by posture alone—Mydei’s right hand.

And behind him came the one every vibration in the ship seemed to anticipate.

Mydeimos.

He hadn’t changed.

His uniform was stripped down to functionality—dark crimson lined with gold circuit-threading that pulsed faintly, almost breathing. His hair caught the chamber light like a blade: beige at the roots, bleeding to molten red.

His eyes—gilded, unreadable—moved across the room like scanners set to find weakness.

He didn’t speak. He didn’t need to. The silence was enough to command the space.

Every Kremnoan in the room shifted subtly, bodies straightening in quiet acknowledgment.

Phainon stopped. His control flickered—just long enough that the color of his eyes shifted, a sudden flicker of gold through the blue. Castorice noticed. Her hand brushed his sleeve, just once, the faintest reminder to breathe.

He forced the light down, pulse steady again.

And then Mydeimos’s gaze found him.

A silence stretched—long, electric, impossible to fill.

Phainon’s mouth curled, the hint of a smile forming.

The kind of smile that never meant peace.

Phainon bowed his head—not deeply.

“Commander,” he said smoothly, voice dipped in silk.

Across the wide glass chamber, Mydeimos regarded him with that cutting stillness of his—like the pause before a blade drops. “You still breathe, envoy,” he said at last. “A shame.”

A grin unfolded over Phainon’s face, bright and unapologetic. “You missed me, then.”

The silence that followed rippled through the Kremnoan officers like static through glass. Someone shifted. Someone else coughed. Mydeimos’s expression did not move, but his tone dropped an inch lower. “I don’t miss irritants,” he said. “I remove them.”

Phainon tilted his head. “Mm. You’d have to touch me for that.”

The sound Castorice made beside him might’ve been a sigh—or a prayer for patience.

Mydeimos’s jaw twitched almost imperceptibly. Then, measuredly, he turned his attention toward the holo-table instead. “Let’s not waste any more time.”

But Phainon, of course, did. “Time spent in your company could never be wasted.”

That earned him a very flat look from Hephaestion across the table.

Castorice, as usual, knew better than to stay too close to the explosion radius. She drifted toward Hephaestion, polite smile already in place. “Hephaestion, I assume?”

He inclined his head. “That depends who’s asking. Researcher Castorice, I presume?”

“That’s right.”

He smiled. “Your reports make for fine reading. Detailed, and slightly terrifying.”

She arched a brow. “That’s because I write them myself.”

Hephaestion laughed—genuine—and Mydeimos’s eyes slid toward him with a look that said please don’t encourage them. He responded with a small shrug that said too late.

Meanwhile, Phainon had settled halfway on the edge of the conference table, idly toying with the corner of his glove.

“So this is where the great Commander of Kremnos holds court,” Phainon drawled, gesturing lazily to the vaulted metal and crystalline glow. “Glass, gold, and the faint smell of superiority.”

Mydeimos’s gaze snapped to him. “I hold court nowhere.”

“Oh?” Phainon hummed in mock thought. “Then I must be terribly lucky. Not many get to stand this close to you without vaporizing.”

Something in Mydeimos’s face shifted—a crack, barely visible, but there.

“Enough,” he said finally, voice sharpening in annoyance. “I’ve had it with your theatrics. Let’s begin.”

A flick of his wrist, and the room adjusted—lights dimmed, projection expanding until the entire space glowed with swirling star maps. The Rift loomed in scale before them: vast, jagged, unstable.

Mydeimos’s tone, when he spoke again, was changed. “The Titanal fragments within the Rift have begun destabilizing harmonic currents along our shared corridors. The imbalance is accelerating. If it continues unchecked, we lose our primary trade vectors by the next quarter-cycle.”

Castorice frowned. “We’ve observed similar readings—harmonic spikes, frequency splintering across the lateral bands.”

Phainon nodded, folding his arms, his earlier smirk fading just enough to show he was listening. “And if the field ruptures completely, containment becomes impossible. Half the interstellar routes collapse.”

“Both sides lose,” Mydeimos confirmed. “Our task is containment. Okhema’s fleet handles harmonic mapping and energy diagnostics. Kremnos provides tactical protection and navigational gridwork through the unstable zones.”

Hephaestion leaned forward, tapping a few panels. The hologram reoriented, showing their dual paths. “Two converging fleets,” he said. “Kremnos enters from the southern corridor, setting the anchor grid. Okhema traces the fissures from the northern vector. Data streams sync every six hours. Any deviation above point-six triggers an immediate recall.”

Phainon’s mouth twitched. “Simple. Almost charmingly predictable.”

Mydeimos’s eyes flicked toward him. “Predictability keeps people alive.”

“Mm. But unpredictability makes it interesting.”

The air tightened, charged. It might’ve stayed that way if Hephaestion hadn’t cut in—good-naturedly, but pointedly. “You two planning to compare philosophies or actually save the corridors?”

Mydeimos exhaled, clearing his throat. “As I was saying—”

Phainon, unrepentant, leaned closer. “You were saying we’ll work together. You should try to sound happier about it.”

“I’m elated,” Mydeimos deadpanned.

“Liar,” Phainon said lightly.

The commander’s mouth curved—barely, a ghost of something. “Careful, envoy. Some of us bite.”

Phainon’s grin brightened, teeth catching the white of the hologram’s light. “That’s the idea.”

Castorice, now deep in a hushed exchange with Hephaestion, pretended not to hear a word of it.

Other than that, the conversation was quite boring.

The deeper logistics were hashed out quickly—relay placement, data relays, interference fields, everything.

Soon after, when the projection dimmed and the final sequence stabilized, the air eased back into its natural rhythm. Mydeimos closed the holo with a gesture. “That concludes the joint coordination session. Data protocols are being transmitted to your flagship as we speak.”

Castorice inclined her head. “Acknowledged. I’ll ensure calibration syncs immediately upon return.”

“Good,” Mydeimos said.

Phainon hadn’t moved. His gaze was still fixed on the commander. “Always so composed,” he murmured, mostly to himself.

Mydeimos finally looked back. “Always so loud.”

Hephaestion smirked. “And yet, somehow, still invited.”

Phainon turned toward him, eyes glinting. “You’d miss me otherwise.”

“Unlikely,” Mydeimos muttered, already turning away.

When the meeting dispersed, the Kremnoan officers filed out with curt nods and metallic murmurs. Mydeimos and Hephaestion remained a moment longer, conferring in low voices by the projection dais.

Phainon lingered, just long enough to catch the sharp line of Mydeimos’s profile against the fading red light.

He didn’t look back.

Phainon smiled to himself. “Do you think monsters know when they’re beautiful?” he asked absently.

Castorice, already walking toward the exit, didn’t even turn. “Let’s get back to our ship, please.”

He followed, boots echoing softly through the crystalline corridor as the Kremnoan light dimmed behind them—red fading into the white of Okhema’s.

Phainon yawned—the kind that came from thirty-six hours of recycled air and soft alarm chimes, deep enough to echo faintly against the metal bulkhead.

Outside the viewport, the Okheman cruiser glided through a corridor of fractured starlight.

The panels beneath their hands pulsed slightly. Harmonic fields thrummed faintly through the deck—the heartbeat of a vessel holding itself together.

Phainon leaned forward on the console, chin propped against his hand. “You know,” he said around another stifled yawn, “for a sector named after a fault, it really likes to prove the point.”

Castorice’s focus never broke, not even when the deck swayed faintly beneath them. “Meaning?”

“Meaning it’s living up to the name. Fractured. Irritating. Unforgiving.” He squinted at a soft pulse of violet flaring across his display, then added more quietly, “And a little too beautiful for comfort.”

From above, a voice chimed in.

“Flux stable… quantum bandwidth holding at eighty-nine percent… we like this percentage!”

Phainon half turned. “You always say that, Tribbie.”

“We always mean it.” she replied, hovering just overhead.

“That’s reassuring,” Castorice murmured.

“Great work as always, Tribbie,” Phainon said, reaching up out of habit to ruffle her hair.

Trinnon and Trianne had gone quiet the day before, shutting down to conserve processing power while Okhema held position in the Rift’s heavier zones. The absence of their chatter left the bridge quieter than anyone liked. Every now and then, Phainon would glance at the empty ports where their signals used to hover, as if expecting them to flicker back.

Castorice had called the silence “unsettling.”

Phainon had said “sad.”

Tribbie had called it both before promising to “hold steady for all three of us.”

Phainon smiled faintly at the memory. “How’s our corridor holding?”

“Stable enough,” Castorice answered, adjusting a few dials. “The southern harmonic line’s syncing cleanly with Kremnos’s outer grids. Their fleet’s maintaining orbit along the second fracture cluster.”

“So,” Phainon murmured, “the plan’s actually working.”

“For now,” she said.

He huffed a quiet laugh. “You’ll make an optimist proud.”

“Don’t count on it.”

“I got another report earlier,” Castorice continued, scanning the readings. “The fragments are beginning to structure themselves—crystalline chains forming along the magnetic fractures. They’re… humming, in a sense. Frequencies we can barely translate.”

Phainon tapped through the analysis logs. “Any chance it’s not just random noise?”

“Doubtful. It’s decaying resonance—echoes of what the Rift used to be before it collapsed in on itself. Harmonic decay, residual motion, memory imprints. Nothing alive, but not nothing.”

He looked at the scrolling waveforms, colors bending softly against the screen. “The sound of dying stars humming their last song,” he said.

“Poetic nonsense detected,” Tribbie announced in mock seriousness. “Logging for future teasing.”

Phainon blinked, then laughed. “That’s mutiny, Tribbie. Mark that too.”

“Logged with affection.”

The bridge lights flickered—the quiet shift of the containment adjusting again.

The hum of etheric flow filled the pause that followed.

Phainon broke it. “You know, our last call with Mydei was short. Almost like he couldn’t wait to leave.”

“Still thinking about your favorite Kremnoan?” Castorice asked.

“Thinking about my least favorite man in the universe,” he said immediately.

Tribbie tilted her head. “That sounds suspiciously like favorite behavior.”

“Traitor.”

“Affectionate observation,” she countered.

Castorice folded her arms. “You’ll have a chance to glare at him again soon. Sync call’s coming up—two minutes.”

Phainon blinked. “Already? That was fast.”

“That’s what happens when you lose track of time.”

“I don’t lose track of time.” He stretched, vertebrae cracking audibly. “Time just refuses to behave around me.”

“That’s definitely how that works,” she murmured.

He picked up a sleek, iridescent device from the console—its surface alive with dim, rippling light—and thumbed through the new readings. “Outer corridor’s holding. Slight flux in the magnetic fold, nothing dangerous. Looks like Kremnos’s side is taking the heavier resonance strain.”

“They built for brute endurance,” Castorice said. “We built for balance.”

He hummed. “And here we are—proof that compromise can be inconveniently effective.”

“Or that necessity makes for strange partners.”

“Poetic,” he teased.

She shook her head, smiling faintly. “I’m learning from you.”

Before he could answer, the holo-channel shimmered to life—light unfurling in geometric strands, each one folding into the next until a translucent sphere hovered between them.

Tribbie’s form brightened as she adjusted signal flow. “Channel steady. Routing uplink now. Please try to sound professional.”

Phainon looked amused. “You’re the one who said we.”

“We includes you,” she said primly.

He grinned. “Alright, let’s start.”

The light stabilized, and then the signal cleared.

Hephaestion came into focus first and beside him, Leonnius lounged against a console, one arm slung casually over a holobar.

“Okhema uplink secure,” Castorice reported.

Hephaestion nodded. “Good to see your end still intact, Researcher.”

A voice came from off-frame. “You sound surprised, Hephaestion.”

Phainon stepped into the holographic wash, crossing the projection radius. His tone carried a lightness—the sort that made people uncertain whether he was being polite or mocking.

“I’m always pleasantly surprised when you’re not the source of interference.”

“Ah,” Phainon said mildly. “And here I was hoping for flattery.”

Leonnius gave a laugh. “Oh, there it is—the envoy himself. I was beginning to think you’ve died.”

Phainon didn’t answer right away. He just looked at Leonnius, the silence stretching long enough that even Tribbie, flickering faintly behind him, hesitated like she was waiting for a cue to giggle.

“Leonnius,” Phainon said finally. “You still talk as though your commander’s listening in. It’s endearing.”

Leonnius’s grin sharpened, all teeth. “Old habits. Especially when the commander’s busy making sure the rest of us don’t die.”

A flicker—brief, barely perceptible—crossed Phainon’s face, a tightening near his eyes that disappeared behind a smirk.

Hephaestion, amused, interjected. “You’re talkative today.”

“Blame the vacuum,” Leonnius replied, leaning back and tapping his console. “Anyway—grid anchors deployed and stable. Magnetic flux readings are steady. We’ve mapped seven of the southern fractures. Pretty ones, too. Shame they’re lethal.”

Hephaestion gave a low hum, eyes flicking toward the readings projected behind them.

Castorice adjusted her own console. “We’re seeing harmonic feedback from those same fractures. The pattern’s faintly rhythmic—pulsing in sequence.”

“Patterned?” Hephaestion’s brow rose. “That’s new. Flux is stable on our side, but temperamental. The commander’s leading the third sweep himself.”

Mydei.

Leonnius’s smirk faded into something almost fond, an ease that came naturally only when the subject was someone they trust. “He’s enjoying himself,” he said idly. “Haven’t seen him go all out in ages.”

That earned a sharper look from Phainon—subtle, but clear. “How lucky for you.”

Leonnius caught it instantly, that edge of careful disinterest. “You’d say that differently if you’d ever seen him pilot up close.”

Phainon’s smile was smooth. “Oh, I’ve seen him. That’s the problem.”

Hephaestion made a sound suspiciously like a stifled laugh. “Easy, both of you. We’re on the same side—for now.”

Castorice cut through the tension. “Okhema’s readings confirm the harmonic split’s widening but not exponentially. The Rift’s fragments are developing crystallized exo-shells. Their resonance is increasing—too deliberate to be random collapse.”

Leonnius looked mildly impressed. “Deliberate?”

She nodded, scrolling through waveforms. “They respond to movement. Each time one of our ships passes, the crystalline matrix adjusts its resonance. Adaptive feedback. It’s… almost aware.”

Phainon brought up a holo beside her, magnifying a shimmering cluster. Tiny filaments twisted through the image like glass nerves. “We broadcasted steady harmonic tones,” he said. “The formation reoriented toward us. Not hostile—more like… recognition.”

Hephaestion frowned slightly. “That’s unnerving.”

“Beautiful,” Phainon corrected under his breath.

Leonnius gave a quiet whistle. “And that’s why we prefer armor over poetry.”

Phainon’s mouth curved. “And yet the poets are still here.”

“Miracles happen.”

Before anyone could respond, Tribbie exclaimed, “Miracle acknowledged. Logging optimism for morale reports!”

That earned a genuine laugh from Hephaestion. “I like your assistant, Envoy.”

“She’s the pragmatic one,” Phainon said. “Keeps the rest of us from drifting into existential despair.”

Castorice sighed. “Someone has to.”

Then the comm line pinged, a sharp chime slicing through the quiet.

Hephaestion checked his console. “Priority link. The commander.”

Leonnius straightened immediately, expression shifting from relaxed to focused in an instant. “We’ll take it.”

Hephaestion nodded once toward the Okhema side. “Appreciate the sync, Envoy. Researcher. Keep that harmonic data flowing—the Council will want comparative readings before the next cycle.”

“Understood,” Castorice replied.

Phainon added lightly, “Try not to get swallowed whole while we’re gone.”

Leonnius smirked, stepping back into the fading hologram. “We’d hate to miss seeing you jealous again.”

Phainon’s answering smile was too perfect to be sincere. “Take care down there.”

The image fractured—light dissolving into particles—and then they were gone.

Tribbie dimmed her light. “Transmission closed.”

Phainon stayed quiet for a moment, staring at the empty air where the projection had been. His jaw flexed once. He bit his inner cheek—a tiny, human thing—before speaking, voice low. “Why doesn’t he ever call us directly?”

Castorice didn’t look up. “Because they’re running the front line. It isn’t his place to—”

“I know,” Phainon interrupted, too quickly. Then softer, almost embarrassed, “I know. Just joking.”

But the joke didn’t land.

Castorice turned her head just slightly, studying him. Whatever she might’ve said stayed unsaid.

Tribbie floated closer, voice barely above a whisper. “Another call soon.”

Phainon smiled faintly, without humor. “Yeah,” he murmured. “Soon.”

Unfortunately, the calls had became more frequent after that.

By the sixth day, the Okhema’s bridge had stopped bothering to dim the panels during rest hours. The Rift’s glow bled through the viewport in unpredictable flashes anyway—sometimes dim, sometimes bright, always too deliberate to be random.

They’d switched to staggered shifts by then. Castorice took the early hours, calibrating data streams and cross-analyzing the harmonics while Phainon slept in the observation cabin just off the main deck. When he woke, she was usually gone—her console cleared, her mug left half full, the faint steam always just cooled. A quiet signature that the day had already started without him.

When their hours did overlap, it was brief—a passing nod, a tired “morning,” sometimes a note left on the holo-feed that read more like a sigh than a sentence. Their conversations had grown shorter as well.

Even Tribbie filled the silence differently these days.

She’d started humming when idle. It wasn’t in her programming, not exactly, but neither of them ever told her to stop.

It would’ve been peaceful, if it didn’t sometimes sound like someone else was with them.

“Resonance stable,” Tribbie announced one morning, bright and chipper as ever.

Then, after a pause—same tone, same rhythm—

“Resonance stable.”

Castorice paused mid-sip. “Tribbie?”

“Yes?”

“You just repeated yourself.”

“No, we didn’t.”

The pause after was uncanny. More than it should’ve been.

“…Did we?”

Castorice exhaled slowly. “You did.”

“Oh.” Her voice dropped a register, embarrassed. “I don’t remember.”

“Check your logs.”

“I did.”

“And?”

“They’re fine.”

The lights flickered once—just once—and outside, the Rift pulsed in perfect sync, like it had been waiting for its cue.

The environmental drift started that same day.

Condensation appeared along the starboard panels—fine moisture on surfaces that shouldn’t have been capable of forming it. The lights dimmed in strange intervals, sometimes following the hum.

When Castorice ran diagnostics, everything came up clear. Except—

a small, persistent deviation: 0.04 degrees off magnetic alignment, identical across every instrument. Too exact to be coincidence. Too minor to justify panic.

Phainon had leaned over her shoulder, squinting at the readout. “It’s probably the Rift flirting again.”

“You joke too easily.”

“That’s my only marketable skill.”

But even he didn’t laugh after saying it. His humor had thinned out lately— still there, but stretched and a little brittle.

They adjusted. That was what Okheman did best.

By the eighth cycle, the fatigue had settled in for good. Their bodies resisted it, but the exhaustion clung like static—persistent, never quite leaving. Okheman physiology wasn’t meant for this kind of isolation; their species thrived on shared resonance, on proximity, on emotional exchange. Yet somehow, Phainon and Castorice held steady—stronger than most, or maybe just too stubborn to admit weakness.

Still, strength had limits.

Castorice started dreaming again—strange, vivid things. Voices like Tribbie’s, slowed down and layered, like hearing an echo underwater. Once, she woke up to find her console already on, data logs open to harmonic readings she didn’t remember pulling.

She didn’t tell Phainon until days later. She knew he’d only make light of it to comfort her, and she didn’t want to hear him sound worried.

His shift came.

Phainon sat alone on the dim bridge, the ship’s systems whispering around him, every pulse half a beat behind itself. He’d gotten used to the rhythm— the mechanical heartbeat of the ship syncing with the slow shimmers.

He caught himself humming again, absently. The tune slipped into that same uneven pattern Tribbie had been using for days.

He rubbed his eyes. “I’m losing it.”
