“You’re not,” Tribbie said brightly.

He looked up. “Did I say that out loud?”

“Of course.” Then, a beat later—same tone, same voice—

“Of course.”

He stared. “…You’re doing it again.”

“Doing what?”

“The repeat.”

Tribbie tilted her head. “I’m not.”

He sighed. “Right.”

The data feed rolled endlessly across his console—energy spectrums, resonance graphs, harmonic fluctuations. All noise, until it wasn’t.

Near the bottom of the latest sequence, something subtle emerged: a low-frequency pulse buried beneath main signature.

Too deliberate to be natural. The intervals followed half-beat rhythms— almost syllabic, almost speech.

He watched the waveform repeat. Then shift. Then pause, like it was waiting for him to notice.

Phainon leaned forward, isolating the frequency through three filters. The pattern persisted in each one—then, faintly, it echoed itself.

Not an error. A response.

“Castorice,” he murmured, opening the comm.

Static met him first—a slow hiss, like breath. Then her voice, hazy with exhaustion. “You’re up early.”

“It’s late. Or… was.” He pinched his eyes shut.

“What’s wrong?”

“I think it’s talking.”

A pause. “Don’t start.”

“I’m serious. Look at the last packet.”

“I’m looking.” Her voice hardened. “It’s feedback. Harmonic interference.”

“Then why does it pause when I stop looking at it?”

“That’s not possible.”

He smiled faintly. “Neither’s condensation on heat panels, but here we are.”

His head throbbed—sharp, rhythmic. He pressed a hand to his temple, eyes watering a little from the pressure. “Six-hour mark just passed. I’ll initiate the next call once the feed stabilizes.”

“Phainon—”

“Relax. I’m fine.”

He wasn’t, but it was easier to lie when she couldn’t see him.

He reached across the console, eyes half closed, and for a brief moment, the outside pulsed in sync with his headache—slow, insistent. The reflection in the viewport shifted a second behind him.

He didn’t notice.

The console’s light bloomed across the room.

“Establishing link,” Tribbie said.

Then again, perfectly mirrored—

“Establishing link.”

He ignored it.

Phainon stared at her display, exhaling through his teeth. “Right. Let’s keep it to one version of you tonight, yeah?”

He tapped the comm node, adjusting the frequency. “Channel four-three, Hephaestion relay. Let’s make sure you haven’t drifted into another dead zone again, old man.”

Tribbie’s face screen lit in bright sequence. “Transmission verified! Stabilizing, stabilizing—”

“Variance at one-point-two percent,” Phainon finished, leaning back in his chair. “You’re starting to sound like me.”

He checked the time—six hours late. The ache behind his temple had turned dull and constant. He rubbed at it absently, eyes flicking up to the viewport again.

The transmission wave rippled outward from the console, spreading rings of light across the deck floor.

Phainon frowned, head tilting. “That’s new. Usually, they at least start with a ‘copy received.’”

“Transmission stable,” Tribbie announced brightly. Then, a half-second later: “Transmission stable.”

The delay was wrong enough to make Phainon glance at her. Her display had flickered—not an error exactly, but as if her code was trying to decide what part of her should be speaking.

“Tribbie, are you—”

“Perfectly operational!” she replied, then blinked, softer. “Perfectly… operational.”

Phainon blinked, concerned.

Footsteps padded behind him—Castorice, hair slightly mussed from her shift rest, datapad tucked under one arm. “Still no response?”

He gave a one-shouldered shrug. “Either the Detachment’s ignoring me again or the environment decided to start screening my calls.”

She leaned against the console. “Bandwidth interference?”

“Already compensated.” He ran another diagnostic just to humor her. The feedback graph jumped, stuttered, and flattened back into a line that didn’t make sense. “Feels like something’s talking back,” he said finally. “Just… not in the right order.”

Before Castorice could answer, the sound shifted. The static hollowed out, the hum of the ship going eerily still for a half-second before a voice broke through—bent, wet, and too close to the ear.

[“…out of…here… alert…”]

Phainon blinked. “Hephaestion?”

The voice warped again, syllables stretching, overlapping.

[“…out—of—here—alert—”]

Castorice straightened, her tone edged with alert focus now. “Playback.”

Tribbie’s display dimmed to gray, then brightened again—confused. “Playback. Playback.” Pause. “No data found.”

Phainon huffed, the sound more nervous than amused. “Selective memory. Great. I’m sure that’s fine.”

Then, abruptly, the feed stabilized.

Light bloomed from the projection core—sharp, too bright. The figures finally resolved: Hephaestion, uniformed, expression taut with urgency, and Perdikkas just behind him, hands moving across unseen controls.

Phainon sighed in reflexive relief. “Finally. Signal confirmed. Is something —”

“Envoy, listen to me.” Hephaestion’s tone hit hard, stripped of its usual easy calm. “You need to turn back. Now. That’s an order.”

“An order?” Phainon raised an eyebrow. “You’re not my superior, Hephaestion.”

“Phainon.” The way Hephaeston said his name wasn’t friendly—it was strained, breath catching on distortion. “You don’t understand. It’s in there with you. Turn the ship—now.”

Castorice stepped closer, frown deepening. “The field hasn’t destabilized. We’re still within safe thresholds. What’s going on?”

Hephaestion’s background flickered—once, twice—like something massive was moving just beyond his feed’s range. “You don’t have time for me to explain.”

The air on the bridge thickened. Phainon’s skin prickled. The hologram shimmered again—its surface distorting inwards, then out, like a breath being taken.

Phainon opened his mouth to ask another question, but the words didn’t make it out. The deck light bent. Everything bent.

He froze mid-motion.

Castorice stiffened beside him, her hand still hovering above the console. Her pupils dilated to near black.

Every empathic panel on the ship ignited—white-red-white—screaming in silent resonance.

Phainon’s body jolted. The air turned solid in his lungs, his neural threads snapping bright behind his eyes. It hurt.

The kind of pain that wasn’t pain at all, but something deeper—like every emotion in his system was suddenly on the wrong frequency.

His vision split.

It hurt.

It hurt.

It hurt.

Something was inside his head, whispering through the wiring of his mind like it had found a door and didn’t plan on leaving. His throat clenched around a sound that wasn’t human.

Castorice gasped beside him—her body arched, fingers clawing into the console until the metal creaked.

Tribbie’s voice fractured into a dozen versions of herself, each speaking over the other—code screaming, mechanical prayers and error strings blurring together.

Hephaestion’s voice broke through the static: “Envoy! Status, respond!”

Perdikkas appeared behind him, shouting something indistinct, then sharper: “Neurological feedback loop! But there isn’t any aetheroots—get them out of resonance—”

Phainon’s knees hit the floor. He didn’t remember falling. Every nerve felt inverted, his heartbeat too loud, his body trying to tune itself inside out.

Then—everything stopped.

Sound dropped out.

Color followed.

The panels dimmed, the hum flattened, and both Okhemans’ biosigns fell to baseline as if nothing had happened at all.

For a few seconds, no one breathed.

Castorice was the first to move, her hands trembling as she lowered them from her temples. “What in the—” Her voice cracked. “What was that?”

Phainon wiped blood from his mouth with the back of his hand, eyes glassy. “That wasn’t Okhema’s aetheroots.”

She blinked at him, still struggling to find words.

The hologram flickered one last time. Perdikkas’ voice bled through, fragmented and urgent:

“Resonant trauma leaves traces. If it happens again—don’t suppress it. Find the sou—“

The feed cut.

…

Phainon took a slow breath, exhaled shakily, then looked at Tribbie.

“Tribbie,” he said, “get us out of here. As fast as you can.”

Tribbie’s eyes dimmed to cold blue.

“Understood,” she said quietly.

The ship began to turn.

Outside, the stars shifted—just slightly—like something enormous was watching them leave.

And for the first time since the mission began, Phainon didn’t feel like they were alone.

The hum of the Okhema’s engines had changed again.

“Harmonics are drifting again,” Castorice muttered. She adjusted the sliders one-handed, eyes flicking between two conflicting graphs. “By three hertz this time.”

Phainon looked up from his own screen, chewing on his stylus like the situation was only mildly inconvenient. “Could be atmospheric interference.”

“We’re in a vacuum.”

“Then it’s emotional interference,” he said, deadpan. “The Rift’s feeling temperamental today.”

Castorice shot him a glare over her shoulder. “You joke when things catch fire too.”

“Only after I put them out.”

The banter bought them about six seconds of normalcy before Tribbie’s voice cut in.

“No significant hardware failure detected. However…”

She trailed off, something hitching in the audio feed.

“However?” Phainon prompted, already typing a command string.

“There’s a harmonic echo,” Tribbie said slowly. “A residual waveform inside my auditory sensors. It’s… not registered as mechanical.”

Castorice’s eyes narrowed. “Meaning?”

Tribbie hesitated, and that alone set both Okhemans on edge. “Meaning I heard someone speaking.”

The bridge went very still.

Phainon raised an eyebrow. “Any chance you’re developing taste?”

“I do not hallucinate, Captain.”

“Didn’t say you did,” he said easily, but his tone sharpened beneath the drawl. “Run a sweep for ghost frequencies. If something’s piggybacking through the comm band, I want to know where it’s coming from.”

Castorice, meanwhile, was pulling up telemetry data. “Thermal readings are off, too. Condensation on the lower panels again—there shouldn’t be water this deep in vacuum.”

“Don’t tempt it.”

Before he could reply, the comm line pinged.

“Signal from Kremnos fleet,” Tribbie said. “Origin tag: Leonnius.”

“Patch him through.”

Static hissed. Then a voice filtered in.

[—testing—line—Kremnos main channel four, confirm receipt—]

Castorice’s jaw flexed. “That’s a temporal desync.”

Phainon glanced at her with faint amusement. “And you were worried about humidity.”

The signal fractured, then snapped.

“Tribbie,” Phainon said quietly, “what’s our distance from Kremnos’s forward detachment?”

“Three point seven clicks,” she replied.

He hummed. “Close enough to hear them die if something goes wrong.”

Castorice shot him a look. “You always know what to say.”

“I’m a conversationalist.”

[…gravitational fluctuation detected—Hephaestion—confirm— Mydeimos’s fleet adjusting trajectory—]

Phainon paused. Every muscle stilled at once, like someone had flipped a switch.

Castorice’s gaze darted up. “That was—”

“Mydei,” he said softly, before the channel detonated into white noise.

Tribbie’s voice flickered faintly back online, glitching like a dying echo: “—fleet—signal—lost—”

Phainon slammed a fist on the console. “Open channels!”

Static.

Then, briefly, the ship ID flickered to life.

HEPHAESTION PRIORITY RED

“—protect—command—”

Cut.

He hesitated at the hatch. “Cas.”

She raised a brow.

“If something happens—”

He smiled. “Fair enough.”

She looked at where he was once, before stepping back. “Five minutes, Phainon.”

Castorice’s voice came over comms, slightly distorted already. “See you soon, partner.”

“Yeah,” he said quietly. “See you soon.”

Gravitational surges clawed at the hull, dragging the pod sideways. The metal howled. Warnings flashed across his visor in angry red.

“C’mon,” he muttered through clenched teeth, adjusting the thrusters manually. “Stay with me.”

A wave of debris spun past—shattered hull fragments, wiring, shards of armor plating. For a second, he thought he saw something moving among them, a flicker of rocks shaped like a hand. Then it was gone.

The beacon pulsed again. Closer now.

Then impact.

The pod slammed into solid mass with enough force to knock the breath out of him. The harness caught, the shock absorbers screamed. Systems flickered, then steadied.

Silence.

For a long moment, the only sound was his breathing.

Then, one by one, the pod’s internal lights flickered back on. The hatch hissed open, releasing a curl of vapor into the dim, fractured glow beyond.

Phainon unlatched himself, stood, and stepped out into the wreck.

Cold air. Silence.

And then he started walking.

Or at least, something close enough to walking. The deck no longer deserved the title—half-bent plating, half-liquefied conduits, all of it groaning in slow, metallic protest. The gravity field flickered every few seconds, switching between syrup-thick and moonlight-thin, tugging at him like an invisible hand unsure whether to pull or let go. Every other step sent him floating half a meter off the ground before slamming him back down hard enough to rattle his teeth.

The wreck was silent in that way that screamed.

His breath fogged faintly in his visor. The air was thin but technically breathable, or at least survivable if you were built like an Okheman. He could feel it scraping at his throat, sharp and electric, the oxygen thinned out to the point it tasted metallic. His lungs burned, but his body compensated on instinct.

Okheman biology had been built—literally—for places like this. Their blood carried a network of adaptive myceles: living micro-filaments that could snatch stray oxygen ions out of air so thin it might as well not be there. The process wasn’t pleasant; it left a faint chemical sting behind the eyes, a ghost taste of rust and copper. Still, it was better than suffocating.

The suit’s biosensors pulsed faintly along his forearms, syncing with his bloodstream’s rhythm. He could almost feel the myceles working—cool, relentless. Okhema had evolved for emotionsand endurance, for surviving the voids between systems where no one else would bother going.

“Yeah,” he muttered under his breath, “real evolutionary masterpiece. Shame it doesn’t help with claustrophobia.”

He checked his wrist display—a soft glow, fractured by dust. The beacon’s pulse trembled across it, weak but rhythmic. Okhema’s tracking tech worked off resonance mapping: not location, but impression. Each Okheman carried a trace field around them, a sort of quantum echo in their biofrequency. The system could read that—translate it, even amplify it—but Mydei wasn’t Okheman.

The only reason Phainon could feel him at all was the link-band Mydei had worn, an Okheman-made device meant to sync heartbeat data across distances. Mydei had kept it on, half because he had to, half because Phainon had forced him to.

It was that band—the most ridiculous kind of sentimental tech—that was now saving Mydei’s life.

Phainon slowed to a stop, closed his eyes, and let the link hum against his ribs. The resonance was faint but familiar, warm, flickering like candlelight in water.

“Got you,” he said softly.

He started to move again, faster now, navigating through the ribs of the wreck. The deeper he went, the redder everything became—the emergency lights pulsing in slow, uneven rhythm, echoing the ship’s death throes.

A warped bulkhead loomed ahead, torn open like the ribs of a carcass. He squeezed through, wincing as the edges scraped against him. Inside, the corridor narrowed. Every sound was too close. The air carried a faint crackle of electricity.

Something moved at the edge of his vision. A shape. A trick. Or maybe not.

He froze. Listened. Nothing.

“Yeah, no, definitely not haunted,” he muttered, voice dry. “Just cursed. Totally different classification.”

He ducked beneath a collapsed beam, boot catching briefly on something slick. A pool of hydraulic fluid glimmered beneath his step, violet and shimmering under the emergency red.

The marks along the walls had also changed the further in he went. No longer burn damage or pressure tears—these were grown. Thin, crystalline etchings cut through the hull, spreading in fractal patterns, glimmering faintly with internal light. They crawled upward like veins.

He touched one experimentally, and his glove sensors pinged low-level energy—unstable but active.

“Castorice would’ve told me not to touch that,” he muttered. Then, quieter, “She’s probably right.”

The beacon’s signal grew stronger, pulsing faster now, in time with his own heart. Mydei was close—he could feel it in the resonance building beneath his skin. The Okheman trait kicked in, that biological matrix that allowed their nervous systems to attune to another’s frequency. It guided him through the wreck like a compass made of intuition.

He broke into a sprint. Carefully, at first—measured steps, pushing off walls where gravity faltered, sliding across uneven plating when it returned. Then faster.

The corridor widened suddenly into a half-collapsed hangar bay. Red dust floated through the air in sheets, catching the faint glow of sparking conduits. The beacon’s pulse was deafening in his ears now, a steady rhythm that wrapped around his heartbeat like a double helix.

“Mydei,” he breathed. “I’ve got you.”

He vaulted a fallen girder, hit the ground hard, and kept going. The hum beneath his skin rose higher, until it wasn’t just sound anymore—it was presence, warmth, the distinct shape of someone alive and scared and waiting.

And then it happened.

The wall to his right didn’t just give way—it burst.

A sound like shattering glass mixed with thunder tore through the hangar. A plume of red crystals exploded outward, jagged and violent, slicing through the air in a fan of light. One shard missed his head by less than an inch, embedding itself in the console behind him with a sound like frozen lightning.

The blast hit him a second later. He was thrown backward, rolling across the deck until his shoulder slammed against a pipe. His visor flickered and the world was a mess of crimson and drifting debris.

The crystals pulsed faintly, their veins glowing brighter with each beat, like they were breathing.

Phainon staggered upright, blinking hard. The beacon on his wrist was gone —no, not gone, but consumed, its signal pouring out from the heart of the crystalline bloom.

He stared, realization sinking in slow and cold.

“…Shit.”

The beacon’s frequency wasn’t just close to the crystals—it was inside them. The same pulse. The same rhythm.

The signal he’d been following—the heartbeat he’d been chasing—was coming directly from the core of the growth.

From inside the red.

He stood frozen, chest heaving, the red washing over him. Somewhere deep within the crystal mass, there was a heartbeat. Faint but undeniable.

Phainon had the distinct, stomach-turning sense that the wreck wasn’t dead at all—

—it was living.

Phainon bit down hard, the copper sting of blood spreading across his tongue. He ignored the pain and kept moving. The once-metal walls had been swallowed whole by red crystal growths that pulsed like veins under a thin layer of flesh.

The glow painted everything in slow, viscous color, each reflection a distorted image of himself walking deeper.

He turned a corner and stopped.

The crystals had devoured the room’s structure completely, sprouting upward in jagged pillars and sweeping arcs, refracting the dim emergency lights into red storms across the walls.

And right at the center, at the eye of the storm, was the source.

Phainon’s breath caught. For one impossible second, he thought the beacon had cracked open and become light itself—but then his eyes adjusted, and he saw him.

Mydei.

Or what was left of him.

He was encased within the crystal bloom—his entire body caught mid-motion, one hand half-raised, face turned slightly toward the floor, as if reaching for something. The red crystal had formed around him, not as imprisonment, but as… protection. Each shard curved along the lines of his body like frozen flame.

Phainon’s jaw slackened. He took one shaky step forward, then another.

Was the crystal keeping him alive? Or feeding on him?

He reached out, gloved fingers brushing the crystal surface. It was warmer than it should’ve been—almost soft under the armor. A faint hum vibrated through his bones, harmonizing with his own heartbeat in a way that was wrongly familiar.

“Mydei…” His voice cracked, barely a whisper. “Hey, it’s me. You can stop hiding now.”

The crystal didn’t move.

He swallowed, flicked his wrist, and the plasma cutter flared to life. The blue flame reflected off the red crystal, tinting everything a molten purple. He aimed it carefully, exhaled, and cut.

The scream that followed wasn’t normal. It sounded almost alive—like the crystal itself crying out in protest.

Phainon winced, teeth grit as the vibrations rattled through his skull. Shards flew like molten snow, burning through the air. The heat pressed against him from all sides, and the oxygen readout on his display began to dip faster than he liked.

“Come on, come on—”

Another cut. The crystal resisted every strike, mending itself in slow waves.

“Fine,” he muttered, kicking free a length of cable from the wall. He twisted it between his hands, rigging it with the flick of his wrist, sparks snapping in the air. The arc torch hissed to life, white and angry, and this time when he struck the crystal, it bled. Cracks spidered outward, glowing bright enough to burn through his visor filters.

The crystal’s hum changed pitch—from low to something jagged, desperate. A piece fractured and fell, revealing the curve of Mydei’s face beneath.

He was beautiful.

Too beautiful for this place.

And that, somehow, startled Phainon more than anything else.

He kept going, ignoring the sudden sting along his arm where a flying shard had sliced through the plating. It buried itself. His blood—golden and iridescent—seeped into the inside of the suit, tracing a slow line toward his wrist. He bit back a hiss, forced himself to keep working.

He didn’t care.

He couldn’t.

Not when he was so close.

The final crack split the air with a sound like thunder underwater. The light within the crystal shuddered, then collapsed inward, releasing a burst of red vapor and sound. Mydei fell forward into his arms.

Phainon staggered back, the weight nearly knocking him over.

The crystals dimmed, their glow flickering like dying embers.

Mydei was cold—too cold—and still covered in a fine dusting of red crystal dust that shimmered faintly along his skin. His pulse, when Phainon pressed two trembling fingers to his neck, was there. Faint. Steady.

Alive.

He laughed, a short, breathless sound that bordered on delirium. “You damn bastard. You just had to make me work for it.”

He shifted Mydei’s weight, ignoring the protest of his injured shoulder. He slung Mydei’s arm around his neck, half-carrying, half-dragging him toward the nearest stable corridor.

“Castorice,” he rasped into the comm, using up his only call, voice breaking slightly, “I’m finished. Pick me up at—hangar deck, lower quadrant, now.”

The signal flickered in and out, fragments of her voice stuttering through: “—Phainon—do you—copy—what’s your—status—”

“Just get me out,” he said sharply, still moving.

And then—Mydei shifted.

Phainon stopped mid-step, eyes snapping down. Mydei’s fingers twitched, brushing faintly against his suit. He blinked once, slow, lashes catching what little light was left. Phainon nearly dropped him.

“Mydei?” The name came out strangled, half a plea. He lowered them both to the ground, sliding to his knees. “Hey, look at me. You’re okay. You’re— Gods, you’re okay, I got you. Just stay still, alright? We’re getting out of here, I promise.”

He brushed a thumb across Mydei’s cheek without thinking, tracing the faint shimmer of dust that still clung to his skin.

For a moment, Mydei looked at him. Really looked—eyes weakly opened, golden, almost too bright. Something moved behind them, a flicker of confusion or memory or nothing at all.

And then he spoke.

“…Who,” he murmured, voice hollow and distant, “are you?”

Everything stopped.

…

What?

Phainon’s mind emptied all at once—the background hum of the ship, the smell of metal and ozone, the pulsing red glow—they all receded into nothing. He was aware of his heartbeat only distantly, a dull, slow echo behind glass. His thoughts didn’t move. They didn’t even exist.

He stared at Mydei’s face—the same face he’d memorized, dreamed about, killed for—and saw no recognition. No warmth. Not even faint curiosity. Just that hollow confusion, sharp enough to cut him open.

The sound in his ears went dull, replaced by a faint high-pitched ring. He was distantly aware of his breathing—too shallow, too fast—and of Castorice’s voice breaking through the comm, words warped by glitching:

“Phainon—status—if you can hear me, proceed to extraction—don’t linger —repeat, do not linger—”

He didn’t move. His fingers twitched once against Mydei’s sleeve, then stilled.

When he finally spoke, it was automatic. His lips moved before his mind caught up.

“…You defected with me from Castrum Kremnos,” he said softly, almost dazed. “You said you wanted peace.”

The words didn’t sound like him. They sounded rehearsed.

The crystals along the walls flickered faintly, pulsing once in response. As if listening.

Phainon didn’t notice. He just kept looking at Mydei, at those gold eyes that looked back through him like he was no one at all.

And for the first time, he wasn’t sure if he was.

The soft, syrupy kind specifically—the kind that made everything below shimmer as though dipped in honey. Two suns hung lazily overhead, taking turns warming the horizon in a choreography so smooth it was rehearsed. The winds here didn’t howl or race; they strolled. —followed immediately by a loud, distinctly real groan.

A head hit a table with a soft thunk.

“Shut up,” Phainon muttered into the surface, muffled, his voice breaking the serene background track.

The holo-display sputtered mid-sentence, as if startled, before cutting out altogether.

The camera—or perhaps just fate—panned out from the glossy brochure fantasy to something smaller, and infinitely less marketed: a sun-bleached café perched on a floating dock, its metal rails warm from the afternoon light. Below, an ocean of clouds stretched forever, slow currents rolling in golden waves. Cruises drifted lazily in the distance, birds flying about.

The air smelled faintly of salt as a parasol fluttered overhead. Somewhere, a drone waiter whirred softly by, chirping an automated “Enjoy your day under the twin suns!” before continuing its route.

Across the table, Castorice sipped from her glass, watching the horizon without much interest. The condensation slipped lazily down her drink, catching the light in miniature rainbows.

“Lovely day,” she said mildly.

Phainon didn’t move, cheek still pressed to the table. “Mm-hmm. Lovely.”

A long breeze drifted by, warm and patient, carrying with it the faint echo of the ad’s last jingle:

Elyon-7… Elyon-7… Elyon-7…

Somewhere out there, the perfect world kept spinning.

Here, two people were just trying to forget why they’d landed on it.

The ship had been grounded for “post-mission maintenance,” as Castorice so politely phrased it. In reality, it was more like being benched. The vessel hung suspended over Elyon-7’s stratosphere docks 2 hours from here, surrounded by a halo of repair drones and diagnostic lights flickering like lazy fireflies. Its engines had purred at idle—recovering, recalibrating, and, according to Castorice, “learning to breathe again.”

“Breathe,” she’d said.

Which, somehow, had turned into “sit in public and pretend everything’s perfectly fine.”

So now Phainon sat across from her at a café suspended on a glass terrace above the clouds. The deck was built around a sprawling synth-tree, its silver leaves rustling in the filtered wind that carried a faint trace of burnt sugar from somewhere around.

Phainon pretended to study the view, then pretended harder not to. His eyes eventually landed on Castorice’s drink—some fancy mineral brew, crystalline blue and faintly shimmering. It sat untouched, perfect, and cold.

He coughed once. Adjusted his sleeve. Coughed again.

“Well,” he said finally, voice a little too casual to be accidental. “What good weather we’re having today, huh?”

Castorice’s gaze lifted from her cup with the slow precision of a targeting system.

“Are we going to address the elephant in the room?”

Phainon looked around, scanning the surrounding tables. A family of tourists, two dockhands, a server drone. No pachyderms.

“I don’t see any elephants,” he said.

Castorice exhaled, set her glass down, and leaned forward, sunlight glinting off the insignia on her uniform. “You know what I mean, Phainon.”

He pursed his lips, tilting his head like a confused puppy. “Elaborate, please.”

Something twitched in her eye. Subtle, restrained, but deadly—a small rebellion in the face of her usual composure. Sweet, measured, endlessly patient Castorice looked seconds away from discovering a new form of homicide.

Phainon, entirely unaware—or pretending spectacularly well—leaned back, his chair creaking under the lazy stretch.

If patience was a virtue, then Castorice was rapidly ascending toward sainthood.

“You know how a Kremnoan Commander—a Commander, Phainon—is currently resting back on our ship, dead asleep, and from what you’ve told me, has forgotten all his memories?”

Phainon’s smile faltered like a ship losing power. “…Vaguely.”

Her mind flickered back, unbidden. The wreckage had still been burning when she arrived—red dust in the air, metal warped into grotesque shapes. The silence had that eerie, hollow kind that only came after chaos, when even sound was too stunned to return. And then, through the haze—him.

Phainon.

Dragging himself through the debris, shirt torn, one arm hanging uselessly at his side, and in the other—someone.

A man. Insignia glinting faintly beneath the grime.

A Kremnoan Commander.

“Imagine my surprise,” she murmured now, mostly to herself.

Castorice’s brow creased. “You could’ve said literally anything else.”

He raised a hand. “Could’ve. Didn’t.”

Phainon exhaled, slouching back into his chair, his expression somewhere between guilt and stubborn pride.

“Phainon.”

The word landed softly, but it stopped him anyway.

Phainon said, quieter this time, “They’re not gone.”

She didn’t agree—but she didn’t deny him that hope, either.

Her silence was mercy.

Her brows lifted slightly, a warning and an invitation all in one. He didn’t immediately answer.
