The avatar flickered once. “We—uh—we are… stable,” Trinnon said, voice stuttering the way it always did when she was nervous. “Reboot sequence is seventy-eight percent complete. Tribbie and Trianne are… um… coming online shortly.”

“Good, good,” Phainon said, leaning back, clearly pleased. “Tell them I’ll run a calibration check myself once—”

Trinnon’s voice glitched, a flicker slicing through her words. “Captain— there’s—uh—we—uh—”

He frowned, setting his glass down. “Trinnon, slow down. What’s wrong?”

The hologram jittered once, the signal stabilizing just long enough for her voice to come through clear—louder, higher than he’d ever heard it.

“It’s that man!” she blurted. “He’s awake!”

For a heartbeat, the words didn’t register.

Then, simultaneously, both Phainon and Castorice froze.

His drink hung halfway to his mouth. Her hand hovered midair over the call.

And then—perfectly synchronized—they both choked.

“Shit.”

Well, after traumatizing a poor skycrawler pilot into driving three-quarters of the way there—and then running the last quarter on foot because somehow, somehow, the damn thing decided to sputter, spin, and die mid-flight—they made it back to the ship in record timing.

It wasn’t a graceful return. Castorice looked like she’d been personally hunted by a windstorm, one boot scuffed, the other half undone. Phainon’s coat had caught on something during the sprint, one sleeve torn clean off and dangling from his wrist by a few loose threads. He didn’t even bother trying to fix it.

They stood there for a moment, panting, staring up at the gleaming hull— their ship, their beautiful, broken, half-disassembled ship—as if sheer willpower could make the hangar doors open.

The universe, unfortunately, remained unimpressed.

The docking platform was a disaster zone of repair drones, stray welding sparks, and people shouting orders over the clamor of machinery. The hull plating was half-peeled open for diagnostics, the engine core sat exposed like a beating heart mid-surgery, and the ship’s comm line repeated its cheerful automated message on loop:

“Maintenance in progress. Access restricted. Please contact your

assigned dock officer—”

Castorice pinched the bridge of her nose, muttered something unprintable, then snapped, “Just open the damn hangar.”

There was a stunned pause. Then, against all odds, the system chirped an affirmative tone. The massive doors rumbled open.

Phainon blinked. “You know, one of these days, you’re going to yell at the wrong AI and it’s going to actually explode.”

She didn’t even dignify that with a response.

A barely restrained argument followed—with two engineers, a flustered dock manager, and one very nervous safety officer—before they were finally granted entry. By the time the airlock hissed open, both of them were out of breath again, leaning forward, hands braced on their knees.

“Next time,” Phainon said between breaths, “we’re requisitioning a proper transport. Preferably one that doesn’t fall apart when it sees a storm cloud.”

Castorice let out a sharp exhale that was halfway between a laugh and a groan. “Next time, you’re flying.”

“That’s the plan,” he muttered, straightening.

Her eyes swept the dim corridor ahead—wires hanging from the ceiling, the hum of auxiliary systems running low. She adjusted her gloves, already shifting back into that crisp tone of hers. “We’ll cover more ground if we split. You take the lower decks; I’ll sweep the maintenance wing.”

“Fine,” Phainon said, already moving before she’d finished. He didn’t even wait for the airlock to finish decompressing before slipping through, the metallic hiss fading behind him as he disappeared into the corridor’s low light.

Castorice watched him go, one brow twitching.

“Kephale help me,” she muttered, before setting off in the opposite direction.

What a great day it was shaping up to be.

Phainon took the lower decks, his boots echoing against the grating with a rhythm too steady to match his thoughts. The air down here was cooler. It should’ve been grounding. It wasn’t.

He tried not to think about why Trinnon had said. Tried not to replay that trembling cry over and over in his head: He’s awake.

The words wouldn’t leave him.

He should’ve felt relief. That’s what any sane person would feel—someone survived, someone woke up, end of story. But instead, there was this awful tangle sitting under his ribs.

Because if he was being honest to himself, Mydeimos had never liked him much. Barely tolerated him on the best of days. And still, Phainon had followed him—too closely, too often. He told himself it was because Mydei was brilliant, indispensable, someone the others relied on. But that wasn’t the whole story, was it?

His flashlight flicked across the corridor walls, light catching on wires and dust motes.

What the hell was he supposed to say to him now? “Sorry about that, Mydei, I panicked”? As if Mydeimos wouldn’t immediately see through it. He could already picture it: that silent, assessing look, the faint twitch of disdain at the corner of his mouth before he turned away again.

And yet, the idea of facing that expression again made Phainon’s chest feel tight.

He stopped at a sealed door, the handle cold beneath his glove. Nothing but noise from the internal machines.

He sighed and moved on.

“Nothing… empty… empty…”

Every door he passed hissed open at his approach, and every time it revealed the same thing. Untouched consoles. Half-sealed storage crates. Air so still it might’ve been frozen.

He frowned.

His footsteps thudded evenly against the deck plating, the rhythm steady enough to keep him anchored.

He’s awake.

He pressed the heel of his hand to his brow. Not thinking about it.

Noise flared softly in his ear. Castorice’s voice followed, clear and clipped. “No signs of forced entry here either. Are you sure Trinnon’s readings are accurate?”

“Trinnon doesn’t panic for no reason,” Phainon said. He crouched to check a maintenance panel. “If she said something’s here, something’s here.”

“Could be a feedback loop. The sensors have been touchy since the refit—”

“Castorice.” His tone flattened. “You heard her voice.”

A pause. Then, softer, “…Yeah. I did.”

He stood, scanning the ceiling ducts, the ventilation grid. “Just stay alert. If she’s right, maybe he’d already left—”

A sound sliced through the comm.

High-pitched. Distant. The kind of sound that didn’t belong anywhere near a ship.

Castorice’s voice vanished. All that remained was that noise—half mechanical, half human. Then it came again, higher, clearer this time.

A scream.

Trinnon’s.

Phainon froze. The beam of his light jerked upward, as if he could pinpoint it through sheer will alone. The sound had come from above—Castorice’s level.

“Castorice?” he barked, already turning toward the nearest liftwell. “Trinnon?”

The comm spat. Then a voice—small, broken, barely coherent.

“W-we—we didn’t mean to—he just—!”

The line cut.

Silence.

Phainon’s pulse dropped into his stomach, cold and heavy. Then came the heat—the rush that overtook everything else.

“Fuck.”

He broke into a run.

The corridor became a blur of flickering amber lights and the pounding in his chest. He nearly slipped on the grated floor as he rounded the first corner, one hand catching the wall for balance, the other fumbling for his comm controls—dead, nothing but whir noise.

He kept running.

“Trinnon! Castorice!” His voice bounced uselessly off the metal bulkheads. No answer.

He took the ladder two rungs at a time, his hands burning against the cold bars.

“Come on, come on…”

The ship groaned around him as he reached the next deck, the lights stuttering overhead. Somewhere ahead, a muffled thud. Then another. Fabric tearing. The scrape of boots against the floor.

He broke into a sprint again, lungs burning. Each step echoed louder until the hallway funneled into a narrower passage choked with fallen debris. He shoved it aside, heartbeat rising to match the rhythmic clang, clang, clang ahead of him.

“Castorice!” he shouted, rounding the final bend.

And then something slammed into him.

The impact hit hard enough to knock the air from his lungs. The world snapped sideways. They hit the grating floor with a crash that sent pain spiraling through his ribs. His flashlight spun away, clattering across the metal.

Instinct took over. He twisted, grabbing at his attacker’s arm, his other hand snapping up to brace against their shoulder. They were strong—shockingly strong. His grip slipped as a forearm pressed down on his chest, pinning him.

“Get—off—” He braced his knee, ready to throw his weight—

Then he saw them.

Eyes.

Brilliant, burning gold that caught the flickering light and turned it molten.

Everything froze. The noise, the pain, the air in his lungs—gone, replaced by that single, impossible detail.

Those eyes.

He knew them.

He’d memorized them once, traced their light like something sacred.

The figure above him hovered in the half-light, breath ragged, expression unreadable—but those eyes blazed through everything else. Familiar. Furious. Alive.

“My—” The name stuck in his throat, barely forming.

The person’s grip faltered for half a second—enough time for the recognition to cut both ways.

Mydeimos.

The word slammed through Phainon’s mind with all the weight of the world.

And the look Mydei gave him said everything before either of them could speak.

For a moment, everything hung still.

Then, from above him, a voice—rough, scraped raw.

“Where am I.”

The sound didn’t even seem human at first. It was low, uneven, guttural, like he was teaching his lungs to work again. The words dragged as though they didn’t fit right in his mouth.

Phainon’s pulse tripped. He didn’t answer. Couldn’t.

Mydei’s chest rose and fell in shallow bursts, muscles tight, every inch of him strung like a live wire. His hair was damp, plastered unevenly against his forehead; his medbay clothes hung half-open, a patchwork of torn seams and clinging fabric. Bare feet against the grating, half-wrapped wrists. He looked more animal than man—sharp, cornered, dangerous.

And yet, somehow, painfully familiar.

“Mydei…” Phainon’s voice barely came out.

The reaction was immediate. Mydei’s head snapped toward him, teeth still bared, gold eyes flashing under the cold lights. For a heartbeat, Phainon swore Mydei was gonna kill him.

Footsteps echoed in the distance—quick, urgent—but Mydei didn’t turn. He didn’t even glance that way. His entire focus stayed pinned on Phainon, like nothing else existed outside the space between them.

Something flickered in his expression—too quick to place. Not recognition exactly, but something that almost resembled it. His snarl faltered, confusion creeping in where fury had been.

“It’s… you.”

The words weren’t a question.

Phainon’s throat tightened. He stared up at him, caught somewhere between shock and blankly staring.

Mydei blinked slowly, as though trying to match memory to face. His voice came softer now, uncertain.

“I remember your face.”

That single line hit harder than any strike could’ve. It cracked through the tension.

And then—

“Phainon!”

The spell shattered.

Castorice rounded the corner with Trinnon clinging behind her, both looking like they’d sprinted the whole way. Her scythe was already drawn, energy flaring down the curved blade. One glance at the scene was enough to have her aiming squarely.

“Step back—he’s unstable—”

Trinnon peeked from behind her shoulder, holo flickering faintly. “L-leave Snowy alone!”

Mydei didn’t even look at them. His attention barely wavered from Phainon, though the growl in his throat rumbled again—warning.

Phainon swallowed, forcing his voice out. “He’s not going to hurt me.”

“Phainon.” Castorice’s tone sharpened. “Look at him. He nearly broke my —”

“He’s not going to hurt me,” he said again. Quieter. But firmer.

Something in his tone made Castorice pause mid-breath. Even Trinnon went silent, her projection dimming slightly.

Mydei’s breathing slowed. His hand—still gripping Phainon’s wrist— loosened just enough to not bruise. The readiness didn’t leave his body, but the hostility did.

“…You helped me escape those crystals,” Mydei murmured after a beat.

Phainon’s breath caught. “You… remember that?”

(What he didn’t say was—is that all?)

Mydei didn’t answer.

Castorice finally exhaled, lowering the weapon a fraction. “Phainon. Either get him to medbay or get out of his reach, I’m not asking twice.”

Trinnon, flickering nervously beside her, whispered, “We said he needed more time before waking, his vitals weren’t even—um—stable—”

Phainon rose slowly, careful not to spook the man in front of him. Mydei’s grip adjusted instinctively, fingers catching his wrist to steady him.

The touch made something electric crawl under Phainon’s skin. Too much. Too easy to want.

“Come on,” he said quietly, his tone gentler than he meant. “We’re not doing this here.”

Mydei hesitated, but he didn’t resist. He followed when Phainon tugged, the faintest pull enough to guide him forward.

Their steps fell into sync without meaning to. Mydei’s eyes stayed fixed on him, studying, remembering—or trying to.

It was the first time Phainon had seen Mydei look at him without hatred. Without the familiar, cold disgust.

Something inside him twisted. Maybe guilt. Maybe something worse. His fingers tightened slightly around Mydei’s wrist before he realized it, before he could stop himself. He didn’t let go.

Neither did Mydei.

They passed under the low hum of the lights and out of sight, their voices fading into the soft rumble of the ship.

Castorice stood there long after they disappeared, scythe still in hand, expression torn

Beside her, Trinnon’s projection flickered again.

Castorice finally sighed and pinched the bridge of her nose.

“…We’re going to need more containment fields.”

Trinnon blinked. “Uh… more than one?”

“Way more than one,” Castorice muttered, watching the corridor’s empty stretch where they’d gone. “And maybe a leash while we’re at it.”

Phainon had all but dragged Mydei with him.

The medbay’s light had been too harsh so he’d overridden the controls and dimmed it until the glow softened to something bearable. It wasn’t cozy, but it was private.

Mydei sat on the edge of the narrow bench, posture coiled. Even cleaned up he carried the look of someone halfway between a briefing and a battlefield. His shoulders stayed squared, his legs planted, as if ready to spring for the nearest exit.

Phainon leaned against the opposite counter, pretending to look casual. He wasn’t.

He’d told himself he’d brought Mydei here to keep him calm. Truth was, he didn’t want anyone else near him.

For a while, neither spoke. The silence stretched taut.

Then, Mydei broke it.

“How long was I out?”

Phainon looked up from the console. “2  weeks.”

That earned a flicker of surprise. “That long?”

“Your body took time to stabilize,” Phainon said. “Those crystal fields— you weren’t exactly meant to breathe them.”

“You make it sound like I was a lab rat.”

Phainon almost smiled. “You were closer to a cardiac event, actually. For me.”

That got him a faint eye-roll—progress, technically.

Mydei’s gaze drifted to the stars outside, reflecting faintly in the dark glass. Then, quieter:

“Where is this place?”

Phainon didn’t miss the suspicion in his voice. “Still in neutral orbit,” he said quickly.

That made Mydei’s head turn. His eyes narrowed. “Neutral orbit,” he repeated, like he was testing the phrase for lies. “You expect me to believe that?”

“It’s safer this way,” Phainon said.

“For who?”

Phainon kept his face still. “For both of us.”

A pause. Mydei studied him for a long moment, unreadable. Then his voice dropped, softer, but edged. “Who else made it out?”

Phainon felt the faintest spike in his pulse. He should’ve seen that coming.

He shifted his weight, leaning back on the counter, fingers tapping against metal to stall. “A few,” he said. “The ones stationed along the western ridge when it happened. Command didn’t hold.”

Mydei’s jaw flexed. “Names.”

He hesitated. “You should rest before—”

“Names,” Mydei repeated.

Phainon didn’t flinch. “…Ptolemy. Peucesta.”

It came out too fast.

He prayed Mydei wouldn’t notice.

He had no idea if either of them had survived—he was gambling, constructing a lie from memory fragments and educated guesses.

“That’s it?”

Phainon forced his tone into something neutral. “The others didn’t make it.”

Mydei’s expression didn’t change, but something in his posture did—a small tightening at the shoulders. “You’re saying I was the lucky one.”

“You are,” Phainon said.

“I don’t feel lucky.”

He wanted to say, you should, but that wasn’t the kind of thing that helped. He wanted to tell him how close it had been, how he’d nearly stopped died, how Phainon had carried him out of the collapse with hands shaking so badly the suit telemetry thought he was injured. But none of that would make sense to Mydei now—not when he still thought they’d defected together.

So instead, he said, “You’re alive. That’s what matters.”

Mydei shot him a look, unimpressed. “You talk like a medic.”

“I’ve had practice.”

“Right.”

The air eased slightly, if only by a fraction. Mydei’s shoulders lowered a little, some of the tension bleeding out, though his eyes never stopped moving. He was cataloguing exits again. Counting. Always counting.

“You don’t have to stay on guard,” Phainon said quietly.

“I don’t trust empty rooms.”

Phainon smiled faintly. “Didn’t think you trusted me either.”

Mydei’s eyes flicked toward him. “Should I?”

Phainon’s throat tightened.

“You trusted me enough to follow me out,” Phainon said instead, carefully wording his speech.

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No,” Phainon murmured, almost to himself. “It’s not.”

Mydei looked away, muttering something he probably didn’t intend to be heard.

Phainon caught himself smiling again, helplessly. He didn’t even know why. Maybe it was the absurdity of it—the fact that he was sitting here, spinning stories to the one person least likely to believe them. Maybe it was the way Mydei’s presence still pulled at him, magnetic, even through layers of suspicion.

He was the one with the upper hand, yet Mydei still made him feel like the one being interrogated.

He tried to keep calm.

And when Mydei turned slightly, profile caught in the half-light of the lab, eyes glinting like the edges of a blade, Phainon could only think one thing:

He was in so much trouble.

When Mydei stood, it should’ve been a simple motion—just standing. But Phainon’s attention caught on it anyway.

Something about it was wrong. The shift of weight, the subtle overcorrection when Mydei straightened, the way his stride carried a weightlessness that didn’t belong to his frame. His balance looked practiced, not natural, like someone walking across unstable ground and pretending not to notice.

Phainon watched him cross the small space, that lightness in his steps setting off an itch at the base of his thoughts until realization slotted neatly into place.

The gravity.

It was too low.

He’d left it calibrated to Okheman standards—comfortable for him, a little over one standard gravity, easy on the joints. But Kremnoans were different creatures entirely. They grew under pressure, shaped by denser air and heavier atmospheres, by planets that pulled harder. The weight of their world lingered in their bones.

And here Mydei was, moving as though the air had thinned to glass.

Phainon’s fingers twitched toward the console. The correction was small, just a few adjustments keyed in manually, but the room responded instantly —metal groaning faintly as the artificial field deepened. The hum of the air changed pitch; the floor seemed to reach up, claiming them both.

1.8g.

He didn’t say anything. He just watched.

Mydei steadied. It happened so naturally that Phainon almost missed it—the small shift in stance, the way his shoulders evened, the fine tension bleeding out of his neck. Even his breathing changed: slower, heavier, grounded again.

And Phainon, damn him, felt a small tug of satisfaction. The sight of Mydei at ease—just a fraction, but enough—felt undeservedly like a victory.

Then Mydei’s gaze cut toward him.

“You changed it.”

Phainon didn’t look up from the console, voice perfectly mild. “You were moving lighter than usual.”

Mydei studied him, one brow raised. “You pay attention.”

Phainon’s mouth curved, more reflex than smile. “Bad habit.”

That earned him a look—part scrutiny, part thought. Mydei turned back to the viewport and sat again, the faint creak of the bench filling the space where a thank-you might have gone.

Phainon shifted his thoughts.

That subtle lightness from before—the way Mydei had been disoriented, his questions clipped and suspicious—it wasn’t just exhaustion, most likely. The crystalline exposure, the neural interference, the fact that he still didn’t remember half of what had happened—Phainon couldn’t just leave it at that.

And then it hit him.

Hyacine.

He could take Mydei to her. She’d know what to do, how to run diagnostics properly, maybe even patch the fragments left behind in his memory. If anyone could help, it was her.

The thought crystallized so abruptly that he froze mid-motion, staring past the viewport like he was watching something only he could see.

Of course. The Grove of Epiphany. He’d have to cross through it to reach Hyacine’s outpost. Not ideal—but better than waiting here and doing nothing.

He must have gone quiet too long, because Mydei turned, eyes narrowing faintly.

“What?”

Phainon blinked, realizing how still he’d gone, the edges of his expression probably betraying more than he meant. He coughed, adjusting his collar as if that could cover it. “Nothing. Just—remembered something important.” His tone softened into that easy drawl again, practiced and harmless. “I need to make a call. I’ll be right back.”

Mydei leaned back, still watching him, one hand resting loosely on his knee. “Then why are you still here?”

Phainon snorted quietly, a huff of breath that almost became a laugh. “Fair question.”

He pushed off the wall, steps steady now under the heavier pull of gravity, and started toward the door. The faint smile ghosted back for a second as he keyed it open.

He didn’t look back, but he could feel Mydei’s gaze following him— measuring, and full of questions that hadn’t yet found words.

And that was fine.

He had enough of his own.

Now he just needed to convince Castorice that dragging a half-amnesiac Kremnoan through the Grove wasn’t completely insane.

God help him.

He scrubbed a hand through his hair, sighed, then keyed in the frequency he wasn’t supposed to use outside emergency channels.

The interface flickered to life, stabilizing into the familiar pale light of Castorice’s projection. She was still somewhere on the upper decks, uniform jacket half unzipped, the glow of her displays painting faint blue rings under her eyes. Calm, professional, maddeningly composed—her gaze always made him feel like a particularly unwashed stray someone had decided to let in out of pity.

He grinned anyway, leaning a shoulder against the wall. “Heyyyyy, Castorice. Fancy seeing you here. Lovely signal weather we’re having, yeah?”

Her gaze didn’t even twitch. “You’re planning to move him, aren’t you?”

The grin froze halfway. “…You’re supposed to be running diagnostics.”

“I did,” she said simply, not breaking eye contact. “And while you were playing babysitter, I prepped two ships.”

He blinked. “Two?”

“We’re splitting.”

Phainon hesitated, caught between surprise and suspicion. “…Well. That was easier than expected.”

“Don’t get comfortable,” she said, glancing toward a side console. “The Council deployed a new trace pulse an hour ago. They’re sweeping for surviving Okhemans.”

“Of course they are,” he muttered. “Wouldn’t want to let a few unsupervised disasters slip through.”

Castorice ignored that. “I don’t mind being found,” she continued quietly. “You, however, should go.”

He frowned, folding his arms. “You’re volunteering me? Why not send—”

“Because if they find me,” she interrupted, “they’ll take me back for review and reclassification, and I’ll be fine. If they find you, same thing. But if they find him…” She paused, her voice softening without losing clarity. “You know what they’ll do, Phainon. They’ll dissect what he knows. Maybe even for no reason.”

Phainon looked away, jaw flexing. “You’re assuming a lot.”

“I’m assuming the obvious,” she said pointedly, her hands moving off-screen as if finalizing the transfer before he could argue. “If we move together, we’ll amplify the trace signature. Split, we’re noise. Two smaller blips are harder to lock than one larger one.”

“Smart,” he said after a beat. “Paranoid, but smart.”

“Both keep you alive,” she replied, faint amusement ghosting in her tone.

He leaned back, watching her. “You’re sure this pulse isn’t a decoy?”

“No.” She hesitated briefly before adding, “But you’re taking him to Hyacine, aren’t you?”

“…You shouldn’t assume.”

“I don’t have to.” Her tone gentled. “It’s the logical next step. Hyacine’s work with crystalline recovery makes her the only one who might help him. You wouldn’t sit still knowing that.”

Phainon exhaled, a sound somewhere between a sigh and a laugh. “You make it sound like a bad weakness.”

“It is,” she said, smiling faintly now. “But it’s the right one this time.”

He looked down at the deck, then back up at her. “You’re letting me go.”

“I’m not letting you. I’m clearing the way before you do something reckless without backup.” She reached for another control panel. “Take the secondary vessel. It’s fueled and warp-stable for short runs. Just—don’t get caught again.”

He tilted his head, lips twitching. “You say that like it’s something I plan for.”

“Phainon,” she said softly, cutting through his grin. “Be careful. Please.”

He smiled again, smaller this time. “Always am.”

The line flickered and went dark.

It wasn’t so bad.

Phainon stood there for a long minute, fingers still resting against the comm panel, replaying the look on her face.

Separate ships. Separate logs. Separate records.

No supervision.

No witnesses if Mydei got his memories back and decided to strangle him.

And still, he couldn’t not go.

Damn it.

With a slow breath, he pushed off the wall and headed back toward the medbay.

The door hissed open to reveal Mydei exactly where he’d left him—sitting with that practiced stillness that wasn’t quite rest, gaze fixed on the window’s edge. The faint starlight framed his profile in silver and shadow. When Phainon stepped in, those sharp eyes shifted toward him instantly.

Phainon gave a faint, lopsided smile. “Well,” he said lightly, “how do you feel about a space trip?”

Mydei’s brow rose. “That depends. You planning to tell me where we’re going this time?”

He considered, then flashed a toothy smile. “Would you believe me if I said it’s somewhere quiet?”

“No.”

Phainon chuckled under his breath. “Didn’t think so.”

He moved to the viewport beside him, the hum of the engines resonating beneath his boots. Out there, the stars stretched endless and patient, like they knew just how small this was in comparison—and still, how much it mattered.

They were really doing this.

And for better or worse, there was no one left to stop him.

That was it.

Today, he was going to talk to Mydei.

Properly, this time. Not the awkward little check-ins, not the occasional muttered “morning,” not the static-filled silence between open comms pretending to be coincidence. Actual words. A conversation. Maybe even something resembling connection.

True to her word, Castorice had prepped their departure fast—two ships ready before dawn, stealth-mode locked, all traces scrubbed clean. They’d barely made orbit before she was found, but by then, they were already too far to recall. Phainon remembered reading the report, smiling faintly to himself. Trust her to survive chaos like it was a hobby.

He’d gone right back to watching the feed after that.

It was supposed to be a precaution—monitoring vitals, keeping tabs, being responsible. That was all. Except, somewhere around the fourth night, it wasn’t about data anymore. He kept the feed open longer than he should’ve, checking if Mydei was still awake, if he’d started pacing again, if his breathing changed when the ship shifted into sublight drift. The rhythm of it had become… familiar. Steadying, almost.

Mydei, for his part, had been restless from the start. He’d spent days circling his cabin like a storm caught in a jar. Sometimes he’d pause right in front of the active feed, eyes unreadable, the faint hum of his breath carrying across the open comm. Phainon never mentioned it. Neither did he.

By now, three days into the flight toward the Grove, the silence had started to ache.

So Phainon decided to break it—forcefully, if necessary.

Which was why he stood now in Mydei’s doorway, smile just shy of manic, holding a tray of what could only be described as edible despair.

“Dinner’s served~” he declared, sing-song, stepping in before Mydei could object.

The other man barely glanced up from the viewport. His eyes flicked to the tray, then to Phainon, then back again, unimpressed. “That’s not dinner.”

“Technically,” Phainon said cheerfully, setting it down, “it qualifies. Nutritional. Caloric. Gray.”

He leaned in slightly, lowering his voice like he was sharing a secret. “Do you always scowl when food’s good, or am I just that talented?”

Mydei—as expected—scowled. Too predictable, really. “You talk too much.”

“Flattery will get you everywhere,” Phainon sighed, dragging a chair over and plopping down beside him.

Mydei poked the gel with the spoon like he was checking if it might bite. When it didn’t, he gave a reluctant hum and took a small bite, wincing at the taste. Phainon watched with all the intensity of someone observing art in motion.

“You know,” he began conversationally, “I would cook if I could, but Cyrene says—oh, that’s my sister, by the way—says no one wants to eat salads every day. Which is ridiculous, because salads are an art form. Crisp greens, balance, color—”

“Cyrene,” Mydei interrupted, tone flat.

Phainon blinked. “Yeah! Cyrene. My sister. How’d I never mention her?”

He leaned back, gesturing vaguely with his hands as if the story needed space. “She’s a menace, really. Smart as hell, mouthy as hell, thinks she’s the second coming of every engineer who’s ever existed. I once asked her to recalibrate the drone rotors, and she reprogrammed them to whistle songs instead. Whole hangar sounded like a haunted festival for a week.”

The faintest, quietest snort left Mydei.

Phainon noticed and smiled, bright and unguarded. “Exactly. You get it.”

He kept going without realizing he’d slipped into a softer cadence. “She’s working under Cipher now. Poor woman probably regrets ever agreeing to it. But Cyrene’s got this thing about her—she just… makes messes sound manageable. Like, even when she’s clearly about to burn down the lab, she’ll smile and say, ‘Don’t worry, I’ve got it.’ And somehow, you believe her.”

He paused, realizing how easily he’d gone off track. “Sorry. I tend to ramble when I start talking about her.”

Mydei tilted his head slightly, going silent. “Continue.”

Phainon froze for a heartbeat, unsure if he’d heard that right. “What, really?”

A faint nod.

He blinked, caught off guard by the sudden curiosity. The air between them felt suddenly closer, sharper somehow. He cleared his throat, trying to sound nonchalant. “Right, uh—well. She’s the only one who can get me to shut up, for starters. Sends me updates every week, mostly stupid jokes or photos of her projects. Or her cats. She keeps rescuing the ones that sneak into the labs, and I keep telling her she’s gonna get kicked out for it.”

A small laugh slipped out—real this time, soft around the edges. “She doesn’t listen, of course. Never has.”

He shifted, rubbing the back of his neck, then suddenly brightened. “Wait— hold on. I’ve got a picture of her somewhere.”

Without thinking, he scooted closer, their shoulders brushing as he scrolled through his teleslate. The contact was brief, accidental—but he felt it anyway. His breath hitched slightly before he found the photo.

“There.” He angled the slate toward Mydei, smiling. “That’s her. Look at her—tell me she’s not gorgeous.”

It was Cyrene, mid-laugh, pink hair catching the glow of the lab lights. A smear of green on her cheek, a half-tamed grin that looked like trouble and kindness at once.

Mydei leaned in slightly, his gaze flicking to the image. For a moment, neither spoke.

“She’s got that kind of look,” Phainon said quietly, a note of fondness threading through his voice. “Sharp but kind.”

He didn’t notice how close he’d gotten, or how his voice had dropped lower without meaning to. He didn’t notice, either, that Mydei’s eyes had shifted —away from the slate, to him.

Phainon only looked up when he heard a faint exhale beside him. Mydei’s expression was unreadable, but his reply came softer than before.

“…Yeah.”

Phainon beamed at that, easy and bright again, missing entirely the way Mydei’s gaze lingered a moment longer than it should’ve. “Knew it. She’d be thrilled you said so.”

And just like that, the tension broke—light, seamless, almost comfortable. Phainon leaned back, scrolling idly as he kept talking, warmth still coloring his tone.

He tapped a finger against the tray, the last hint of a smile lingering on his lips. He should’ve let the quiet stay—let the ease between them breathe— but silence, when it came to him, was a luxury he rarely allowed himself.

He turned, humming under his breath. “Say, Mydei,” he began, tone light but deliberate, “we’ve got a room that passes for a training deck onboard. Have you ever been there?”

Mydei looked up. “No.”

Phainon’s excitement spiked up suddenly, a duel with Mydei? Who wouldn’t be happy. “Then I’ll have to give you the tour sometime. Show you how Okheman tech actually behaves when you’re not threatening to dismantle it.” He leaned an elbow on the table, voice dipping to something closer. “I could even… reacquaint you with it. Properly, this time.”

Mydei blinked, faintly skeptical. “Properly?”

“Well, the first step is learning that our systems don’t respond to logic alone,” Phainon said, gesturing as though drawing circuitry in the air. “They read intent. They can tell when you’re irritated, or impatient, or trying too hard to hide either.” His smile turned slow. “You have to coax them a little. Like they’re listening.”

“That sounds inefficient,” Mydei replied, dry as ever.

“Maybe,” Phainon allowed. “But they’re honest about it. Most things that react to emotion are.”

A beat passed—soft, suspended—and Phainon found himself watching him too long. Mydei’s attention had drifted to the viewport again, the reflected starlight tracing faint silver along the line of his jaw. Something in the sight of it, calm and unaware, made Phainon want to keep talking just to see if he could draw another flicker of expression from him.

He leaned forward slightly, resting his chin in his palm. “You know,” he said, “you look better when you’re not trying so hard to be mysterious.”

That earned the smallest shift—the briefest flicker of eyes toward him, like surprise caught too late.

He almost smiled again, softer this time. “There it is. Don’t worry,” he added under his breath, “I promise I don’t bite. Not unless you try to override my calibration settings.”

Mydei exhaled a quiet, nearly imperceptible sound—half a scoff, half a laugh. It was fleeting, but real.

And then—

A vibration shuddered through the deck, faint but immediate. The air seemed to tighten.

Phainon straightened, every trace of teasing gone. “What was that?”

Before Mydei could answer, a low warning tone rippled overhead—subtle, but carrying the ship’s unmistakable hum of alert.

He was already on his feet. “Stay here,” he said, and this time there was nothing casual about his voice. The ship’s ambient lighting wavered with his pulse as he crossed to the control junction, teleslate already activating in his hand.

“C’mon…” He murmured to the ship, half command, half coaxing. Pain sensors whispered under his skin when he linked in—small stings that mirrored tension, grounding him in the Okheman vessel’s shared feedback loop.

The diagnostic data flowed fast, elegant, familiar. Everything seemed normal—except for one faint flicker at the edge of the schematic.

A trace of red. Subtle, too subtle, like infection woven into clean code. It pulsed once.

“What…” He zoomed in, eyes narrowing, fingers brushing across the interface. The anomaly didn’t react to direct input. He adjusted parameters, prodding gently at its edge—

And in the next instant, it vanished.

No alert, no trace, nothing. Just the ordinary grid of energy lines as if it had never been there.

The system chimed: All clear.

Phainon stayed there, hand hovering over the display, his reflection faint in the glass.

He didn’t know what that was.

He didn’t know why it had felt alive.

And he definitely didn’t see the faint, unsettled color that had touched Mydei’s face when he’d bolted from the room.

VESSEL STATUS: IN TRANSIT—Estimated Arrival at the Grove: 72 Hours Crew Activity Log: Stable. No further anomalies detected.

At least, that’s what the ship kept saying.

Phainon had learned to stop trusting the ship’s tone after day one—it had the smugness of someone who knew it was smarter than him. But it wasn’t wrong. It had been three days since that flicker in the system, three days since the strange pulse that had crawled under his skin and refused to leave his mind.

And in that time, he’d accomplished something arguably more miraculous than stabilizing a ship’s code:

He’d gotten Mydei to talk to him.

It had started small. A quiet response here, a nod that lingered a moment too long, a question that wasn’t strictly necessary. Phainon would call that communication. Hell, he’d call it a breakthrough.

And now—well, now he had a plan. A bold, brilliant, slightly reckless plan.

Okheman tech training.

Educational, productive, and, best of all, conveniently hands-on.

Which was why he currently found himself dragging a very unwilling, very disheveled Mydei down one of the glowing corridors toward the ship’s training deck.

“Come on,” Phainon was saying as they walked, grin audible in his voice. “You’ll like this one, I promise. No chance of getting electrocuted unless you really try.”

Mydei didn’t answer, though he didn’t pull away either. His hair was uncharacteristically messy, the soft edges of his composure frayed just enough to make Phainon’s brain short-circuit for entirely unrelated reasons.

He’d looked… docile, earlier. That was the word. Like a cat too tired to fight being carried, tail twitching but otherwise resigned.

Phainon definitely wasn’t going to admit how adorable that had been.

By the time they reached the deck, the air felt charged already. The space was broad, clean-lined, and dimly lit by the pulsing threads of Okheman circuitry tracing along the walls and floor—each pulse syncing faintly with the rhythm of whoever stood near.

Phainon stretched, cracking his neck with the easy confidence of someone who’d done this hundreds of times. Mydei stood beside the circular training interface, yawning, his eyes tracking the faint movement of light beneath the translucent floor.

“Alright,” Phainon began, rolling his shoulders. “We’ll start with resonance control. Nothing too intense. Just… feel for the hum in the current. Don’t overthink it—it’s like breathing. You let the tech match your rhythm, not the other way around.”

Mydei nodded once, wordless, and pressed his hand against the surface.

The lights flared obediently at first. Perfect symmetry. Perfect alignment. Then—

A sharp crack, followed by a burst of static light that made the air pulse.

Phainon didn’t even blink. A thin wisp of smoke curled upward from the interface.

“…”

He inhaled slowly, counted to three, and smiled. A perfectly composed, perfectly I-totally-meant-for-that-to-happen smile.

“Well,” he said brightly, clapping once. “Progress! You didn’t vaporize it this time.”

Mydei stepped back, his expression unreadable but the faintest trace of contrition flickering in his eyes.

Phainon tilted his head, amused. “Don’t tell me you actually feel bad for it. You’ll hurt the ship’s feelings.”

“I misjudged the output,” Mydei said quietly.

“You don’t say.”

There was the faintest twitch at the corner of Mydei’s mouth, there and gone in a heartbeat.

“Alright then,” he said, tone softening. “Let’s try again.”

They’d switched to resonance training after Mydei’s strength made short work of the more physical drills. In any other context, Phainon might’ve been… distracted by that. The way his hands fit against the equipment, the effortless tension in his arms—

He cleared his throat. Professionalism, yes. Focus.

Mydei’s gaze flicked toward him again, uncertain. Then, after a long beat, he nodded.

Huh. The bastard actually did feel bad.

How endearing.

Phainon motioned toward one of the auxiliary pedestals gleaming at the edge of the deck. “Alright, let’s try something a little different,” he said, tone pitched somewhere between challenge and charm. “Here—”

He picked up a sleek crystalline rod, translucent with veins of faint blue light pulsing just under the surface. “This,” he said, holding it up between them, “is a vein conduit. It regulates emotional output through resonance alignment.”

Mydei raised an eyebrow, arms crossed. “Emotional output,” he echoed.

“Yes,” Phainon replied, undeterred, holding it up like a holy relic. “Okheman tech reads feeling as data. If your focus slips, it mirrors that instability. Which is why I’m going to—” He made a vague gesture that could’ve meant anything. “Help you stabilize the flow.”

Mydei stared at him for a moment longer, as though weighing the risk of asking what that meant. Then, with the barest sigh, he extended his hand. “Fine.”

Phainon smiled—small, genuine, a little too pleased. “Atta boy.”

He stepped closer. Close enough for Mydei to feel the faint glitch that always seemed to follow him when he worked with tech—like the circuitry itself charged under his touch. “Here,” Phainon said, offering the conduit and guiding Mydei’s grip until both their hands overlapped along the smooth, humming surface.

Mydei’s fingers were steady but tense. “And now?”

“Now,” Phainon murmured, moving behind him, “we calibrate it.”

He positioned himself close—close enough that his chest nearly brushed Mydei’s back, his breath grazing the edge of his hair. There was no teasing in his tone when he spoke again, he was focused. “Don’t lock your wrist. Let it move. Feel for the pull in the current—”

The conduit flickered in response, the soft blue light trembling like a pulse.

“Better,” Phainon murmured. His voice dropped unconsciously. “You’re connecting. The conduit draws from both of us now—my signal balances yours. If either of us spike emotionally, it’ll throw the flow off.”

Mydei’s jaw flexed, but his focus didn’t waver. “Convenient,” he said, voice mellow, though it came out quieter than before.

Phainon smiled faintly. “It’s why I make such a good diplomat. Comes with built-in damage control.”

He adjusted his stance, one hand lifting slightly to hover over Mydei’s, fingertips brushing the back of his knuckles—not quite touch, but near enough that Mydei’s breath hitched before he caught it. “Alright,” Phainon said softly. “Steady. Let it resonate with you. Don’t force control—just let it learn you.”

For a few long moments, the hum of the conduit deepened, its glow spreading like veins of living light across its surface. Phainon could feel Mydei’s concentration sharpen, all that composed stillness drawn into a singular point of focus. He could almost see it—the way Mydei’s energy aligned.

Then, suddenly, the light brightened—no stutter, no flicker—just a clean, steady pulse that filled the space between them. The air hummed like a held breath.

Phainon blinked. “Well I’ll be damned.”

He eased back half a step, happy despite himself. “You actually did it.”

Mydei exhaled, lowering the conduit. The look on his face wasn’t defensive —it was earned. The faintest flush of pride crossed his features, gone almost as soon as it appeared.

Phainon laughed, delighted. “See? Natural talent. Should’ve known you’d show off once you got the hang of it.”

A corner of Mydei’s mouth curved into a small smile that caused Phainon’s chest to do something strange and unhelpful.

“These weapons,” Mydei said after a pause, tone thoughtful, “are difficult to hold.”

Phainon tilted his head. “Yeah?”

“They feel…” Mydei hesitated, searching for words. “Foreign. Like something that doesn’t want to fit.”

The smile faltered, just slightly. “Huh.”

Phainon forced an easy chuckle. “You’re not wrong. They were designed by a bunch of eccentric engineers who think ergonomics is a myth. You’ll get used to it.”

But even as he said it, something about Mydei’s words lingered—an itch just out of reach. Doesn’t want to fit.

He smiled again, softer this time, but the look in his eyes gave away the flicker of unease beneath.

Phainon watched him for a moment longer. Mydei still held the conduit with that same carefulness, the glow dimming to a faint pulse in his palm. There was something almost reverent about the way he regarded it— entirely absorbed.

It struck Phainon, suddenly and without warning, how foreign that sight was.

Had they ever even fought together? Not as in training—but fought. Shoulder to shoulder. He couldn’t recall. He remembered the way Mydei moved through a room, yes, the authority that made people part before him, but not the way he fought. Not truly.

The only image that surfaced was fragmented—a flash of light, a shout, the edge of claws slicing through smoke. Mydei, incandescent and terrifying, cutting through the dark like he’d been born to it. Beautiful. Blazing. Untouchable.

And Phainon, idiot that he was, had been watching him even then.

The memory tugged at him like wired under his skin. Huh, he thought. I wonder if—

He stopped. Then his lips curved, the kind of slow, dangerous smile that never meant anything good.

“Well,” he said suddenly, stepping back into Mydei’s line of sight, “I have an idea.”

Mydei blinked, wary. “That usually means trouble.”

“You wound me,” Phainon said, already swiping a hand through the air to call up the holographic weapon matrix. The grid hummed to life, geometric light tracing itself into being until a greatsword solidified in his hand— sleek metal, black-veined with pale gold light.

He twirled it once, easy and fluid. “Meet Dawnmaker. My personal weapon.”

Before Mydei could respond, Phainon tossed it lightly toward him. The blade hummed midair, and Mydei caught it without looking, the weight settling into his palm like it belonged there.

“Wanna have a quick spar?” Phainon asked. “Don’t worry, I don’t bite.”

The look Mydei gave him was unamused, but Phainon caught the faintest smirk forming on his mouth. Even without his memories, of course he was bloodthirsty. “You bite,” Mydei said pointedly.

Phainon spread his hands. “Only when provoked.”

Mydei exhaled softly through his nose—half sigh, half reluctant amusement —and looked down at the sword. The weapon’s light reflected against his eyes, gold against blue, and for just a moment, he looked… conflicted.

Phainon tilted his head. The Kremnoans had a saying: You don’t know someone until you’ve fought them. For them, sparring wasn’t aggression—it was intimacy. A communion of will. The first time Phainon had learned that, he’d laughed. Now, watching Mydei trace the edge of Dawnmaker with gloved fingers, he wondered if there was something in him that missed it.

He grimaced inwardly. Gods, Phainon, you’re pathetic.

Still, the thought wouldn’t quite leave him. He doubted Mydei remembered a single Kremnoan custom after the amnesia—he doubted he remembered Phainon, for that matter—but still, the temptation to see what was left, what instincts lingered, burned bright.

Besides, what harm could it do? Mydei might have been a legend but that was before the memory loss. Phainon doubted the old edge still lingered.

Right?

He forced his focus back to the moment. “You use that,” he said, nodding toward Dawnmaker. “I’ll grab something less intimidating. Wouldn’t want to bruise your ego and your ribs.”

He turned and reached for one of the practice blades hanging nearby— lighter, shorter, with dull-edged lines glowing faintly down the fuller. He spun it once in his palm, the motion smooth, practiced.

When he turned back, Mydei was still studying him. Not the sword, surprisingly.

Phainon’s theatrically sighed. “Oh come on,” he said lightly, stepping onto the sparring deck as the floor flared alive with containment lines of pale blue. “It’ll be good for you. Builds character.”

There was a pause, long enough for Phainon to start wondering if he’d pushed too far—then, slowly, Mydei nodded once.

That single nod hit harder than any yes.

Phainon felt the shift immediately—the air thickening, the faint hum of the deck responding to their movement, calibrating for combat mode. He rolled his shoulders, raised his blade, and let the grin return.

“Alright,” he said, eyes glinting. “Don’t worry. I’ll go easy on you.”

A dry voice replied, “I’d rather you didn’t.”

Phainon blinked, startled—then laughed, delighted. “Oh, you’re serious. Even better.”

He took a step forward, blade angling up, a spark of anticipation running through him like lightning through wire.

“How hard can it be?”

Harder than he thought.

Phainon had gone in expecting something simple—light sparring, a touch of showmanship, maybe the kind of lazy back-and-forth where he could sneak in a few jokes and coax a reaction out of Mydei. Maybe even a smile. But the instant their blades crossed, all those expectations cracked clean through.

The first strike hit with surgical precision. Mydei met it like he’d been waiting for it—one smooth deflection, one seamless turn of the wrist, redirecting Dawnmaker’s weight as though it were nothing. The shock bit up through Phainon’s arm, nerve to shoulder, bright and sharp.

His eyes narrowed. “Oh,” he said lightly, shaking out his wrist. “So that’s how we’re playing this.”

No reply. Mydei simply reset his stance, his gaze gilled with intent. He moved with the kind of stillness that made Phainon’s instincts twitch— loose and unassuming, but ready to strike at any second.

Something in Phainon shifted. His casual swagger thinned into something sharper, his weight balancing just right on his heels. The lazy smile stayed, but now it was edged—an expression worn by someone who finally felt a challenge in his bones.

They circled, the sound of the training field pulsing faintly underfoot.

Phainon lunged first—testing, teasing, the kind of opening meant to draw out the other’s rhythm. Mydei met every swing cleanly, every parry precise.

Sparks of kinetic light spilled across the floor like molten stars.

“You sure you don’t remember any of this?” Phainon asked, laughing as their blades clashed again.

Mydei’s response came in that calm, even tone of his, not even a flicker of emotion. “My muscles do.”

That threw him off more than he wanted to admit. The rhythm of his strikes faltered for half a heartbeat before he laughed again—lower, breathier. “Unfair. I liked you better when you were bad at this.”

He barely caught the next blow. The pace had picked up without warning— each strike sharper, faster, heavier. Mydei didn’t waste a single motion. It wasn’t brute strength. Every movement said, I’ve done this a thousand times before.

Phainon couldn’t help it—his excitement increased. Gods, he’s reading me.

It wasn’t fear that shot through him—it was exhilaration. A rush he hadn’t felt in too long. He wasn’t used to being the one chased into focus, hell most the time he wasn’t even fighting. He was a diplomat for goodness sakes. Maybe it made him a freak, but that realization alone lit a fire in his chest.

So what if I’m a little freak? It’s not like anyone’s watching.

He feinted left, then snapped right. Mydei parried, slipped inside his guard, and—without warning—Phainon’s sword was gone, skittering across the polished floor.

“Oh, come on—”

Before he could blink, Mydei caught Dawnmaker mid-air, turned it effortlessly, and leveled it right at Phainon’s chest.

Phainon blinked once. Then he laughed. Full-bodied, delighted. “Oh, that’s beautiful.”

And then Mydei smirked. Small. Dangerous. The kind of expression that shouldn’t have been half as attractive as it was.

Phainon felt his pulse spike so fast it was ridiculous. Oh, I am so screwed.

He lunged for a nearby rack, grabbed another blade, and came back swinging before Mydei could get a word out. Their swords clashed again— fast, hot, relentless. The simulation lights above them flickered, struggling to keep pace with the energy output.

The deck vibrated faintly beneath their feet. Heat rolled off the air in waves.

Phainon ducked under a swing, clicking his tongue. “We’re breaking the training deck.”

“You’re the one heating it up,” Mydei replied without missing a beat.

“Oh, I’m the problem?” Phainon twisted around him, catching his sword against the other’s, forcing their faces close enough to share breath. “You’re not supposed to try and kill me!”

“You told me not to hold back.”

He exhaled through a laugh that came out closer to a groan. “Why am I into these types?” he muttered, almost to himself.

Mydei’s eyes flicked up at that, expression incredulous.

A twist, a parry, a push. Mydei caught his wrist mid-swing; Phainon turned the grip over, reversed it, and shoved him back. The sound of their blades locking was almost like music.

Gods, Phainon thought, no wonder the Kremnoans turned this into a courtship ritual.

Mydei came in low, forcing Phainon to pivot—fast, defensive. When their blades met again, they didn’t part. Shoulder to shoulder, each pushing for ground.

Phainon could feel the other’s breath brush his jaw, heat ghosting between them, both of them smiling like lunatics.

For a moment, the world narrowed to just that—breath, motion, heartbeat.

He looked up, and Mydei’s face was lit from below by the simulation field. Focused. Wild. Hair clinging to his forehead, eyes with the kind of focus that shouldn’t be possible mid-fight. Beautiful, in that dangerous, too-alive way.

Phainon almost forgot to move.

Their swords twisted together again, guards locking, and the momentum shoved them closer still—too close.

“…You’ve done this before,” Phainon murmured, voice rougher than he meant.

It wasn’t a question.

“…Maybe,” Mydei said.

He tensed, heartbeat catching—then smiled, that sharp, wicked kind of smile that promised trouble. “Then don’t hold back.”

The next strike came without hesitation.

Mydei didn’t.

Alas, Phainon would’ve loved to keep going. Gods knew he could have.

But the simulation’s temperature was peaking, the air sharp with electricity, and the glow from the floor panels flickered dangerously between them. So, they had to end it—preferably before the deck burned itself out.

One final exchange.

Phainon feinted left. Mydei mirrored perfectly, their swords flashing in mirrored arcs. Both twisted, stepped in, and stopped—an inch from each other’s necks.

Silence.

The energy fields dissolved in a quiet ripple, their blades dimming to silver and steel.

Phainon stayed there a moment, breath heaving, shoulders rising and falling with the aftershock. Mydei wasn’t much better off—his stance solid, but the fine tremor in his wrist gave him away. Sweat ran down the curve of his throat, caught in the line of his collarbone.

For a second, neither moved.

Then Mydei lowered his blade first. His voice a second later, edged with something between disbelief and amusement. “You call that easy?”

Phainon barked out a breath of a laugh, rubbing at his shoulder. “Harder than I thought.”

Mydei tilted his head. “You underestimate poorly.”

“Maybe I just like surprises.”

The answer earned him a look—flat at first, then curious. Mydei studied him for a moment too long, as if trying to read something behind his face. His gaze lingered on the line of Phainon’s jaw, the faint cut at his lip, the easy rise and fall of his breathing.

He didn’t look away when Phainon caught him staring.

Instead, Mydei asked quietly, “Does everything amuse you?”

“Only the good things.” Phainon said in response, deciding to forgo the taunts. “You’re one of them.”

For all his composure, Mydei faltered for half a heartbeat—eyes narrowing as though unsure whether to take it as mockery or not. The silence stretched.

Finally, he huffed out something like a laugh, barely audible. “You talk too much.”

“And yet you’re still standing here.”

That earned him the faintest smirk. Mydei looked away, brushing damp hair out of his face with the back of his wrist. “You fight like you mean it.”

“Should I not?”

“No,” Mydei said, glancing at him again. “It’s… good.”

That shouldn’t have sounded as serious as it did, but it was. There was something almost fascinated in his tone—not admiration exactly, but something similar.

It should’ve been flattering.

Phainon didn’t know why it caused him to tense up suddenly.

“You’re not so bad yourself.” Phainon rolled his shoulder, winced, then said, “Next time, I’m setting ground rules.”

“Next time?”

“Oh, you think I’m letting you end it here?” Phainon scoffed. “You owe me a rematch.”

Mydei’s smiled again, slower this time, less restrained. “You’d lose.”

“Maybe,” Phainon said easily. “But I’d have fun doing it.”

The simulation lights flickered back to normal, the hum of the ship returning as if it had been holding its breath too. Finally, Mydei twirled his sword and threw it to Phainon to catch, voice threaded with something new —interest, maybe.

“You’re strange,” he said, almost to himself.

Phainon smiled, head tilting just slightly. “And yet you don’t seem to hate it.”

Mydei didn’t respond, but the silence was an admission without words. That was enough.

And when Mydei started toward the exit, Phainon let him—mostly because he couldn’t think of a good excuse to make him stay. Not yet, anyway.

[TIME UNTIL GROVE ARRIVAL: 10 HOURS]

The ship purred along the edge of an asteroid belt, coasting steady and slow. Outside the viewport, fragments of rock turned lazily in orbit, catching stray streaks of starlight as they passed. The glow reflected faintly against the hull, like ripples on water.

Phainon leaned over the console, humming to himself as he adjusted the gravitic stabilizers. The field sensors had been flickering on and off since they’d entered the belt—nothing serious, just annoying enough to keep him from getting bored. Every time a larger chunk of debris drifted too close, the radar chimed softly, and he nudged it away with a flick of his wrist.

“Not today,” he murmured, smirking faintly as another small boulder spun off into the void.

He’d woken up about an hour ago. Technically, Okheman didn’t need sleep (for long periods of time at least), but it was nice to pretend sometimes. There was something satisfying about waking up groggy, stretching, and realizing he didn’t have to be anywhere for a few hours.

Now, he sat cross-legged in the pilot’s chair, barefoot, wrapped in a too-big blanket he was pretty sure he’d “borrowed” from the medbay. His shirt was wrinkled, hair half-dried from a quick rinse, and he looked every bit like someone still mentally in bed.
