Phainon reached for his mug, found it still warm, and smiled. “Good ship,” he said absently, as if it could hear him.

He flicked open a few displays, checking the asteroid density maps, then idly rerouted the ship’s external shields to redistribute impact load— completely unnecessary, but it gave his hands something to do. There was something calming about it, like knitting for people who grew up with star drives.

He glanced at the countdown clock. Ten hours until Grove arrival. Not bad. Enough time to breathe, to pretend the universe wasn’t constantly trying to kill him, and maybe even nap again if he felt like it.

“Could be worse,” he said, echoing his own thought aloud, voice warm and lazy in the still air.

He reached out and dimmed the remaining lights until the only illumination came from the starfield. The glass canopy reflected his outline. It wasn’t glamorous. But gods, it was comfortable.

Phainon tilted his chair back, drawing the blanket tighter, and watched the asteroids drift by. They spun slow and steady, glimmering with every rotation, and for once, he didn’t mind the quiet.

There was no one demanding a report, no crisis alarm, no eldritch alien being screaming through the comms. Just the sound of metal and stars and a single man keeping them alive.

“Alright,” he said to the empty bridge. “You win, universe. This’ll do.”

He tapped one last command into the console, setting the ship to autopilot, and settled in.

Phainon had sunk deep into the pilot’s cradle—more a half-cocoon than a chair at this point—and the blanket wound tighter around him until—

He exhaled a slow sigh, fingers flicking idle patterns across a console’s edge.

“You could just tell me what the problem is, you know,” he said at last.

Silence answered him. Then, the subtle change in the air—weight shifting against the bulkhead, the faint rustle of fabric. Someone pretending not to exist.

Phainon didn’t turn around. “I don’t like to think of myself as a rude host,” he went on, conversational, “but I can’t exactly fix what I don’t know, Mydeimos.”

For a while, there was nothing. Then, a shadow detached itself from the dim amber of the wall.

Mydei stepped forward, the soft light catching in his pale hair and the faint redness of his cheek (was he cold? He’ll have to adjust the ship’s temperature later.). His tone was quiet, almost neutral. “You’re up early.”

Phainon finally turned, unimpressed. “As are you. And, if I’m recalling correctly—this whole week?”

A pause. One of those short silences that say you’re right, but I’m not giving you the satisfaction.

Instead of answering, Mydei drifted closer to the viewport. He looked out at the asteroid field, where distant rocks gleamed in slow, silvery arcs.

“What are you doing?” he asked idly.

“Adjusting our trajectory,” Phainon said easily. “Field’s dense, but manageable. We’re riding the edge to stay off scans. Efficient and scenic— my favorite combination.”

Mydei made a quiet sound in his throat. Not quite agreement, not quite disapproval.

Phainon chuckled faintly. “Something on your mind, captain?”

For a long moment, the other man didn’t answer. Just stood there, gaze fixed on the window, jaw set tight in a way that made Phainon want to kiss his worries away.

Then, quietly—too quietly:

“When we reach orbit, I’ll leave.”

Phainon stilled. His hand hovered over the console.

Ah.

So that’s what this was about.

He should’ve known. Mydei never lingered anywhere he couldn’t navigate himself. Never trusted what wasn’t his to command.

Still—it hit harder than he wanted to admit.

He leaned back a little further, letting the cradle shift with him, pretending nonchalance. “I see,” he murmured.

Mydei didn’t stop there. “You’ve done enough,” he said, still looking out at the stars. His reflection shimmered faintly on the glass. “You got me off Kremnos, kept me alive long enough to get this far. That’s… more than I can ask for. Once we reach the Grove, I’ll handle the rest.”

Phainon arched an eyebrow, tone casual. “Should I be flattered, or worried that you sound like you’re resigning from a job?”

Mydei’s scoffed. “Neither.”

He turned then, and looked directly at Phainon.

“You shouldn’t concern yourself with what happens next.”

Phainon tilted his head, smiling. “Things that aren’t my business, you mean?”

“That’s one way to put it.”

Mydei started walking again, slow, unhurried. It had that cinematic rhythm —like a dream half remembered, his voice calming even as he moved past.

“I meant what I said. You’ve done more than enough.” He didn’t look at him as he spoke. “You don’t owe me anything, Phainon.”

Phainon watched him go. Mydei’s hand brushed the back of the cradle in passing—close enough to feel the static hum between them, but not close enough to linger.

He could let him leave.

He could.

But where was the fun in that?

Phainon’s hand shot out, catching Mydei’s wrist before he could take another step.

Mydei froze, startled but not alarmed—his head turned just enough for Phainon to catch the faint raise of an eyebrow.

“Now, now,” Phainon said, “let’s get to know each other first, yeah? No need to rush off. We’ve still got ten hours to kill.”

Mydei’s eyes narrowed. “Deliverer,” he said lowly.

Ah. That again.

Phainon almost smiled. The title had started as a joke a few days ago— Mydei, in one of his rare dry moments, had called him Deliverer after catching him hauling a crate twice his size without breaking stride. The name had stuck, though Phainon was still undecided whether it was meant as mockery or reluctant endearment.

“Mm,” Phainon hummed, feigning thoughtfulness. “That’s the tone you use when you think you’re in charge of a conversation.”

Mydei’s brow ticked. “And that’s the tone you use when you think charm substitutes for sense.”

Phainon shrugged. “You’d be surprised how often it works.”

Mydei tugged his wrist, intent on pulling away—but Phainon’s grip held firm. A subtle twist of movement, deceptively relaxed, and the momentum tipped.

A startled breath—then gravity took over.

Phainon caught him easily, arm braced around his back, the other still wrapped around his wrist. Mydei’s knee landed against the edge of the cradle, body half-hovering over Phainon’s lap.

The proximity was instant and dizzying. Mydei’s hair brushed Phainon’s cheek; the fabric of his shirt bunched where Phainon’s fingers pressed.

For once, Mydei looked almost uncertain.

Phainon tutted softly, tilting his head, hand sliding up to nudge Mydei’s chin until their eyes met. “You never listen, do you?”

The blanket slipped halfway off Phainon’s shoulder, catching on Mydei’s sleeve. The console light painted them in soft gold and shadow.

Neither moved.

Mydei’s expression barely shifted, but the sound he made—a low, dismissive humph—gave him away. He turned his head aside, eyes flicking toward the viewport instead of Phainon.

“Well? I’m waiting.”

He almost let out a victorious whoop when Mydei finally gave in.

Albeit very reluctantly.

“…I have trouble sleeping here.”

Phainon tilted his head, curious. “Yeah?”

Mydei exhaled slowly. “It’s unfamiliar here. The air’s too thin. The lights dim, then flare again when the systems cycle. Every noise sounds closer than it is.” He paused, lips downturned. “It’s like the ship’s alive and it’s watching me breathe.”

He hesitated, fingertips brushing the edge of the pilot cradle. “It keeps me alert. On edge. Waiting for something to happens”

Phainon blinked once, then made a small, drawn-out sound of understanding. “Ohhh.” His mouth curved, tone playful. “Why didn’t you just say so?”

Before Mydei could ask what that was supposed to mean, Phainon’s hands settled lightly at his waist.

Mydei startled, jerking back instinctively. “What the—”

Phainon’s grip held firm—not harsh, but undeniably strong. His smile widened, bright in the dim light. “Relax.”

“Phainon.” The name came out as a warning.

Too late. With a deft pull, smooth and practiced, Phainon drew him closer. Mydei’s balance tipped forward, and the ship’s pilot cradle responded to the movement with a quiet mechanical hum—widening, reclining, reshaping itself to fit them both.

By the time Mydei caught his breath, he was fully seated on Phainon’s lap.

“What the hell are you—”

“Helping,” Phainon interrupted lightly, one arm braced behind Mydei to keep him from sliding off. “You’re wound up. I’m fixing it.”

“The chair is fixing it,” Mydei muttered, glaring down at him.

“The chair’s doing great,” Phainon said, amused. “You, not so much.”

The cradle shifted again—another gentle recline—and the blanket pooled around them like a second heartbeat. Mydei looked ready to snap a retort, but the absurdity of it all got the better of him. His glare dulled into disbelief.

“You have three seconds,” he said as warning, “to explain yourself before I —”

“—help you sleep.” Phainon’s voice was gentle, as he rubbed at one eye with mock drowsiness. “You said you’re tense. I can regulate emotional feedback—pulse rhythm, hormonal drift, all that fun bio nonsense. Most Okhemans can’t, but I can.”

Mydei gave him a flat, disbelieving stare. “You expect me to believe—”

“—that proximity makes it easier?” Phainon interrupted again, leaning his head back. “Obviously. Go on. Tell me you don’t feel better already.”

Mydei opened his mouth. Closed it again.

Silence lingered—then he frowned faintly, realizing the tightness in his chest had already eased. The constant alertness had ebbed into something quieter, softer.

“…I suppose it does,” he admitted at last, the words quiet and grudging.

Phainon’s teasing faded into something gentler. “Good to know,” he murmured, his tone shifting lower, sleepier. “I used to do this with Cyrene when she was little. She’d wake up whenever the gravity flux hit. Said the air felt ‘too much.’ I’d hold her until it smoothed out. Always worked.”

Mydei blinked, surprised by the warmth in his voice—that easy fondness threaded through memory.

After a while, Mydei’s posture softened, the rigid edge easing as he let his weight settle more naturally. His hands rested near Phainon’s shoulders, fingertips brushing the soft fabric of the blanket pooled beneath them.

Outside, the asteroid field drifted in slow motion, their faint light blinking in and out across the hull.

Phainon’s breathing had slowed, eyelids fluttering as sleep tugged at the edges. “You can stay here tonight if you’d like,” he murmured, voice dropping to something almost inaudible. “Or go. I won’t stop you.”

For a long time, Mydei didn’t answer. Then, in a tone so soft it barely disturbed the air:

“…I’ll stay.”

Phainon smiled at that—a small, content curve that reached his eyes. “Good,” he whispered, half-asleep.

The chair adjusted one last time, recognizing the shift in weight, and Mydei instinctively leaned closer—drawn toward the warmth, toward stillness. His head found its way against Phainon’s shoulder, the steady pulse beneath calming, grounding.

Outside, the stars drifted. Inside, only quiet breathing.

By the time the control lights dimmed for the night cycle, Phainon had dozed off—and the quiet, steady warmth still pressed against his chest did not move away.

Usually, there would’ve been hours of prep work before setting foot on the Grove of Epiphany.

Ship clearance. Identity verification. Half a dozen bureaucratic headaches wrapped in polite language. The Scholars were notorious for it—every visitor expected to crawl through protocol before being allowed within a kilometer of the planet’s surface.

But Phainon, of course, was an exception.

He always was.

Once a student of the Grove, now something between guest and anomaly, the gates opened for him without a fuss. The world below welcomed him back with a soft hum, the air alive with electric fragrance and chlorophyll haze.

And besides—he had other things on his mind.

The wind here carried warmth; sunlight dappled through silver-veined leaves that whispered with soundless energy. Mydei knelt amid it all, just off the walkway’s edge, beside a patch of flora that glimmered faintly with bioluminescent veins. A translucent pot cradled the bloom he’d been tending since they left orbit—an Asterion filament, glowing brighter the longer his hands lingered near.

Phainon lingered at a distance, one hand in his pocket, the other shading his eyes as if the sight might blind him. Not the plant. Mydei. The rare quiet that came over him when he thought no one was watching.

“…You know,” Phainon called, tone teasing, “if I didn’t know better, I’d say you’re trying to charm that thing more than you ever try with me.”

Mydei didn’t even glance up. “That’s because the plant listens when spoken to.”

“Ouch. Brutal.”

He wandered closer, boots crunching softly over the crystalline gravel, hands clasped behind his back in mock authority. “Alright, Doctor Doom-and-Bloom, tell me—how long until you start lecturing it about proper soil pH?”

A quiet sigh left Mydei as he brushed a fingertip over one of the petals. “The plant doesn’t need to be lectured.”

“Sure, but I do?”

“You just volunteered yourself,” Mydei murmured.

Phainon crouched down beside him. “Hey, I was being supportive.”

“You were being distracting.”

“Same thing, really.”

Mydei sighed.

Phainon leaned in, pretending to study the flower with the gravity of a man solving cosmic mysteries. “So, what is this one, anyway? It looks like it’s trying to glow itself into another dimension.”

“An Asterion filament,” Mydei said, looks like someone’s been doing their research. “They react to kinetic energy. The more movement nearby, the brighter they get.”

Phainon blinked. “So it likes attention.”

“Unlike some.”

“That’s rude.”

He reached out before Mydei could stop him, brushing a knuckle against one of the petals—

A flare of gold light burst outward, bright enough to sting the air.

“Whoa—”

Mydei’s hand darted out, steadying the pot before it tipped. “You are going to make it combust at this rate.”

“Reflex test!” Phainon said quickly, raising his hands in mock surrender. “And you passed with flying colors.”

Mydei exhaled slowly, looking every inch the man debating whether the flower or his companion would be more deserving of being thrown into the compost. “You’re insufferable.”

“And you adore me.”

He ignored him.

Phainon tilted his head. The air shimmered faintly between them—hazy sunlight through glass. Something too gentle to name.

Then, as if on cue, Phainon broke it. “Anyway, back to the topic—we’re almost there.”

Mydei brushed his hands off, his composure sliding neatly back into place. “How far?”

Phainon sing-songed, “Very close~,” already taking a few steps ahead. Then, without warning, he reached back, caught Mydei’s hand, and tugged.

“Phainon.” Mydei said, carrying that mild warning that usually preceded an act of violence. “Where are we going?”

Phainon didn’t slow, glancing over his shoulder with that infuriating half-smile. “Looks like you’re getting your tour a bit early.”

“…Tour?”

“Of course. You said you wanted to see the Grove.”

“I thought we had to—”

“We do, but that’s boring, and this isn’t.” He patted his shoulder. “Trust me. I’ve got the perfect first stop.”

Mydei sighed quietly, but didn’t resist. He followed, still holding Phainon’s hand like it was an inconvenience he didn’t truly want to remove.

The path curved—and suddenly, the Grove opened before them.

It was like stepping into a waking dream.

The world here was color, alive and endless—buildings that shimmered with breathlike pulses, grown instead of built, veined with light from the petrified bones of Cerces herself. Great tendrils of vine and circuitry wove together across the skyline, a marriage of nature and mind, of life that refused to die.

Phainon slowed, letting Mydei take it in. His expression softened, a rare thing—open awe, unguarded. The light caught in his eyes, refracting gold and green.

Phainon watched him quietly.

There was something satisfying in it. The sight of Mydei in color. In light. In this world.

And something else—something that tightened faintly in his chest as he thought, absurdly, don’t get used to it.

But he smiled anyway. “And for what could it be,” he began dramatically, sweeping an arm wide, “except the humble, world-renowned, ever-prestigious medical institution—the Twilight Courtyard!”

He stopped walking, beaming, gesturing grandly toward a towering structure of iridescent crystal whose surface rippled like water when the wind brushed against it.

“Tada!”

Mydei blinked at him, expression perfectly neutral. “That was unnecessarily dramatic.”

Phainon coughed. “Nevermind.”

He strode ahead, waving to a few passing Scholars who lit up at his presence, offering cheerful greetings that he half-returned. His steps quickened the closer they got, as though pulled by something familiar.

Finally, he stopped before a door at the far end of the courtyard. Its metal shimmered faintly with embedded sigils that pulsed softly when he approached. Phainon pressed his palm against it—the glyphs brightened, recognizing him, and the door slid open with a low sigh.

He turned and swept into a theatrical bow. “After you.”

Mydei regarded him a moment—then stepped forward without comment, brushing past him as he entered.

Phainon’s laughter followed quietly, soft as the door sealed behind them.

Mydei glanced around once they stepped inside, taking in the gleaming walls and the faint antiseptic tang in the air. “Now what?”

Before Phainon could answer—

“Phainon?”

He turned fast, instincts snapping taut before his brain caught up.

Then he blinked, tension uncoiling the second he recognized the voice.

“Hyacine!” He beamed instantly, disarming and bright. “Perfect timing, actually—long time no see! Here, I wanted to introduce you to—”

He didn’t get the chance.

“Not here,” she said, voice quick and light but carrying that unmistakable don’t argue undercurrent. Before he could even react, she seized his wrist, caught Mydei’s sleeve with her other hand, and hauled both of them down the corridor.

Phainon barely managed to keep his footing. Mydei, predictably, didn’t so much as trip.

They were swept through a pair of automatic doors that hissed open just long enough for Hyacine to shove them into a compact infirmary before slamming shut again with a decisive click.

The silence that followed was immediate and profound.

Phainon blinked, slightly winded, and looked from her to the sealed door. “…Alright. Definitely stronger than I remember.”

Hyacine straightened, smoothing her dress with both hands. “You make me sound fragile.”

“Not fragile,” he said. “Just deceptively sparkly.”

Her eyes narrowed—but the sigh of relief she had after gave her away. “You haven’t changed.”

“And you have?” he shot back, light as ever.

That earned him a full smile this time—bright, genuine, and terribly at odds with the look that followed.

Then she fixed him with a stare sharp enough to cut through alloy. “You’ve already told me about your… companion.”

“Oh,” Phainon said.

There was a pause.

Then another, slightly more painful one.

Right. The transmission. The one where he may or may not have described Mydei as “some guy who he lied to not remembering he was a galactic commander.” Yeah. That.

And yelling Mydei’s name the second she appeared—possibly not the smoothest choice in retrospect.

He cleared his throat, trying for composure. “…Yes. That companion. Hyacine, this is Mydei.”

Hyacine’s expression shifted almost instantly; her tone gentled, bright again. “Ah—so you’re the one he’s been worried about.” She smiled, extending a hand that shimmered faintly with the light from her wrist device. “It’s a pleasure.”

Mydei inclined his head slightly, every movement respectful. “Likewise.”

There was a brief, quiet moment of mutual study—Hyacine’s open, assessing gaze against Mydei’s subtle one.

Phainon could practically feel the polite silence expanding between them.

He sighed under his breath. “Fantastic. Two statues. My favorite social dynamic.”

That earned him twin looks—one unimpressed, one mildly disbelieving.

“So!” he said, clapping his hands once, too brightly. “Should we get started before I’m executed for breathing too loudly?”

Hyacine’s cracked; she huffed a small laugh, shaking her head. “Right, yes —let’s. Before you break something.”

She brushed a strand of pink-blue hair behind her ear, stepped closer to the medbay cot, and gestured for Mydei to sit. “Here, please. It’ll be easier to get a full read from the diagnostic core.”

Mydei obeyed without question, perching neatly on the edge.

“And you,” Hyacine said, turning toward Phainon, “either sit quietly or wait outside. According to your very dramatic message, this is going to take a while.”

Phainon immediately dropped onto a nearby counter, crossing one leg over the other. “Do continue. I’ll be quiet as a star in vacuum.”

“Mm-hm.”

She didn’t bother responding further, only turned her attention back to her instruments. Her hands moved with practiced precision—quick, sure, gentle. The scanner hummed softly, light drifting across Mydei’s profile.

Phainon leaned back, watching the two of them—the healer at work, the patient perfectly still. He smiled faintly, chin in hand.

The day had barely begun, and already, he could feel the headache blooming behind his eyes.

It was going to be a long one.

At some point, Phainon must’ve dozed off.

That was the only explanation for why he jolted like a man electrocuted when a very gentle tap brushed his shoulder.

He flailed, nearly catapulting himself out of the chair—only for a strong hand to catch him before his skull could introduce itself to the floor.

When the blur settled, he found himself half-hanging off the cot, Hyacine standing beside him with an expression that was disappointed but not surprised, and Mydei holding him upright with one effortless grip. Both wore identical looks: unimpressed, faintly exhausted.

They could’ve been siblings.

Phainon cleared his throat and wriggled free, tugging his coat straight like dignity was a fabric he could smooth back into place. “Ahem. Right. So… you guys wrapped it up?”

Hyacine’s smile was kind, but her eyes carried the quiet, terrifying calm of someone who spent years keeping warriors alive through sheer willpower, and about to do the same to him. “For now,” she said lightly, stylus tapping against her tablet. “Everything reads within range—mostly.” Her tone cooled a few degrees on that last word, and when she glanced up at him, the look said we will discuss this later.

Phainon managed a polite, long-suffering look of his own that translated neatly to yes ma’am, later ma’am.

Her answering nod said, good.

To anyone else, it would have looked like gibberish.

“Well,” she continued, locking the tablet, “while you were peacefully drooling into my patient’s linens, I called up Professor Anaxa. He should be here within thirty minutes.”

Phainon blinked. “You called Anaxa?”

“You did say urgent,” she replied, smoothing a strand of hair behind her ear.

He gave a low whistle. “That’s… a decision.”

She looked like she had a migraine incoming. “And yet one of us had to make it.”

“Fair.”

The faintest crease of exhaustion marrowed her features, and for a moment the clinical medbay lights caught on the fine, translucent markings under her skin—Skyfolk vascular lines, threads that pulsed in time with her heartbeat. The air around her always smelled faintly of rain, a side effect of the microcurrents her kind naturally generated.

“While we wait,” she said, glancing at him, “you still wanted that checkup, didn’t you?”

Phainon sighed theatrically but nodded. “Might as well. Haven’t had one since you last bullied me into it.”

“That sounds about right.” She smiled sweetly. “Try not to move.”

She stepped closer, her presence a comfort as she retrieved a thin diagnostic scanner. Its soft sound layered over the distant buzz of filtration vents, the Grove’s heartbeat somewhere deep below the station’s floor.

Phainon relaxed into the chair while she worked, eyes half-lidded. “You know,” he murmured, “you’re wasted on the Grove. You could open a clinic anywhere and people would line up just to have you scold and treat them.”

“Scolding keeps them alive,” she said, not looking up. “Now stop talking or I’ll find a reason to keep you here overnight.”

He shut up immediately.

Mydei sat a short distance away, relaxed as ever. Polite. Still. Almost distant—except for the faint tilt of his head that suggested he was listening to everything.

It wasn’t until Hyacine leaned forward to steady Phainon’s arm, her fingers brushing his skin, that something imperceptible shifted.

It was so subtle at first that he almost dismissed it—a slight drop in temperature, the faint drag in the flow of space around them. But being Okheman meant he felt it, like a dissonant note caught under the skin.

Phainon frowned faintly. “Hm.”

Hyacine paused mid-motion, hand still on his wrist. The light from the scanner flickered once.

“…You feel that?” he asked quietly.

She didn’t answer. Her eyes were focused past his shoulder, pupils narrowing.

He tilted his head, following her line of sight. “What—”

He turned—

—and the chill vanished like it had never existed.

Mydei sat exactly as before, composed, serene. The soft glow from the nearby panel haloed his hair, his expression calm and faintly bored.

For half a second, Phainon wondered if he’d imagined it.

Then, because he didn’t know what else to do, he raised a hand with a lazy, playful wave. “Hi~”

Mydei blinked slowly, and lifted his hand in the smallest echo of the gesture.

Phainon smiled, turning back around, tone bright. “Anyway! You were saying something about how stunningly healthy I am?”

Hyacine hesitated for just a heartbeat too long, then smoothed her voice. “Yes. Surprisingly, everything looks normal.”

“Surprisingly?” he said.

“For someone who never sleeps, eats like a wayward pigeon, and insists on wandering into crossfire for fun? Miraculous, really.”

He grinned sheepishly. “Talent.”

She gave a small huff of laughter before returning to her screen. The scanner light shimmered against her hair, and he caught the faint scent of rain again as she moved.

They stayed like that for a few minutes—quiet, familiar, easy. When she finally withdrew the scanner, she set it aside with a soft click.

“Well,” she said, tone warm again, “still reckless, still loud, still alive. I’ll take it.”

“Hey, consistency is key.”

“Consistency,” she echoed, amused. “That’s what you’re calling it now.”

Their shared smile felt like sunlight through glass.

After a beat, Phainon leaned back, stretching his arms behind his head. “Say, where’s Professor Anaxa anyway? Thought he’d—”

He didn’t finish.

The door slammed open hard enough to rattle the ceiling panels. Hyacine jumped, nearly dropping her tablet.

Phainon closed his eyes and sighed, already regretting his life choices. “… Of course.”

“Professor Anaxa,” he said after a pause, not turning around, “you certainly know how to make an entrance.”

A cold voice answered, each syllable clipped like the edge of a blade. “It’s Anaxagoras.”

Phainon winced. “Ah. Right. Some things never change.”

Phainon waited a full beat before daring to turn around.

Anaxagoras—because stars forbid you ever call him “Anaxa”—stood framed in the doorway, one gloved hand still resting on the metal rim like he owned it. The man hadn’t aged a day. Same immaculate posture, same composure that made people instinctively straighten their backs. His voice, when it came, could still make a classroom go silent out of sheer survival instinct. (Partially because he would pull a weapon on you if you interrupted his lecture. Only once, but the legend stuck.)

Phainon cleared his throat and pasted on his best smile. “Well, uh—this is awkward timing but, uh—Professor, this is Mydei.” He gestured toward Mydei, who stood at his usual level of tranquil that bordered on eerie. “Mydei, meet Professor Anaxagoras, my lovely former instructor back when I was still pretending to be a model student.”

Anaxagoras didn’t even spare him a glance. His gaze snapped straight to Mydei—sharp, assessing, as if trying to read the entire man in one go.

“You’re coming with me,” he said flatly.

Phainon blinked. “Now, now, let’s not be too—”

“Okay,” Mydei said.

Phainon’s jaw nearly hit the floor. “I—wait, what?”

Hyacine coughed delicately into her hand. Phainon swore she was smiling.

He whipped around, offended. “You agree that easily? Where was that cooperative spirit when I was trying to stop you from almost touching a live reactor core?”

Mydei just tilted his head in mild apology, a ghost of amusement flickering in his eyes.

Before Phainon could gather enough outrage to keep going, Hyacine— sweet, deceptively gentle Hyacine—rested a hand over his mouth and turned to the professor with a radiant smile. “That would be wonderful, Professor Anaxagoras. Thank you for taking the time.”

Phainon muffled a protest, something along the lines of “wonderful my ass”, but one look from her—polite, serene, deadly—made the words die a quick, merciful death.

Right. Message received. Shut up.

Anaxagoras gave the faintest nod, his coat whispering against the floor as he turned. “Follow me,” he said.

Mydei didn’t hesitate. Just walked out after him without so much as a backward glance.

The door shut behind them with an airtight hiss.

Phainon stared for a long moment, hands on his hips. “Well,” he said finally, “that wasn’t ominous at all.”

Hyacine set her tablet aside, exhaling softly. “To be fair, that’s mild for him.”

“Mild? I once saw him reduce a Council member to tears for mispronouncing ‘axial inversion.’”

Hyacine gave a faint laugh, but it didn’t reach her eyes.

Phainon squinted. “What’s got him all ruffled anyway? He looked ready to vivisect the air itself.”

She hesitated—always a bad sign. “I may have… forwarded him the results from my diagnostic earlier.”

He perked up. “Oh, that.” He leaned back against the counter, arms folded. “Right, you said you wanted to wait till we were alone to talk about it. And look at that—” he gestured broadly, “privacy achieved.”

Hyacine didn’t immediately answer. She turned toward her workstation, flipping through a few sheets of synth-paper. The hum of the medbay filled the silence, accompanied by the soft pulse of the hydroponic vents.

Phainon waited, for once not rushing her.

When she finally looked back, her voice was quieter. “The readings were strange,” she said. “There was something… old. Titanal resonance.”

Phainon’s smile faded. “Titanal? You’re kidding.”

“I wish.” She pressed a hand against the console, eyes flicking to him. “Not residual, either. Active. Traceable.”

His tone shifted instantly, the levity dropping away like a mask. “Whose signature?”

Hyacine’s expression tightened. “Nikador’s.”

For a second, the only sound was the hum of the diagnostic screens.

Phainon went still. “You’re sure?”

“Triple-checked. It wasn’t a misread.”

He rubbed his temples, muttering something under his breath that might’ve been a prayer or a curse. “That’s impossible.”

Hyacine shook her head. “I know. And yet.” She drew in a deep breath, her bioluminescent markings dimming slightly. “Everything else was normal— organ health, energy flow, cognitive rhythm. He’s perfectly fine. But the Titanal levels were through the roof. If I didn’t know better, I’d say he’s acting as a conduit.”

“That hasn’t happened since—”

“The Fall,” she finished quietly.

Phainon looked down, jaw tight. “You think it’s connected to the recent distortions? The ones eating at the fringe colonies?”

“Maybe.” She exhaled, pressing the heel of her palm against her forehead. “The readings don’t match the usual anomaly patterns, but they’re close enough to make me uneasy. Whatever’s going on, it’s not just a fluke.”

When she lifted her gaze again, her voice softened. “Be careful, Phainon. Please. If Mydei really is tied to that signature, we might be standing too close to something we don’t understand.”

He smiled faintly, though it didn’t reach his eyes. “When have I ever not been careful?”

“Do you want the list alphabetically or chronologically?”

He laughed, short and genuine, though it dissolved quickly. “Point taken.”

A beat of silence passed between them, quieter now, less professional— something more like friendship resting heavy between the words.

Then Phainon straightened, adjusting his coat with that overdone flourish of his. “Well, looks like I’ve overextended my welcome. As always, Doctor Hyacine, a delight.”

She sighed, but there was fondness behind it. “Phainon—”

“I’ll see myself out,” he said, already halfway to the door.

“Give them a few hours,” she said suddenly.

He paused mid-step, back to her. “…You always know everything, don’t you?”

“Someone has to.”

He snorted, the corner of his mouth twitching.

“Maybe,” she continued, “take that time to go out. Get some air. Do something not self-destructive for once. You’ll be here longer than planned anyway.”

He turned just enough to flash her a look. “Shopping therapy. How very clinical of you.”

But something lit up behind his eyes—mischief, sudden and bright.

Hyacine immediately groaned. “No. Whatever you’re thinking, no.”

“Oh yes,” he said, far too pleased with himself. “Mydei’s got a sweet tooth. Maybe I’ll bring him something nice. Chocolate, maybe. Or those crystalline sugar leaves from the Grove markets.”

“Phainon.”

He waved her off, strolling out before she could finish.

The doors hissed closed behind him.

Hyacine stood there for a moment, hand over her eyes. “Trouble,” she murmured. “Every damn time.”

The medbay hummed back to its usual rhythm, faintly smelling of ozone and rain.

The Grove was at its loudest during midday.

Music bled from every corner—bells, laughter, the rhythmic clatter of glass trinkets being shaken for attention. The air shimmered with scent and color: spice, pollen, ozone. Phainon wandered through it like someone who’d lost his purpose halfway through the journey and decided to just enjoy the detour.

He had a bag slung over his shoulder, weighed down by… things. He wasn’t even sure what half of them were anymore. Some merchant had pressed glowing seed-pods into his hand, swearing they “improved mental conductivity.” Another had sold him a pair of floating glass fish that “symbolized equilibrium.” He didn’t even like fish.

Whatever. He had time.

By the time the Grove’s skies dimmed from gold to violet, the noise had thinned, and Phainon realized he hadn’t seen Anaxagoras since morning. The man had shut himself and Mydei away in the study and hadn’t emerged since.

He didn’t actually see him again until dawn.

“You’d think you were a damn dog with how long you’ve been parked out here.”

Phainon cracked an eye open. He was sitting cross-legged against the wall outside Anaxagoras’s office, coat half-buttoned, hair a mess, an open bag of sweets in his lap.

“Four hours,” Anaxagoras added mildly, like he was commenting on the weather.

Phainon yawned. “I call it dedication.”

“I call it a waste of floor space.”

He grinned. “Missed me?”

“Desperately,” Anaxagoras said dryly, stepping over him to unlock the door.

Phainon stretched his legs and stood, brushing himself off. “So,” he said, tone casual but his curiosity edged in it, “you and Mydei finally done in there?”

Anaxagoras didn’t answer immediately. He adjusted his gloves, straightened a sleeve, a deliberate pause before replying, “Who knows?”

That… wasn’t normal.

Phainon blinked. “I’m sorry—what?”

“Curious patient you’ve brought me.”

“Yeah, he’s adorable. What about him?”

Anaxagoras’s gaze flicked toward him briefly. “Adorable,” he echoed, with the kind of tone that suggested deep scientific offense.

“Uh-huh.” Phainon squinted at him. “You’re being weirdly vague, and it’s scaring me a little.”

“I’m being accurate,” Anaxagoras said, not missing a beat.

“Right. And I’m being patient,” Phainon muttered. “So maybe you could tell me what you actually found?”

That finally earned him a look, more a side-eye really. “You want the short version or the one that makes you regret asking?”

Phainon raised a brow. “Let’s gamble.”

Anaxagoras folded his hands behind his back. “He’s not just recovering memories. It’s more so he’s reconstructing them.”

Phainon frowned. “Isn’t that the same thing?”

“No.” He said immediately. “Recollection is retrieval. Reconstruction is creation. He’s piecing things together that may not have survived in their original state.”

“So he’s… improvising?”

“In a manner of speaking.” Anaxagoras’s aqquited, but there was something beneath it—a note of concern. How odd. “That’s the danger. Reconstruction breeds deviation.”

Phainon tilted his head. “You mean he’s—what—rewriting himself?”

“That’s one way to describe it.”

Something about the way he said it made the back of Phainon’s neck prickle.

“So what are you suggesting? That I stop him?”

“I’m suggesting,” Anaxagoras said, turning to face him fully now, “that you pay attention. If what he rebuilds isn’t what you remember… you’ll need to decide whether you still recognize who’s standing in front of you.”

Phainon blinked, caught off guard by the sudden weight in his tone. “Bit dramatic, don’t you think?”

Anaxagoras’s expression didn’t change. “If he ever looks at you like he remembers you,” he started, “Just run. Nikador’s signature isn’t one to be underestimated. Don’t take any chances.”

Then he stepped past him, hand briefly brushing Phainon’s shoulder in a gesture that felt more like punctuation than comfort. “He’s still inside. Try not to distract him.”

Phainon watched him go, the air in the hallway still humming faintly from the exchange.

“…Right,” he muttered to himself. “That’s definitely not ominous at all.”

He stood there a while, running the words over again. “Run.”

Yeah, sure. That sounded like Anaxagoras’s version of affection.

He shook it off with a sharp exhale and adjusted the strap of his bag. No sense getting worked up over riddles. Whatever weird theory Anaxagoras had cooked up, it didn’t change what he came here for.

Besides, Mydei was fine. Probably.

He started walking.

The study door slid open with a soft hiss, and light spilled out—soft blue, tinted with gold from the crystalline lamps.

Phainon stepped inside, already reaching for the bag. “You know,” he said casually, “some of us age while waiting outside, and—”

He stopped.

Mydei was at one of the tables, hair loosely tied back, strands of blonde falling against his cheek. He was bent over one of Anaxagoras’s scanning lenses, eyes narrowed slightly in concentration. A soft hum filled the space —the device running, his faint breathing, the quiet world that formed around him when he focused.

Phainon leaned against the doorframe, watching him for a beat too long.

He looked… unfairly pretty like that.

Phainon sighed helplessly. “You really like stealing other people’s labs, huh?”

Mydei didn’t look up. “Borrowing,” he corrected mildly.

“Sure, sure. That’s what thieves say before prison.”

“Prison implies they caught me.”

Phainon laughed under his breath, crossing the room. “Touché.”

He stopped beside the table, set the bag down, and nudged it toward him. “Brought you offerings.”

Mydei finally glanced up. “Offerings?”

“Tribute. Payment. Bribe. Take your pick.”

He peeked inside, lifting out one of the sugar petals. “You bought these from the central market?”

“Technically, yes. Realistically, I think I was scammed.”

“Most likely.”

Phainon pressed a hand over his chest, mock wounded. “Your faith in me is astounding.”

Mydei smiled faintly, then popped one of the petals into his mouth. “Sweet.”

“Right? I figured it fits your personality.”

“Questionable taste?”

“Addictively pleasant.”

He melted when Mydei’s ears turned faintly pink at that, though the man’s expression didn’t otherwise change. He just went back to his instruments, movements careful.

Phainon leaned against the table again. For a second, everything Anaxagoras said earlier dimmed, replaced by this small, quiet moment—the rustle of paper, the hum of machines, the faint sound of Mydei crunching on another sugar petal like nothing else in the universe mattered.

And maybe that was enough.

“Hey,” Phainon said softly.

Mydei hummed, eyes still on the scanner. “Hm?”

“Just making sure you’re real.”

That earned a small, sidelong glance—half confusion, half question— before he looked back down again.

“Unfortunately for you,” Mydei said, “I am.”

Phainon felt himself loosen up. “Lucky me.”

“Welp,” He started finally, stretching his arms until his back popped. “Guess we’re stuck here a bit longer. Doubt Anaxa’s gonna stop poking at your brain anytime soon. He’s probably printing copies of your thoughts as we speak.”

Mydei looked up from the counter, idly picking at the edge of another sugar petal before popping it into his mouth. “He mentioned something about ‘extended observation.’”

“See? I told you.” Phainon gestured with both hands like he’d just been proven right in court. “You’ve officially become the world’s prettiest lab rat.”

“I don’t mind,” Mydei said thoughtfully.

Phainon stared. “That wasn’t a compliment, y’know.”

“It sounded like one.”

He blinked. “That’s… honestly worse.”

Mydei hummed, completely unfazed.

Phainon sighed, dragging a hand through his hair. “Alright, fine. While our beloved mad scientist does whatever he’s doing, we might as well figure out where we’re staying. Any preferences for your temporary living arrangements?”

Mydei didn’t even hesitate. “Can I sleep with you?”

Phainon inhaled wrong. “—I’m sorry, what?”

Unbothered, Mydei brushed a crumb off his sleeve. “It helped before. It was calming.”

Phainon froze mid-cough. “Oh. Oh, you mean—sleep sleep.”

“Yes. That is what I said.”

“Right. Totally. Sleep sleep. Naps. Innocent, platonic, medically recommended sleep.” Phainon nodded like a man trying to convince himself of gravity. “Yeah. Sure. Why not. Love that for us.”

Mydei just blinked. “You look flushed.”

“Do I?” Phainon croaked, rubbing his neck. “Probably—uh—low blood sugar. Nothing to do with the topic. Completely unrelated.”

He cleared his throat, desperately changing tracks. “So! Anything else? Blankets? Pillows? You like soft lighting or more of a candlelight-gothic thing? Need me to hum lullabies? I do a mean impression of ocean waves —”

“No.” Mydei’s tone shifted faintly—absent, half somewhere else. “The sooner we start, the better, no?”

Phainon blinked. “Start what—oh, right, the study. Yeah. Of course. That.”

Before he could embarrass himself further, Mydei stood, adjusting his sleeves with that quiet grace that made Phainon forget words for a second. “I’ll meet you outside. From what I’ve overheard, I’m assuming you already found us a place?”

“Caught red-handed!” Phainon exclaimed, throwing up his hands. “You got me.”

“Show me, then.”

“Gladly,” Phainon said, maybe too quickly.

They looked at each other eye to eye before Mydei slipped out the door.

Phainon stayed behind for a beat, reaching for his bag. He was halfway through tightening the cord when his fingers stilled.

Mydei was humming.

Soft, rhythmic, something familiar.

Phainon frowned. It took him a moment to place it—and when he did, he couldn’t help but still.

A Kremnoan hymn.

Old, very old. The kind sung under breath in temples.

Phainon’s hand hovered mid-air. For a heartbeat, his chest tightened.

Then he huffed out a shaky laugh. “Right. Because that’s not at all ominous,” he muttered. “He probably just… likes the tune.”

He slung the bag over his shoulder, raising his voice. “—coming!”

And just like that, the tension cracked. His cheer slid back into place, easy and bright as ever, as he jogged after Mydei down the hall—sweets clinking faintly with every step.

Whatever it was, he’d figure it out later.

For now, there was someone waiting.

It happened slowly, the way things that change your life usually do.

One day he was pacing sterile halls, arguing with Anaxa over containment parameters and caffeine limits. The next, he was here—somewhere between sunlight and dreamlight—watching dew roll down glowing roots while pretending this was still part of the job.

It had been about three weeks, give or take. Long enough for the Grove to start recognizing his footsteps. Long enough for him to forget what silence without breathing trees sounded like.

And long enough for Mydei to start taking morning walks.

Phainon told himself he only followed out of routine—security detail, supervision, nothing personal. But the truth was far less professional. Mydei would drift through the outer paths at dawn, hair unbound, the pale gold of the sun catching on it like threads of fire. He always carried tea. Always seemed to know which roots not to step on, like the Grove itself bent around him.

Sometimes Phainon would walk a few paces behind, pretending to check readings on his wristband while memorizing the shape of Mydei’s silhouette against the light. One morning, Mydei had smiled at something in the fog—soft, almost private—and that had been that. Phainon decided no sunrise was worth watching unless that smile came with it.

Their quarters—shared purely for logistical reasons, he reminded himself far too often—had fallen into rhythm. Mydei brewed tea with an impossible kind of blend, timing the pour down to the second. The air always smelled faintly of flowers and citrus, and he always hummed while he worked. Phainon never admitted how much those little tunes stuck in his head… or how every so often, they carried the echo of something that didn’t belong here on the Grove.

He didn’t bring it up.

In exchange for tea, Phainon handled breakfast, which mostly meant getting in the way while Mydei tried to stop him from weaponizing sugar. There’d been an incident with a syrup explosion that both of them had mutually agreed to pretend never happened.

He told himself the warmth between them was normal. A side effect of proximity. Familiarity.

(It was also, unfortunately, golden and unbearable—the kind that crawled under the ribs and stayed there long after you’d laughed it off.)

The area itself had begun… responding.

At first, it was small things: vines that brushed his sleeve instead of recoiling, lights that brightened when he entered the room. But lately, the timing had started to feel too exact. The way the glow swelled when Mydei laughed. The way the air pulsed—soft, rhythmic—as if syncing to a heartbeat that wasn’t theirs.

He kept telling himself that was normal too.

It wasn’t.

Then there were the calls.

The first time Tribbie’s holo-link flickered to life, Phainon nearly fell out of his chair. One second he was reviewing data, the next there was a floating pastel cube hovering in front of him, voice crackling with static.

“Snowy, are you nesting??”

Her tone was pure delight, glitchy laughter breaking through the interference. “Domestic bliss achieved! Oh, this is rich. We leave you alone for a few weeks and you go feral and start cohabitating with military.”

“It’s called mission parameters, thank you,” Phainon said dryly, trying and failing not to groan.

“Uh-huh. Parameters. That’s what they all say.”

“You’re just jealous I’ve got sunlight and breakfast.”

“Please. Castorice gave us a new shell. It has cup holders.”

“…damn, okay, that’s fair.”

Their conversations never lasted long. The connection—whatever channel she was using—wasn’t supposed to exist. Even Anaxa didn’t know how she was managing it. Tribbie brushed off the question every time, exclaiming, “Classified protocols! Don’t worry about it!” like that wasn’t the single least reassuring phrase in the galaxy.

Once, when he asked about Okhema—about what happened after the recall —she froze. Her cube-body stuttered midair, flickering between frames.

Then, bright as ever, “Can’t talk about that, Snowy! Sorry! Totally fine though! Everyone’s great!”

And the link cut.

It was weird.

He’d sat staring at the dark space where her projection had been, his surroundings pressing in like a living silence.

He trusted Tribbie. Always would. But the way her code wanted to speak and couldn’t—it made his stomach twist.

He told himself it didn’t mean anything. It always did.

At least he had distractions.

Mydei had somehow revealed himself to be an unreasonably competent cook. The food was—there was no polite way to put it—sinful. Phainon would make noises that should’ve been classified, then try to pass them off as coughs.

“Too sweet?” Mydei asked once, head tilting with genuine concern.

“Perfect,” Phainon rasped, halfway between admiration and cardiac arrest.

But under the comfort, something was… off.

It started with the water. He’d noticed ripples in still bowls when Mydei passed. Then the lights—bioluminescent veins along the walls—would flare in time with his breath. Sometimes, even the air shimmered, faint distortion waves rolling through the room when Mydei was relaxed or distracted.

It wasn’t violent, more so wrong. Like a system glitch trying too hard to be organic.

Hyacine had been monitoring it quietly. She didn’t say much, but one morning she handed him a datapad over breakfast.

“Biotic response indicates recognition,” the note read.

Recognition.

Phainon didn’t like that word. He’d stared at it long enough for his tea to go cold.

He told her not to overthink it. He told himself not to overthink it.

After all, Mydei was just—Mydei. Warm tea, quiet hums, absent-minded grace.

Surely the Grove wasn’t alive enough to recognize him.

Right?

He kept telling himself that, even as the lights dimmed softly when Mydei slept.

Even as the vines shifted to make room when they walked side by side.

Even as the Grove seemed to breathe with them.

Phainon chose to ignore it. The sun was too bright, breakfast too good, and Mydei—too close—for anything ominous to settle for long.

And so the days went on—sweet, steady, golden—like a dream that didn’t quite know it was a dream.

“How does your lattice measure empathy? Is it quantifiable?”

Phainon nearly winced. Oh, great. We’re doing those questions today.

He didn’t even get the chance to open his mouth before Anaxa, seated behind his usual mountain of diagnostics, answered instead.

“Empathy isn’t measured,” the man said without looking up. His voice was perfectly level, like he’d sanded it smooth from years of exhaustion. “It’s correlated. We observe how affective resonance patterns align with behavioral shifts, then archive those alignments as harmonic signatures.”

“Ah.” Mydei’s head tilted slightly. He was perched on the edge of the scanner platform, posture graceful even when relaxed. “So, you store emotions.”

“Responses to emotions,” Anaxa corrected automatically, adjusting a dial. “Okheman latticework doesn’t hold feelings. It records the echoes they leave behind.”

Phainon leaned lazily against the doorway, arms crossed. “Ease up, professor,” he said. “He’s gonna start billing you for therapy if you keep this up.”

Anaxa gave him the kind of look that belonged to a man who hadn’t slept in a week and blamed him personally for it. “He’s not a patient.”

“And you’re not a comedian,” Mydei added mildly, eyes still fixed on the faintly glowing readout in front of him.

Phainon raised his hands in defeat. “Not today, I’m not. Today, I’m moral support with style.”

Anaxa muttered something about “biological interference” under his breath, fingers dancing across the console. The scanner’s lattice shimmered to life around Mydei—a faint, fluid geometry of light that pulsed in rhythm with his heartbeat. Pale blue at first, then shading warmer when Mydei exhaled.

Phainon found himself staring despite himself. The colors always fascinated him—the way they moved like tidewater, alive and sensitive, catching every flicker of thought. He’d seen scans before, but something about this one moved differently.

“How does it store it?” Mydei asked quietly, still watching the light ripple. “The resonance data. Does it degrade over time?”

“Not linearly,” Anaxa said. “Connections formed through sustained or strong affective bonds retain coherence longer. Think of it as a frequency loop—memory by proximity.”

Mydei nodded. “So, memory and emotion are linked.”

“That’s one interpretation.”

“It’s also the only one that makes sense.”

Anaxa hesitated just long enough for Phainon to notice. “Perhaps,” he allowed.

Phainon broke the tension with a sigh

and facepalm. “You two realize you sound like a philosophy major and his dissertation advisor, right? Next thing I know, someone’s bringing up the meaning of love.”

Neither of them responded.

He stepped closer, placing a hand lightly on Mydei’s shoulder. “Hey. Don’t fry your brain on him too early in the morning. You’ll start seeing equations in your dreams.”

The contact was nothing—just a casual touch—but the scanner’s light flared sharply, twin pulses overlapping, then snapping apart with a soft hiss of static.

Anaxa’s head jerked up. “Wait—”

But by then the waveform had stabilized, as if nothing had happened.

Phainon blinked. “Did I break something?”

Anaxa hesitated.

“…No.” Anaxa’s voice was quiet now, careful. “Just interference.”

He didn’t sound convinced. Phainon opened his mouth to ask but stopped when he caught Mydei’s gaze watching Anaxa with an unreadable patience that made the atmosphere around them feel thick.

Whatever Anaxa had been about to say, he didn’t.

The scan continued. Mydei’s tone turned almost conversational. “So if the lattice records resonance patterns, can it recognize familiar ones?”

“In theory,” Anaxa replied. “If the harmonics align strongly enough.”

“And can those harmonics affect the host in return?”

“That depends on exposure levels.”

Mydei hummed thoughtfully, eyes following the flickering light that wove between his fingers like it was listening. “Then what happens,” he asked, “if two fields resonate at the same frequency?”

Anaxa hesitated again. “That would imply synchrony. Which—under normal conditions—shouldn’t occur without intentional calibration.”

Phainon added idly, simplifying it. “Translation: that’s a fancy way of saying it’s impossible.”

“Unlikely,” Anaxa corrected.

Mydei’s gaze slid briefly to Phainon. “Not impossible, though.”

There was that tone again—light, curious, like he didn’t realize he was dissecting a live wire. Phainon forced a laugh, rubbing the back of his neck. “Right, well, I think we’ve maxed out the existential dread quota for the morning. Markets are calling. You done with him yet, doc?”

Anaxa glanced down at the last string of data, then, after a beat, powered down the scanner. “For now.”

Phainon clapped his hands together. “Perfect! Come on, Mydei. If we hurry, I might even buy you that tea you keep pretending not to like.”

He had just turned toward the door when Anaxa’s voice cut through, crystal clear. “Wait.”

Phainon stopped mid-step, glancing back.

“Could Mydei stay a little longer?”

“Uh, sure,” Phainon said slowly. “A little longer as in…?”

Anaxa didn’t look up. “A while.”

Phainon blinked. “Oh. Right. ‘A while.’ My favorite unit of time.” He gave a weak laugh. “Okay then.”

He turned toward Mydei, half expecting some protest. But Mydei was still seated, posture straight, gaze locked on Anaxa.

Phainon lingered, awkward now. “So, uh… I’ll just wait outside?”

“Mydeimos,” Anaxa said softly.

Mydei didn’t look away. “Phainon.”

“Yeah?”

“Go home.”

Phainon blinked. “…Okay.”

He gave a salute that was more flustered than formal and backed toward the door. “Guess I’m… dismissed. Again.” Under his breath, he muttered, “I swear I’m turning into a house pet.”

The door hissed shut behind him, cutting off the sound of his voice.

Silence.

Anaxa’s gaze drifted toward the scanner still faintly glowing beside Mydei. The harmonics hadn’t settled—they pulsed faintly, residual energy shimmering in paired signatures.

“Curious,” he murmured, almost to himself. “Your harmonics reacted before he even touched you.”

Mydei didn’t answer.

The lattice light flickered once, dimmed, and faded to black.

Phainon had planned to head straight home after the scan. Really, he had.

But the Grove had a way of keeping him longer than intended.

It started simple enough—a call from one of the outer domes. An apprentice linguist had somehow managed to erase three hours of rare vocal data from the archives and was now on the verge of tears. Then came the second favor, and the third. And by the time he realized what was happening, he was already knee-deep in the day’s chaos with a polite smile and a resigned sense of purpose.

Because apparently, when people saw Phainon, they saw “friendly and competent and available.”

By noon, he’d recalibrated an entire team’s light filters, repaired a sensor grid that had been short-circuiting since the last storm, and been conned into carrying crates of luminescent roots across the main walkway because —quote—“You’ve got good balance, sir.”

He did not have good balance.

But he smiled and did it anyway.

“Careful—careful—those are volatile specimens!” a harried botanist shouted as Phainon stumbled slightly, the crate humming ominously in his hands.

“Volatile?” he repeated, steadying it. “You could’ve led with that part!”

“Don’t drop it!”

“Thank you, invaluable advice!”

When he finally set the crate down, a few nearby students clapped like he’d just prevented a catastrophic explosion. Phainon gave a small, dramatic bow.

“All in a day’s work,” he said lightly. “Try not to hand me anything that glows next time, yeah?”

That set the rhythm for the rest of the day.

He stopped by one of the field labs to help a group of students struggling with harmonic resonance equations. “No, no—see here,” he said, leaning over a display. “Your calibrator’s off by 0.002. That’s why your waveform keeps collapsing. There—perfect.”

Then he got pulled into a heated argument between two biologists over whether the Grove’s bloom cycles were lunar or purely artificial. “You’re both right,” Phainon announced, deadpan. “Congratulations, you’ve discovered that science is subjective suffering.”

They threw paper filters at him. He deserved it.

Later, he fixed an archive pod that refused to sync to the central system. It had apparently been offline for months. He got it running again in fifteen minutes.

For all his self-deprecation, it turned out his hands still remembered what they were doing. He was rusty, sure—but not lost. Life might’ve taught him how to survive chaos; Anaxa had taught him how to navigate it.

Still, between the laughter and the noise, his thoughts kept drifting back to the one thing he was trying to avoid.

Aglaea.

The idea of reaching out to her made his stomach twist.

She’d been the one to pull him out of the wreckage of his own mistakes once. The one who’d refused to give up on him when everyone else already had. A leader, yes—but also the closest thing to home he’d ever had.

And now he had to tell her that not only was he alive, but he was harboring Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos—the man she’d spent a decade raging about due to how notoriously difficult he is.

He could already imagine it. The tight-lipped calm. The pointed silence. The inevitable, disappointed sigh. Then, maybe, a smack to the head. She wouldn’t hit him, not really—but she’d want to.

And then she’d start asking questions. Questions he wasn’t ready to answer.

Because what was he supposed to say?

Hi, surprise, I’m alive. Also, I may or may not be gaslighting a Kremnoan commander into emotional recovery while hiding from two governments. Hope you’re well.

Yeah. That’d go beautifully.

“Phainon?”

He blinked, realizing he’d been staring into the soft glow of a data terminal for far too long. A young researcher—Tavi, one of the new recruits—was watching him nervously. “The resonance readout’s still oscillating. Did I… mess it up again?”

Phainon leaned over, glancing at the display. “Nope. You’re fine. You’re just overcorrecting—ease the modulation by one point three. There. Now watch the stabilizer.”

Tavi adjusted the control, eyes widening as the oscillations flattened into a steady rhythm. “It worked.”

“Of course it worked,” Phainon said with mock indignation. “You think I’m here just for decoration?”

Tavi opened their mouth, reconsidered, then shut it.

“Good choice,” Phainon said cheerfully, handing back the datapad. “Keep at it. You’ll get it down before Anaxa invents another crisis to keep us all up at night.”

He left before Tavi could ask if he was joking.

By midafternoon, he’d somehow acquired a trail of stragglers—students, researchers, technicians—all orbiting him for “a quick second opinion.” He didn’t mind. Their questions kept his hands busy, their chatter filling the space that guilt and dread would otherwise occupy.

Now and then, though, something flickered—a pulse of blue across a research display, the faint echo of harmonic feedback that made the back of his neck prickle. It reminded him of the scan earlier. He tried not to think too hard about it.

Instead, he helped an engineer troubleshoot a sensory relay that refused to stop beeping. “You know,” Phainon said as he crouched beside the console, “I could’ve been home two hours ago. Drinking apple juice. Pretending to read a report.”

“You volunteered,” the engineer reminded him.

“I was manipulated by the power of polite suggestion.”

“Uh-huh.”

“Don’t judge me for being a people pleaser,” Phainon said, reconnecting the last cable. “There. Try it now.”

The relay hummed to life with a soft chime. Perfect.

The engineer blinked. “How did you—?”

“I’m magic,” Phainon said solemnly. “Don’t question it.”

It wasn’t until he stood up, stretching out the stiffness in his shoulders, that he noticed the light had changed. The Grove’s canopy had darkened from amber to deep indigo, and the biolights along the walkways had begun to glow, one by one, like grounded stars.

Huh.

He hadn’t realized how late it had gotten.

Around him, the domes were beginning to quiet. Researchers packed up their notes, voices soft and tired, laughter carrying faintly between the paths. Somewhere above, a student was playing something on a string instrument—slow, delicate, drifting.

Phainon sighed, pushing his hair back and glancing toward the glowing path leading home. “All right,” he muttered. “Enough accidental productivity for one day.”

The air smelled faintly of moss and silver, the night cycle settling across the Grove like a gentle exhale.

Time to head back.

His kitchen was a mess courtesy of him.

Well—him more so than the kitchen.

He’d told himself he’d go straight to bed. He’d even tried. For approximately seven minutes.

He knew exactly why.

Because somewhere along the line, he’d gotten used to sleeping with someone.

A certain Kremnoan who slept like gravity didn’t apply to him, took up most of the bed, and radiated heat like a forge. Mydei had an infuriating talent for curling into his side until their limbs tangled, and Phainon—very much against his own better judgment—had adapted.

He rubbed his temple and muttered, “You’ve gone soft.”

And maybe he had.

It wasn’t just the warmth he missed—Okhemen ran hot enough to rival a small star. It was the quiet beside him. The steady rhythm of breath against his back. The weight of another person’s body, anchoring him in a way he hadn’t realized he’d wanted until it wasn’t there.

Mydei’s hair came to mind first, as usual—wild and heavy, like he’d wrestled with the wind and won. He could still feel it brushing his face when Mydei shifted closer, the faint mineral scent of the soaps he favored— clean, with an undertone that always reminded Phainon of sky and storm and flight.

Sometimes he caught himself absently carding his fingers through it, just for the feel of it—thick, soft, ridiculously soothing. He’d never admit it aloud.

Gods. He was down bad.

He leaned forward, cheek pressed to the cool tabletop. The metal warmed faintly beneath his skin. It felt grounding. His eyes fluttered shut. Maybe he could pretend for a moment—pretend that warmth was still there beside him.

Which, apparently, was the exact moment someone decided to throw something over him.

“Mydei?”

“Not tired?” he asked, voice soft enough that it didn’t break the quiet.

Phainon dragged his hand down his face, half laughing under his breath. “Depends,” he said after a pause. “Do you have the energy to talk?”

Instead of answering, Mydei reached over and took the glass from his fingers. He drank from it without ceremony, throat working in a slow swallow that somehow demanded too much of Phainon’s focus. Then he set it back down with deliberate finesse, eyes glinting faintly with amusement.

“Is that even a question?”

And then—because apparently he enjoyed making Phainon’s night more complicated—he licked his lips.

Phainon’s brain shut down for one full, dignified heartbeat.

The blanket slipped further down his shoulders. Outside, the night cycle deepened, painting everything in shades of blue.

And suddenly, Phainon didn’t mind being awake.

Yeah, okay,” Phainon said at last, rubbing at his jaw with a small sigh. “Let’s talk.”

“Is it?”

“It’s on your cuff.”

“Do you ever miss home?”

“Do you miss yours?” he asked before he could stop himself.

Mydei hesitated, gaze flickering toward the window. “I wouldn’t know,” he said finally. “I don’t remember what it felt like.”

The word.

Mydei’s brows drew together. “Phainon—”

Phainon paused, one hand braced on the doorframe. His voice, when it came, was apologetic . “You didn’t,” he murmured. “I just—need a minute.”

Mydei sat there for a long while, unmoving, eyes fixed on the empty chair opposite him—on the faint, invisible warmth still clinging to it.

Outside, the night pressed closer, heavy and silent.
