“Separately?”

“Precaution,” she said simply. “I’d rather not risk both of you—and the subject—on one vessel.”

Anaxa’s smirk was almost audible. “Sensible. I’ll take the longer route with Mydeimos to ensure containment stability.”

Phainon shot him a flat look. “You’re enjoying this.”

“Immensely.”

Aglaea ignored them both. “The Council will need official notice within the hour. I expect coordination from you both.”

She turned slightly, her profile stark against the projection light. Phainon opened his mouth before he could stop himself.

“Wait.”

Her head turned back.

He hesitated, then said, quieter, “After this is over… can we talk?”

A pause.

When she finally spoke, her tone was hard to decipher. “Of course. Depending on how quickly this is resolved.”

Not a promise. Not quite a dismissal either.

Then the feed flickered once, and she was gone—leaving the room dimmer and far too still.

Phainon stood there for a moment, hands loose at his sides. His pulse refused to slow.

Behind him, Anaxa sighed, as if the whole thing had been mildly inconvenient. “Well. That went better than expected.”

Phainon turned slowly. “You are unbelievable.”

“I’m aware,” Anaxa said, already tapping a sequence into the console. “You should start packing. I’ve prepped a ship for you—west hangar. I’ll brief Mydei myself.”

Phainon frowned. “I can—”

“You won’t have time,” Anaxa interrupted smoothly. “Knowing her, she’ll have Council documentation ready before you finish a sentence. Best you leave before she decides to change her mind.”

Phainon hesitated. It was reasonable. Logical. Too logical, maybe.

Still, he nodded once. “Right.”

He lingered a moment longer, hand tightening on the table’s edge.

Anaxa’s tone had been perfectly calm, perfectly measured.

Too perfect, actually.

Phainon knew that voice.

It was the one Anaxa used when he was keeping something to himself.

“Name and clearance?”

The officer didn’t even bother to look up. His voice was flat enough to sand wood.

Phainon handed over his ident-chip, the motion brisk and polite—mostly out of habit. The scanner whirred, pulsed white, then, with all the enthusiasm of divine mockery, flickered gold.

He stared at it. The light shivered once, like a heartbeat deciding whether to bother.

Back home, and already flagged. Wonderful.

The officer frowned faintly. “You’ve been marked for secondary verification. Record mismatch.”

“Yeah,” Phainon said dryly. “That tends to happen when you’re declared dead.”

The officer’s expression didn’t so much as blink. “Please refrain from sarcasm. It interferes with the empathic conduit.”

Immediately, the air around them rippled—a low, quivering pulse that glowed faintly along the archway’s edges. The structure itself seemed to bristle, like a cat reacting to raised voices.

Phainon exhaled slowly through his nose. “Oh, for the love of—”

“Please also refrain from irritation,” the officer added blandly. “It causes resonance feedback.”

He muttered something under his breath that definitely wasn’t in the Conduit Regulation Handbook. The light nearest his shoulder flickered in subtle agreement, as though the architecture itself was quietly rooting for him.

The officer continued typing at a pace that could only be described as vindictive. “Purpose of visit?”

“Existence,” Phainon said. “Maybe a dash of redemption.”

A bored blink. “Scientific or diplomatic classification?”

He dragged a hand down his face. “Research,” he said finally. “Definitely research.”

A hum of data processing followed—long enough for him to mentally draft and delete six different complaint letters.

While the officer squinted at an uncooperative hologram, Phainon’s thoughts drifted—against his better judgment—to the trip here.

The shuttle had been half-empty, the cabin silent and cold, recycled air hissing at him. Aglaea had insisted on separate transports “for safety,” which in Okhema-speak meant control.

He’d spent most of the ride trying to write his report—then deleting every version after realizing how insane it sounded to put “resurrected self” and “amnesiac war criminal roommate” in the same summary.

Eventually, he’d given up and stared out the viewport instead. The stars passed by in quiet accusation. Somewhere out there, Anaxa and Mydei were probably arguing—or worse, getting along—and he couldn’t decide which thought horrified him more.

When the officer finally cleared his throat, Phainon looked up.

“Is anyone accompanying you?”

“He’ll arrive a few days after me,” Phainon said. “Lucky bastard.”

The officer blinked, clearly unsure if that qualified as information. “Specify identity?”

“No.”

A pause. “That was not a yes-or-no question.”

“It was when I said it.”

The scanner light pulsed again—judgmental—as if considering whether to flag him for insolence.

“I require additional identification,” the damn officer said.

Phainon rummaged through his coat, produced another chip, and slid it across the counter. The scanner accepted it with a thin whine before half-melting the corner into a hiss of steam.

He winced. “Damn it.”

“Emotional disturbance in the conduit field,” the officer said without missing a beat. “Please wait for recalibration.”

He pressed a glowing cube onto the console. It began to hum softly, releasing a faint scent of bureaucracy. The light surrounding them dimmed from gold to a sluggish violet, vibrating in quiet disapproval.

Phainon crossed his arms, watching the cube hum like it was performing interpretive suffering. “You know,” he said, “I used to teach half of you this system.”

“Then you should remember the importance of patience.”

“Funny,” Phainon muttered. “Didn’t remember it being this inefficient when I left.”

“Technically,” the officer replied, “you didn’t leave. You expired.”

Oh so they had jokes now.

The cube chirped brightly, pleased with itself.

Phainon stared at it for a long moment. “You people are terrifying.”

The officer’s mouth formed into a smile. “Welcome home, Diplomat Phainon.”

“Thrilled,” Phainon said flatly.

He was still trying to salvage the molten remains of his ident-chip when a voice cut through the sterile hum of the checkpoint.

“Move, you damn bureaucratic fossil.”

Phainon froze. He knew that voice.

And for the first time since landing, he almost cried actual tears of joy.

Because really—who else could it be but Castorice, looking every bit like someone who’d finally decided to stop asking nicely.

She breezed past the officer, coat sweeping like she was late to her own coup, and flashed a sigil so high-level the scanner let out a pitiful beep and shut itself off.

“He’s with me,” she said crisply.

Phainon tilted his head. “Apparently not officially.”

“Apparently officially enough,” she shot back, grabbing his arm before he could earn himself another flag and dragging him through what used to be a functioning checkpoint.

The officer just stared at the smoking console.

By the time they made it through integration—three signatures, two recalibration scans, and one emotionally unstable cube—they were finally stepping into the outskirts of Okhema.

And gods, it hit him harder than he expected.

The city spread out like a living map of memory. Streets curved through open air, held aloft by the slow pulse of glowing aetherroots. Buildings shimmered faintly, edges breathing with color as if the skyline itself were alive. People passed in loose clusters, and each movement left behind faint traces—ribbons of light or soft threads of sound that wove briefly into others before fading.

Above it all, the sky rippled a gentle gold—the kind of hue you only got when the city’s emotional systems were stable.

Phainon exhaled, tension loosening in his shoulders. It was ridiculous how much he’d missed this.

“You’ve been back all of five minutes,” Castorice said, glancing at him sidelong, “and already managed to get flagged. That has to be some sort of personal record.”

“I didn’t realize ‘coming back from the dead’ came with paperwork,” he said.

She laughed, and the air brightened with her mood—the Lattice responding like an affectionate pet.

For a moment, it almost felt like old times. Almost.

“The Council’s losing its collective mind,” she said eventually while walking. “Half want to interrogate you, half want to sanctify you, and the rest are still debating whether you count as legally alive.”

“Effective as always,” Phainon said.

“Aglaea’s keeping them from tearing each other apart. She’s been balancing Styxia’s Oceans against Adonia’s Winters since dawn.”

He gave a low whistle. “So I’m under escort now?”

“‘Protective supervision,’” she corrected, overly formal. “Aglaea’s orders. You’re technically on house arrest until Mydeimos and professor Anaxa arrive—thirty-six hours, give or take.”

“Doesn’t trust me to walk myself home?”

“She trusts you just fine,” Castorice said. “She doesn’t trust the thirty-two factions currently drafting theories about your resurrection.”

“That’s comforting.”

“Think of it as an honor guard,” she said lightly. “Except without the honor. Or the guard part.”

He gave her a look. “You missed me.”

“Barely,” she said, but her excitement gave her away.

They walked in companionable quiet for a while before she asked, offhand but not really, “So—after you left for the Grove… what happened out there?”

He blinked. “I was wondering the same thing on your end.”

The air rippled before he could say more—an almost imperceptible vibration that built until it felt like it was drilling through his skull.

Both froze.

A flash of white split the Lattice like a nerve spasm. Pain hit a moment later, sharp and resonant, a frequency that made thought itself go brittle.

Phainon staggered, teeth clenched. Castorice hissed through hers, hand pressed to her temple.

Then it passed. Just like that. The air steadied, embarrassed, pink returning to their quiet gold.

She was the first to speak, voice thin but controlled. “Can’t… talk about it. Apparently neither can you.”

Phainon tried to reply, but his throat locked—words cutting off like someone had switched off language.

He exhaled through his nose. “Fantastic.”

Castorice grimaced, testing the edges of her own thoughts like she might trigger it again. “About your companions…” she said carefully, each word measured, “I don’t know why, but it might take longer for you to see them again. Something about timing—on their end.”

That earned her his full attention. Whatever Aglaea had told her, it wasn’t meant for him. He could see it in the tension around her mouth, the way she didn’t quite meet his eye.

His instincts shifted, clicking into the cold, professional mode he’d spent years cultivating. Questions formed, too many of them—but he wasn’t about to push her into another psychic feedback spike.

Instead, he just nodded once. “Appreciate the warning.”

Her shoulders eased a little, and she gestured toward the street ahead. “Almost there.”

He followed her around the next curve—and stopped.

It took him a second to place it: the soft glow of the wards, the ivy trailing through the aetherglass, the faint pulse in the entry gate that still recognized him. His residence. Exactly as he’d left it.

Castorice glanced at him, a half-smile ghosting across her face. “Welcome home, Phainon.”

He looked at her, then at the house, not sure how to feel.

“Good to be back,” he said.

And this time, it almost sounded true.

House arrest was going great, actually.

Phainon cleaned up his house, ate breakfast and dinner, watered his plants, took a bath, and slept.

Then he did it again.

Then again.

And again.

No big deal though, right?

A few days and then Anaxa and Mydei should arrive. That was the plan. The delay Castorice mentioned, the political interference, the orbit clearance—all of it was temporary. That’s what everyone said.

Hell, he’d even heard from one of the insiders (read: Hyacine, who he doesn’t even know how she gets her information when she’s still in the damn Grove, but he’s learned not to question her methods) that their ship was finally in Okhema’s orbit.

Right?

Well, imagine his fucking surprise when the second he got confirmation they’d landed, the same insider sent another message that began with:

“Before you get excited—Mydeimos convulsed and passed out.”

Phainon blinked at the message, reread it twice, and then, very calmly, stood up, grabbed his coat, and said aloud to absolutely no one,

“Well, fuck house arrest.”

By the time Aglaea realized he’d left, he was already halfway across Okhema—cutting through the city’s mirrored bridges, coat half-buttoned, muttering something about “totally fine, just visiting the ER,” like that would make it true.

The treatment wing of the Aetheric Research Hall smelled like sterilized regret.

He spent hours there, pacing.

No one told him anything. He tried polite first, then charming, then quietly terrifying, and finally gave up and parked himself by the door.

When they finally let him in, it was already what passed for “night” in Okhema—the hour when the lights dimmed just enough for shadows to remember they existed.

Phainon didn’t walk; he practically ran inside. “Mydei—”

And then stopped.

There he was.

Mydei sat upright on the examination cot, posture still too straight for someone who’d just died for a second, a shimmer of half-dried circuitry across his neck where the stabilizers had latched on. His hair was a mess— well, a controlled sort of mess, like it had decided to rebel just enough to stay fashionable.

Anaxa stood beside him, green hair catching the pale glow from the monitoring screens. He looked like he’d been carved out of restraint.

They were talking in low tones about something Phainon couldn’t hear. Probably about him.

Didn’t matter.

“Mydei—” He started again, but it came out softer this time, halfway between relief and disbelief. “You’re— you’re awake.”

Mydei’s gaze slid up to him, slow. Not startled or even surprised. Just… restrained.

And suddenly, Phainon forgot how to keep moving.

For one beat too long, neither of them said anything. The monitors hummed, steady and impersonal.

Something about the way Mydei looked at him—it wasn’t blank, but it wasn’t the same either. Like someone had quietly rearranged the person behind his eyes while Phainon wasn’t looking.

“Mydei?” he tried again, quieter.

That seemed to break the silence. Mydei blinked, expression smoothing into something almost too impassive. “Phainon.”

His voice was there. Familiar, even. Except it wasn’t. The cadence was different—unperturbed at the edges, aloof in a way that made Phainon’s pulse jump.

“Are you alright?”

It was an innocent question.

Mydei tilted his head slightly, almost curious. Then he breathed out a quiet, unamused laugh. “Define alright.”

Phainon’s stomach did an unpleasant flip. He wasn’t sure why.

When Mydei looked down, it wasn’t dazed like he’d expected—it was sober.

“I’m fine,” he said, tone monotone.

It should’ve been reassuring. Somehow, it wasn’t.

Anaxa hadn’t moved. Phainon turned to him. “What’s going on?”

Anaxa finally met his eyes. Polished, practiced, perfectly diplomatic. “We’re relocating Mydei to one of the lower residences. My supervision for the next few cycles.”

“No.” Phainon’s reply came out before he’d decided to speak.

Both of them glanced at him, the same look mirrored twice.

He could already hear footsteps in the hall—official ones. Great. Aglaea had probably sent half a squad to haul him back to confinement.

“You’re staying with me,” he said, addressing Mydei more than Anaxa now. “He’s staying with me.”

Mydei blinked once. Slowly. “That’s against regulation.”

Phainon shrugged. “So is this conversation.”

For the first time, something resembling amusement ghosted across Mydei’s face. It was small, almost imperceptible—but the kind that made Phainon’s chest ache because there it was. That impossible, quiet arrogance that had always driven him insane.

And maybe it was stupid, but he smiled too.

No big deal, right?

As long as it was Mydei.

He took a step back, half-turning toward the door as the hall lights flared brighter—guards incoming. “I’ll… see you later, alright?”

“Sure,” Mydei said, voice so vague it could’ve meant anything.

Phainon hesitated, but didn’t push it. He was already in enough trouble.

As the door closed behind him, he realized his hands were still shaking a little.

He told himself it was from running.

He didn’t quite believe it.

Three days.

Three days since he’d seen Mydei, and still nothing. No visits, no messages, not even a rumor except the standard, sterile update from the Council feed: Stabilization successful. Patient under observation.

So now he was pacing his room again, half-dressed, hair a mess, lights dimmed to a muted amber while the communicator glowed faintly on the desk.

“I’m not overreacting, Hyacine,” he hissed, low and defensive, like someone expecting to be told he was. “I’m observing.”

On the other end, Hyacine’s voice was the same brand of flat she used on reports that ran too long. “Observing what, exactly? The patient you’re banned from visiting not sending you a personal thank-you note?”

He groaned and dragged a hand down his face. “That he’s different, Hyacine. And don’t—don’t give me the ‘psychological trauma’ line again. You didn’t see how he looked at me. It wasn’t like before.”

“I didn’t see it because you broke house arrest and breached a restricted ward.”

“Technically, the guards broke me in.”

“That’s worse, Phainon.”

He stopped pacing, glaring at the air like she was physically standing there to receive it. “I’m serious. There’s something off about him. Not bad— just… wrongly calibrated. His aether resonance was cleaner than it should’ve been. Like something scrubbed him down to the bone and hit restart.”

A pause. Then Hyacine’s voice, a little softer but no less skeptical: “You’re projecting care onto a phenomenon you don’t understand.”

Phainon’s jaw worked. “It’s not like that.”

“Then what is it?”

“It’s—” he waved a hand helplessly, searching for the right word, “— pattern recognition. He doesn’t behave the way he used to. It’s like he remembers the outline of himself but not the rest. Like he’s trying to reinhabit his own skin.”

She sighed. “Phainon, your risk index has been climbing since you left the Grove. If it spikes again, I’ll have to file it. You know what that means.”

He winced. “Yeah, I know. More appointments, fewer travel permissions. Great for morale.”

“Then stop acting like the universe revolves around one man who—”

“It’s not—” He broke off, laughed a little too hard. “Okay, maybe it’s a little like that. But come on, you saw what he did to the Grove before he left. His presence alone bent the flora network. What if it’s happening again? What if—”

“Phainon.”

That tone again. “You’re chasing ghosts. That’s dangerous.”

He turned toward the window, jaw tight, the glow of the city outlining his reflection. The skyline pulsed with slow, living light. He stared at himself a long moment. His reflection looked tired, almost like it was tired of him.

“…What’s dangerous?”

The words weren’t his.

He froze.

The communicator slipped slightly in his hand as Hyacine’s voice pressed through—distant, muffled: “Phainon? What was that? Hello?”

Arms slid around his waist, unhurried. A head came to rest on his shoulder, warm breath ghosting his collar. His pulse stuttered.

A quiet voice, curious and faintly amused, spoke against his ear:

“Didn’t mean to interrupt. Just curious about what your talking about.”

Every muscle in Phainon’s body went taut.

He thumbed the line off without looking, Hyacine’s voice cutting out mid-syllable. The room fell still again—so quiet he could hear his own heartbeat.

He turned slowly, forcing his body to obey even as it screamed not to.

The first thing he saw was the shimmer of red tracing down an arm. Ink and light both.

“Mydei.”

The name came out halfway between breath and disbelief.

Mydei tilted his head. “You were talking to Hyacine.”

“When did you—where were you?”

Mydei’s eyes flicked down briefly, as if thinking, then back up. His smile was small, almost distracted, but something about it made the it hard to breath. “Here,” he said softly. “Listening.”

Phainon blinked. “You—how long—”

But Mydei was already speaking again, his tone conversational, like they hadn’t skipped a beat.

“You said something about resonance. And danger.” He hummed faintly, the sound vibrating against Phainon’s back. “Let’s get back to that, shall we?”

Phainon’s breath caught.

Shit.

His brain short-circuited for a half second before his mouth jumped in to save face.

“It—uh—wasn’t anything important,” he said, too quick, the lie slipping out like muscle memory. “Just… diagnostics talk. You’d rather die than listen to that.”

Mydei’s arms, which had tensed when Phainon spoke, eased. Slowly, almost lazily, he let go—his fingers catching briefly on the fabric of Phainon’s shirt before trailing away. It wasn’t long enough to mean anything. Which was exactly why Phainon’s pulse spiked anyway.

He forced an exhale and turned around like nothing had happened. “Diagnostics, huh?” Mydei said. His tone was neutral, but his eyes had that faint spark of humor that always made Phainon feel like the punchline to a joke he hadn’t heard yet. “You lie like you’re auditioning for it.”

Phainon crossed his arms, expression dry. “Or maybe I’m just trying to stop you from biting me.”

“That would only work if you stopped talking.”

“You see what I deal with?” Phainon muttered to the ceiling. “I save your ass one time and suddenly you’re a menace with free housing.”

“Free housing,” Mydei repeated. “I recall you offered.”

“Yeah, before I knew you’d take ‘make yourself comfortable’ as a binding contract.”

That earned the faintest flicker of amusement—blink and you’d miss it.

“Why are you here, anyway?” Phainon asked finally. He didn’t mean it to sound suspicious, but it came out that way.

Mydei looked at him like a cat humoring a question. “Did you not say I’m staying with you? I can leave if you’d like.”

“No,” Phainon said too fast, the word snapping out before he could stop it. He coughed into his fist, trying again. “No. I just meant—where’ve you been the last few days? You vanished.”

“Resting.”

“Resting where?”

“Wherever I ended up.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the one I have,” Mydei said shrugging, the damn bastard. “You can be suspicious if it makes you feel better.”

“I’m not suspicious,” Phainon said—then winced. “Okay, I’m a little suspicious. You say creepy shit like that and expect me not to be?”

Mydei raised an eyebrow. “Creepy?”

“Yes, creepy. The kind of thing people say right before they sprout extra limbs and start reciting prophecy.”

“Would it bother you if I did?”

Phainon paused for half a second, unsure if he was joking. “…That depends. How many limbs are we talking?”

“Enough.”

Phainon sighed, pinching the bridge of his nose. “You’re impossible.”

“So I’ve been told.”

“Yeah, by me. Multiple times.”

Mydei rolled his eyes. “Then you must be an authority.”

Phainon snorted. “Unfortunately.” He studied him for a second longer, frowning. “I’m serious, though. You’ve been off since you came back. You keep… saying weird things. Like you’re testing me or something.”

Mydei’s gaze flicked toward him. “Would you prefer I pretend?”

“That’s not what I—”

“You talk like I’m one of you,” Mydei said abruptly, with a faint smile. “You wouldn’t, if you had more sense”

“Mydei—“ “Shush. I’m also being serious. If you knew what kind of man I am,” Mydei said, almost laughing, “you’d stop pretending I’m one.”

Phainon’s brows furrowed. What an odd and abrupt thing to say.

Was he… feeling sick?

A pause.

Then idly, he added, “But you’d still look at me, wouldn’t you?”

Phainon was still confused but did answer the question after a reluctant moment. “I’d call you you. That’s enough for me.”

Mydei’s eyes lingered on him for a long moment, something complicated flickering there before it smoothed out again.

“Good,” he murmured. “I’ll remember that.”

They stood there a moment longer—close enough that Phainon could feel the faint signs of aether still thrumming beneath Mydei’s skin. It made his hair prickle. It also made him not want to move.

Then, as if sensing that he’d dug deep enough, Mydei’s tone shifted—light again, smooth as though the last few seconds hadn’t happened. “I heard there’s going to be a festival soon. In Okhema.”

Phainon blinked, thrown by the sudden turn. “Uh… yeah. The Festival of Kephale. Celebration of the Titan’s birth—worldbearing, moons aligning, all that mythic fanfare.”

“Will you come with me?”

Phainon opened his mouth, closed it, and then opened it again, his brain lagging behind his heart. “What, like… with you?”

“That was the question, yes.”

He felt the corner of his mouth pull upward before he could stop it. “What, you asking me on a date or something?”

“If that’s what it takes to get you to agree.”

“Oh, I’d have said yes either way,” Phainon said, grinning despite himself. “But sure. Let’s call it that.”

Mydei looked almost pleased—almost. “Then it’s settled.”

“Gods, you’re efficient,” Phainon said with a laugh, rubbing the back of his neck. “Can’t even give a guy time to make himself look mysterious first.”

“Too late for that.”

“Rude. I was going for charming.”

“You overshot.”

“Okay, that’s it, I’m rescinding your free housing privileges.”

Mydei stepped past him, glancing around the room with the faintest smirk. “You wouldn’t.”

“I might.”

“You won’t.”

Phainon sighed dramatically, then swept into an exaggerated bow, one arm out like he was introducing royalty. “Fine. Since you’re already here, my terrifyingly enigmatic houseguest, allow me to show you around my very humble abode. Try not to destroy it with your… mystical presence or whatever.”

Mydei glanced his way and dipped into a bow of his own—graceful, poised, and way too princely for someone doing it just to be polite. Typical showoff.

“Lead the way.”

Phainon straightened, fighting the smile threatening his face as he turned toward the hall. “Yeah,” he muttered, half to himself. “I’m definitely doomed.”

Phainon got used to having Mydei around again faster than he cared to admit, again.

It started with small things—an extra mug on the counter, the faint scent of Mydei’s preferred tea steeping before dawn, the quiet sound of someone else moving through the house like they’d always been there.

He told himself it was fine. Normal, even. Then Mydei started straightening his collar in the mornings, brushing a hand down his sleeve before handing him a cup of coffee, and somehow “temporary” started to stretch further and further out of reach.

Phainon pretended not to notice how domestic it all felt.

Mostly because he didn’t hate it.

Like before, the kitchen stayed organized. Breakfast appeared on time. His paperwork—how, he had no idea—kept ending up sorted into tidy stacks. Half of his chaos disappeared before he could even complain about it. And when he did catch Mydei humming under his breath while setting the table, it was quiet, tuneless, but oddly steady—like he was syncing himself to the house somehow.

It should’ve been comforting.

It was comforting. Mostly.

The Council finally decided Phainon wasn’t a flight risk. House arrest: lifted.

Mostly.

He didn’t argue. The first thing he did was reconnect to the Tribios’s network. It’d been ages since he’d seen Trianne, Trinnon, or Tribbie face-to-face—or core-to-core, technically.

The reunion should’ve been happy.

It wasn’t.

Their AI core had been damaged—badly enough that Tribbie had been running on fragmented projections for weeks. Those phantom visits in the Grove, the flickers of Tribbie chatting like nothing was wrong—yeah. Not a trick of the light. She’d been burning herself out just to check in on him.

Now she was offline entirely, in deep hibernation mode, conserving what energy was left. Anaxa had taken over repairs, which was… odd. Engineering wasn’t his thing. But lately, Anaxa had been doing a lot of odd things.

Phainon didn’t question it. If Anaxa wanted to play mechanic, fine. Better him than someone careless. He trusted Anaxa—well, mostly. The alternative was staying up all night imagining worst-case scenarios, and he was already bad enough at sleeping.

The real weirdness was the way Mydei and Anaxa kept working together.

“Research,” apparently.

Phainon had walked in on them more than once—screens everywhere, diagrams spilling across every surface, the technology screeching in the walls. Mydei always looked right at home there, sleeves rolled up, asking questions that made even Anaxa pause.

“What would happen,” he’d said just yesterday, “if a harmonic failsafe was removed from a Titanal core?”

Anaxa had sighed without looking up. “Theoretically?”

“Theoretically.”

“It would destabilize everything tied to it. Let’s not make that a trend.”

Phainon had left before they could rope him in, assuming they were just nerding out. Which, to be fair, they were.

Probably.

Still, the halls buzzed with quiet rumors—missing calibration logs, re-indexed files, anomalies in the archive drives. He told himself it was nothing. Just the usual bureaucratic noise.

Because right now, he had better things to think about.

Okhema was gearing up for the Festival of Kephale—streets draped in gold-white banners, air rich with incense and static light. The annual celebration of the Titan whose body became the world itself.

And for once, Phainon wasn’t scheduled to save or supervise anything.

He had a festival to attend.

And, apparently, a date to keep.

“Are you trying to make us late?”

Phainon yawned mid-step, dragging his feet while Mydei towed him forward by the wrist. His other hand clutched a half-finished drink like it might justify his pace.

The irony wasn’t lost on him—usually, he was the one doing the dragging.

“Relax,” he muttered, stifling another yawn. “It’s not like we’ll miss anything.”

“That’s exactly what people say,” Mydei replied without looking back, “right before missing something.”

And then they stepped into the light.

Okhema had transformed overnight.

The city no longer hummed—it sang. Gold-white banners stretched between the spires like ribbons of trapped sunlight, shifting as though alive. The avenues below pulsed with color and sound: dancers in mirrored masks moved in perfect formations, their reflections scattering the light into shards that danced across glass walls. Drones spiraled above them, releasing bursts of shimmering dust that coalesced into miniature suns before dissolving into the haze. The breath left his chest. “Confirmed? You mean they’re actually here?”

[Approaching vector thirteen.] Her tone was all business now, battle calm layered over exhaustion. [Listen to me. If this fails—if I don’t come back —you’ll need to assume command.]

He froze. “…What? Aglaea, don’t start talking like that—what the hell is happening? You can’t do this, it’s too sudden, c’mon just yesterday we were having dinn—”

[There’s no other way. The lattice is feeding back into itself. The only path left is integration. If I merge with the core, I can halt the cascade before it reaches the outer network.]

His hand clenched against the console.

Was she serious?

“That’s suicide.”

[It’s time. Someone has to hold the structure together from inside. I can do it—buy everyone else enough time to evacuate.]

“Aglaea, no. There’s still time come on, we can reroute from here—”

[There isn’t.] Her voice softened, the distortion pulsing around it like a heartbeat. [You’ll need to protect the city. And Phainon—find Castorice. She’s working with Cipher as well as Hysilens. The core they’re using is unstable. If Kremnos reaches it first, the collapse won’t stop at Okhema. It’ll chain-react across the entire network.]

The line dissolved into noise. He could barely catch fragments through it— containment, resonance, don’t let it spread.

Phainon was already moving, grabbing his coat, breath unsteady but his mind burning through panic. “Alright. Okay. I’ll get the Council online, initiate evacuation. Mydei’s with me now—we can—”

The transmission stuttered, went silent.

Then, abruptly—

[…Mydei?]

He blinked. “Yeah. Why?”

The static began to climb, frequency scraping higher, sharper.

[He’s—] a burst of feedback so violent it made his teeth ache. [Heir… of… Nika—]

“Aglaea?”

[—RUN.]

The line split open into a scream of static, blinding red streaking across every display.

Then nothing.

Silence swallowed the room. Phainon stood frozen, the glow of the monitors washing over him like the last light before a blackout.

His pulse wouldn’t slow.

Behind him, Mydei’s voice broke through.

“Well,” he said conversationally, as if the world hadn’t just dropped out from under them, “we should move fast. If Kremnos really is inbound, Castorice will still be near the Scepter. Docking bay shouldn’t be far— assuming the lower decks haven’t sealed yet.”

Phainon didn’t answer. His attention stayed fixed on the flickering light where Aglaea’s signal had died, that last pulse of red still echoing behind his eyes. Then, slowly, he turned.

“You said lower decks,” he said.

Mydei glanced over his shoulder. “Yeah?”

“The lower decks were decommissioned two cycles ago,” Phainon said carefully. “Only the central engineers ever had the blueprints. Not even the Council has clearance.”

A quiet settled between them.

Phainon’s voice came softer, careful. “How do you know that?”

For a heartbeat, Mydei didn’t react. His expression stayed the same— steady, unbothered—but something subtle in him stilled. The small, unconscious movements—the blink, the faint fidget of his hand—just… stopped.

Then he sighed.

“I suppose I shouldn’t.”

Phainon’s stomach dropped. “What?”

“You heard me,” Mydei said easily, like this was a casual chitchat and not a shattering realization. “You seriously ask too many questions, you know.”

His voice stayed level, but something in his stance changed. The ease in his tone wasn’t poise anymore—it was the disinterest of someone who’d stopped pretending to care.

“You really don’t know when to shut up, do you?”

He said it with a laugh that didn’t reach his eyes.

Phainon’s body moved before thought did—muscle memory, survival instinct, both screaming run. He tore himself free and spun, bringing the closest thing he had up in a clean, defensive arc—

—but the space between them vanished.

He didn’t even see the transition. One second, Mydei was standing a few feet away. The next, he was there—close enough that Phainon could feel the heat radiating off him. His hand caught Phainon’s wrist mid-swing and twisted with just enough force to make the weapon clatter to the floor.

Pain cracked up Phainon’s arm, but he pivoted anyway, driving a knee, a strike—anything. It didn’t land. Mydei’s other hand caught his shoulder, redirected his weight, and slammed him back against the console hard enough to rattle the panels.

Phainon gasped, breath knocked out of him—then felt it.

Not pain—pull.

It started deep under his ribs and crawled outward, a cold ache running through every nerve. His fingers tingled, then went slack. The world flickered at the edges.

“Mydei—what—”

He didn’t get the rest out. Mydei caught his other wrist, pinning it easily, and the contact made the sensation worse. Like something in his chest was unraveling thread by thread.

The faint pulsing of the earrings was made worse against his skin—alive, wrong, synchronized with the energy siphoning through him.

Mydei’s gaze flicked to them, then back to Phainon’s face. His voice was soft, almost pitying.

“You should’ve taken them off when you had the chance.”

Phainon tried to twist away. Mydei didn’t even have to tighten his grip. The pressure itself was enough—a reminder of how completely outmatched he was.

“What did you do?” Phainon rasped.

“I didn’t do anything,” Mydei said, almost thoughtful. “You just never asked what they were connected to.”

Then that faint, crooked smile returned. “But it’s cute you thought I’d give you something harmless.”

It took a second to process what he meant.

The earrings.

Phainon’s pulse jumped. He tried to lunge again, but his legs didn’t answer. The drain had sunk deeper, numbing everything it touched.

Mydei leaned in, voice dropping to a whisper. “You always were so good at seeing through people. Shame you never tried it with me.”

“Mydei,” Phainon rasped, his breath catching against the pressure in his chest. “What—what the hell is happening to you?”

Mydei’s gaze lifted, almost lazily, as if Phainon’s question amused him.

“Who said anything’s happening to me?”

Phainon swallowed hard. “Then who the hell are you?”

“Does it really matter?”

That answer hit him harder than it should’ve. His thoughts scattered, tripping over each other—Aglaea’s final broadcast flashing behind his eyes, fragmented and distorted. Heir of Nikador.

That name rang through the haze, ancient, heavy with meaning. Nikador— the Titan patron of Kremnos. The old royal line had sworn their blood to it before the purge. But Kremnos’s monarchy had been erased centuries ago— burned from history, its survivors executed or exiled.

There wasn’t supposed to be a line left.

Unless…

He blinked hard. The Rift.

The way Mydei had been found—suspended inside that crystal, alive when no one should’ve been. Barely a pulse, barely a data signature, just a body the encasing refused to let go. He’d joked once he’d gotten over it with Mydei—half out of disbelief—that maybe some old god had claimed him.

Now, that didn’t feel like a joke.

Phainon looked up. Mydei hadn’t moved. He stood watching him with quiet fascination, as though he’d been waiting for Phainon to finally catch up.

“You’re—”

“Careful,” Mydei interrupted. “Say it only if you’re sure.”

Phainon didn’t finish his sentence.

He pivoted the topic.

“Mydei,” he said again, softer now. “You lied to me.”

A blink. “You lied first.”

Well he’s not wrong.

Phainon’s mouth twisted. “So what was this then? You play at loyalty, get what you need, and throw the rest to rot?”

“Don’t make it sound so cheap,” Mydei clicked his tongue. “I liked you. Still do, in a way.”

That in a way burned worse than venom.

He tried to pull his wrist free; Mydei didn’t let him. The grip stayed—firm, almost loose, except for the pulse of strength beneath his skin.

“You’ve been pulling the strings this whole time,” Phainon managed. “Aglaea—”

“Handled herself,” Mydei interrupted. “I simply didn’t interfere.”

It took a second for the meaning to register, and when it did, something inside him splintered.

“You killed her.”

“I said I didn’t interfere,” Mydei corrected. “There’s a difference.”

He leaned closer.

“She was going to stand in the way. You won’t.”

“You’re fucking insane.”

“Maybe, but you can’t seriously say you hadn’t expect anything to happen.”

The draining intensified. Phainon’s knees threatened to buckle. His vision ghosted at the edges, but Mydei’s voice kept threading through it all.

“Okhema’s command will fracture before dawn. Their fleets, their data lines—all gone. No one left to order you around. No one to tell you who to save.”

Phainon forced out a broken laugh. “You’ll kill everyone I’ve ever known, and call that mercy?”

“Mercy for you,” Mydei corrected. “You can stop choosing, right? You had complained about this before, if I recall correctly. I’ll take care of the rest, and if it happens to benefit me as well, then...”

He lifted a hand, tracing the edge of Phainon’s jaw with his thumb.

“You’ve got that habit,” Mydei said suddenly. “Picking people apart, seeing what makes them tick. I wonder, did you figure out mine?”

Phainon’s glare deepened. “You think I’m afraid of you?”

“No.” He tilted his head, meeting Phainon’s eyes directly. “You’re just scared of being right. Honestly—how many red flags did you need before getting to this point?”

Phainon tried to move, to strike, to do something—but his muscles wouldn’t listen.

“You’re—Castorice and—” he started, and his voice cracked.

“Don’t say her name,” Mydei cut in suddenly as his grip shifted—a small warning that bit deep into bone.

Phainon stared at him, dazed and furious. “What, jealous now?”

“You have no idea.”

He leaned in.

“You keep bringing up everyone else when I’m right here. Look at me.”

Phainon’s gaze lifted before he could stop himself. Mydei’s thumb rested against his throat, tracing the pulse that wouldn’t calm.

“I only want your attention,” Mydei murmured. “The rest of it can burn.”

The words slid under his skin like a blade wrapped in silk. The pressure at his throat tightened, not tightly—just enough to remind him who held him there.

“You don’t get to decide that,” he managed, though the strain in his voice betrayed him.

Mydei’s expression loosened, but it wasn’t kindness. “You think you still have a say?” His tone was almost admiring. “You’re adorable.”

Phainon jerked against the hold. His fingers bit deep, cutting a harsh red against his wrists.

“Mydei—let me go.”

The earrings responded before Mydei did, splitting his vision into shards of light.

He violently lurched away—or attempted to at least.

Mydei caught him easily, one arm looping around him. “Careful,” he said. “You’ll hurt yourself for nothing.”

“You—think this is—winning?”

“Of course not.” Mydei’s hand lingered at his side, fingers splayed. “Winning’s such a pedestrian term. This—” he tapped the pulse at Phainon’s throat, “—is a cooperation of sorts.”

Phainon tried again to wrench free, a rough noise catching in his throat. His muscles rebelled, trembling under invisible weight. Every movement felt dragged through syrup—thick, impossible.

“Stop fighting it. You’re embarrassing us both.”

“Go to hell,” Phainon bit out.

“Already been,” Mydei shrugged. “Didn’t like the company.”

Phainon felt his vision darkening as he kicked his legs weakly.

“Even now,” he sighed, “you refuse to understand that you’re safe with me.”

Phainon’s breath hitched. “You… can’t…”

“I can,” Mydei interrupted, tone honey-sweet. “And I will.”

His thumb brushed along Phainon’s jaw, tracing the tremor beneath his skin. “You’ve done enough damage to Okhema bringing me here already. Let someone else decide how this ends, alright?”

Phainon tried to speak, but the sound wouldn’t come.

Mydei’s voice followed the collapse like a lullaby. “Sleep, Phainon.”

He fought it—once, twice—but the current beneath his skin had already chosen its path. His knees gave out. Mydei guided him down with infuriating care, the motion practiced.

“Always fighting,” Mydei tutted. “Even when you’ve already lost.”

Phainon’s lips moved; nothing followed.

The last thing he heard was the voice that undid him—low, coaxing, certain.

“See you tomorrow.”

The words sank into him like a hand closing over a wound.

Darkness gathered at the edges of his sight and folded in, slow as a door sealing shut.

Then—static.

A ragged crackle tore through the quiet, bright and cruel.

“Hephaestion, secure the perimeters. Leave the Adonian researcher to me. I’ll handle her personally.”

The comm cut out with a final pop of distortion, leaving the air hollow.

Mydei looked down at the body in his arms. Phainon’s breath still hitched faintly against his wrist; the light from the earrings pulsed once, twice, as though refusing to die.

Something in Mydei’s face turned thoughtful.

He brushed a thumb over Phainon’s temple, smearing a trace of light that wasn’t his to touch. “Always the difficult ones,” he sighed. “You make me work for it.”

He straightened, still holding him, eyes catching the faint red of the console lights. For a heartbeat, his voice eased again—gentle in the way a knife is when it slips between ribs.

“Goodnight, Deliverer.”

The station dimmed around them, machinery powering down one echo at a time until the room was nothing but breath and pulse.

His own heartbeat steadied, syncing unconsciously with the one pressed against him.

A slow smile ghosted across his mouth.

The kind that promised endings—and beginnings no one asked for.

Truly, the start of a love story worth burning worlds for.
